item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ defense looked abysmal while committing four errors in Game 2 of the ALDS. Their baserunning — or Austin Wells’ baserunning — may have cost them in Game 1.
But their _l. While the Yankees put together a lowlight reel fit for the Benny Hill theme in other facets of the game, that shouldn’t be overlooked with the team on the brink of elimination.
“The Rays’ pitchers, like they have all year, they’ve done well these last couple games and executed pitches,” said Ben Rice, who supplied those aforementioned runs with a pair of solo shots in Monday’s 5-2, Game 2 defeat. “We mixed in some good swings here there that we didn’t have much to show for, but we gotta find a way to get runs across.”
One of those good swings that didn’t yield results on Monday came from Cody Bellinger, who ripped a ball 102.9 mph with the bases loaded in the fifth inning. Unfortunately for him and the Yankees, it landed in Jonny DeLuca’s glove on the warning track in center.
While Bellinger hit the ball well, he acknowledged it “ultimately wasn’t good enough.” The same can be said of an entire offense that mustered just one hit in Saturday’s 1-0 loss and four more in Monday’s.
“We’ve got to be able to score some runs and do a better job of preventing than we did tonight,” Aaron Boone said after Game 2.
With the Yankees dominated by longtime nemesis Drew Rasmussen in Game 1, Boone opted for an identical, left-heavy lineup in Game 2 despite stewing on some changes. While the Bombers were able to get Freddy Peralta out after 4.2 innings, Rice was the only one to do damage, and they only drew two walks.
The Yanks were also held to two walks in Game 1, and Rasmussen fanned them 10 times.
Even though the Yankees beat up on Boston’s bullpen in the Wild Card — not Red Sox starters, mind you — it’s not surprising to see them scuffling at the plate with Aaron Judge absent from this lineup and roster due to a calf strain. The pinstripers have struggled in the past when the three-time MVP is hurt, including earlier this season when Judge missed 99 days with a fractured rib.
The Yankees had one of the worst offenses in baseball during that IL stint, ranking last in K% (26.1%); 29th in wRC+ (90) and average (.227); 28th in wOBA (.299); 27th in OPS (.681); and 24th in runs scored (341) from June 2 through Sept. 7
But even without Judge, the Yankees’ offense should be better than this. Rice, recently named a Hank Aaron Award finalist, held up his end of the bargain while batting first on Tuesday, but the Yankees need more from those behind him, especially in the heart of the order.
So far this series, the Yankees’ starting 2-through-7 hitters are 1-for-41.
That’s not going to cut it, even if the club cleans up its play in other parts of the game.
“You just got to take it game by game, at-bat by at-bat, and keep trying to win pitches,” Rice said with Game 3 coming on Wednesday. “When you think about how it’s an uphill battle or whatever, it can seem a little daunting. That’s why we just gotta keep staying focused on the next one.”

item.content:encoded:
Oct 6, 2026, 11:31 AM ET
New York Yankees designated hitter Ben Rice provided the offense in the Yankees' 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the ALDS on Monday. Rice was 2-for-3 with two solo homers and a walk on his night in Tampa. The Yankees were bothered by four errors and the Rays made them pay, but Rice was the lone bright spot for New York. Rice is hitting .467 in the postseason with a .556 on-base percentage. The two homers bring his postseason total to four homers and his RBI total to eight this postseason. Rice has been powering the Yankees offense all postseason long, but the Bronx Bombers find themselves down 2-0 to Tampa Bay in the ALDS. Rice has done his part offensively but needs some help as the Yankees are trying to piece things together without an injured Aaron Judge.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: ESPN.com
More Recent News
Braden Montgomery Drives in Two With Clutch Double


Brian Buckey




Oct 6, 2026, 11:25 AM ET
Chicago White Sox outfielder Braden Montgomery came up with the biggest hit of Game 2 against the Cleveland Guardians. The outfielder came up with two runners on and two outs against left-handed relief pitcher Erik Sabrowski and ripped a ball down the right field line to drive in both runners and put the White Sox ahead 3-2. Montgomery was then driven in by a clutch single by White Sox second baseman Chase Meidroth to give Chicago a 4-2 lead. Montgomery was 1-for-4 in the game and struck out twice, but he delivered the big blow of the game on his huge double. Facing a left-hander in Sabrowski, Montgomery, a switch hitter stood his ground and delivered a right-handed hit when it mattered most for his team.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: ESPN.com
Sean Burke Turns In Elite Relief Outing


Brian Buckey




Oct 6, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Chicago White Sox pitcher Sean Burke came out of the bullpen in Game 2 against the Cleveland Guardians and pitched masterfully as the team earned a 4-3 comeback win to go up 2-0 in the series. Burke came in after Anthony Kay and Sean Newcomb already pitched and calmed things down with 5 1/3 innings of work with one earned run on one hit and one walk with six strikeouts. Burke came out of the pen to throw 83 pitches and didn't give up a run until Grant Taylor allowed an inherited runner to score. Burke mixed his fastball with his offspeed pitches brilliantly and kept the Guardians' hitters off balance during his whole outing. The right-hander entered the game with the White Sox trailing and saw the team score three runs to take over the lead and take a commanding lead in the series.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 5, 2026, 10:58 PM ET
Boston Red Sox general manager Craig Breslow said that left-hander Garrett Crochet (lat, shoulder) is expected to have a "fully healthy, normal" offseason, per Gabrielle Starr of the Boston Herald. Crochet only made six starts during the regular season before shoulder and lat injuries caused him to miss the final five months of the year. However, the 27-year-old was able to battle all the way back and pitched out of the bullpen during Boston's American League Wild Card Series loss to the New York Yankees. While Crochet struggled in that appearance, it seems as though he made it through the outing ok from a health perspective and is now on track to go through his regular offseason routine. If Crochet can make it back to his peak form, he could re-establish himself as one of the top pitchers in baseball in 2027.--Will Brady
Source: Boston Herald - Gabrielle Starr
Roman Anthony Likely to Avoid Surgery


Will Brady




Oct 5, 2026, 10:49 PM ET
Boston Red Sox general manager Craig Breslow said that outfielder Roman Anthony (hand) "likely doesn't need surgery," per Chris Cotillo of MassLive. Anthony strained multiple muscles in his right hand during Game 1 of Boston's American League Wild Card Series loss to the New York Yankees. 2026 was largely lost to injury for Anthony, who missed a large chunk of the regular season after tearing the ligament that connects his right index finger to his wrist in early May. Given that his right hand/wrist appears to be giving him persistent issues, Anthony's health should be of at least some concern for fantasy managers going into 2027. The 22-year-old remains a potentially high-upside bat, but he will need to prove he can avoid injuries for an extended stretch.--Will Brady
Source: MassLive - Chris Cotillo
Josh Naylor Undergoes Right-Wrist Surgery


Will Brady




Oct 5, 2026, 10:40 PM ET
The Seattle Mariners announced that first baseman Josh Naylor (wrist) underwent surgery on his right wrist on Saturday. Naylor is expected to be fully recovered in time for the start of 2027 Spring Training. The 29-year-old had a down year in 2026, hitting .261/.317/.350 with 10 home runs, 57 RBI, 58 runs scored, and 30 stolen bases across 650 plate appearances. Naylor's 4.4% barrel rate and 35.5% hard-hit rate were both his worst marks since the shortened 2020 season. If Naylor was battling discomfort in his wrist for a chunk of the year, it could help explain why his numbers regressed across the board. Assuming Naylor is able to make a full recovery ahead of 2027, he could be worth buying low on in fantasy drafts.--Will Brady
Source: Seattle Mariners
Cal Raleigh Undergoes Left-Shoulder Surgery


Will Brady




Oct 5, 2026, 10:32 PM ET
The Seattle Mariners announced that catcher Cal Raleigh (shoulder) underwent left-shoulder surgery on Saturday. Raleigh is expected to be fully recovered in time for the start of 2027 Spring Training. After finishing second in the American League MVP vote in 2025, Raleigh's numbers crashed back down to earth in 2026. Across 530 plate appearances, the 29-year-old hit .182/.296/.368 with 23 home runs, 69 RBI, 49 runs scored, and two stolen bases. Raleigh spent time on the injured list during the year due to an oblique strain, and it appears he may have been battling a shoulder ailment for some or most of the season as well. As long as Raleigh can recover on schedule, he could be in line for a bounce-back season with improved health in 2027.--Will Brady
Source: Seattle Mariners
Gavin Williams Strikes Out 11 in Game 2 Loss


Will Brady




Oct 5, 2026, 10:24 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians starting pitcher Gavin Williams was not able to pitch his team to victory in Game 2 of the American League Division Series against the Chicago White Sox. However, Williams did his part, striking out 11 while allowing two earned runs across five innings of work. The 27-year-old was one of the best strikeout pitchers in baseball during the regular season, recording a 14-8 record with a 3.76 ERA, 1.11 WHIP, and 248 strikeouts across 184 1/3 innings (32 starts). The Guardians are now down two games to zero with the series heading to Chicago and face an uphill battle to fight their way back to a Game 5. However, if they can win the next two games, Williams would be in position to start a theoretical Game 5 on regular rest.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 5, 2026, 10:15 PM ET
Chicago White Sox right-hander Sean Burke was one of the heroes of his team's 4-3 win over the Cleveland Guardians in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday. Normally a starting pitcher, Burke entered the game out of the bullpen in the third inning and dominated, allowing just one hit, one walk, and one earned run while striking out six across 5 1/3 innings of work. Burke was a breakout arm for the White Sox during the regular season, recording an 11-7 record with a 3.34 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, and 185 strikeouts across 172 1/3 innings (32 games). The 26-year-old allowed three solo home runs in his first postseason appearance against the Houston Astros, but he's now logged 14 strikeouts in 9 1/3 playoff innings. Given his success on Monday, the White Sox could choose to continue using an opener in front of Burke in future postseason outings.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 4, 2026, 10:58 PM ET
San Diego Padres starting pitcher Michael King did his part in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday, allowing just three hits and one earned run while striking out six across five innings of work against the Milwaukee Brewers. King left the game with the Padres holding the lead, but Milwaukee mounted a late comeback to win the game 4-3 and take a 2-0 lead in the series. The 31-year-old was San Diego's top starting pitcher during the regular season, recording a 12-10 record with a 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, and 159 strikeouts across 185 innings (32 starts). King has been excellent across two starts so far in the postseason, allowing just four hits and one earned run while recording 14 strikeouts across 12 innings of work. If the Padres can win the next two games of the series against Milwaukee, King could potentially pitch on three days' rest in a theoretical Game 5.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 4, 2026, 10:41 PM ET
Milwaukee Brewers right-hander Logan Henderson did not have the sharpest outing in his postseason debut in Game 2 of the National League Division Series, but he managed to keep his team in the game. Henderson allowed two hits, three walks, and two runs (one earned) while striking out four across five innings of work in Milwaukee's 4-3 win over the San Diego Padres. Henderson emerged as a front-line starter during the regular season, recording an 11-3 record with a 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, and 110 strikeouts across 98 1/3 innings (18 starts). The 24-year-old averaged only 93.0 miles per hour on his fastball, but he logged an excellent 29.6% strikeout rate while walking just 5.1% of the batters he faced. If Milwaukee is going to make a deep postseason run, it will need Henderson to carry over his strong production from the regular season to the playoffs.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Ty France Drives in Two in Game 2 Loss


Will Brady




Oct 4, 2026, 10:28 PM ET
San Diego Padres first baseman Ty France carried his team's offense in its 4-3 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 2 of the National League Division Series, recording two hits and two RBI in three at-bats. The 32-year-old has been hot to begin the postseason, logging seven hits, two RBI, and two runs scored in 15 at-bats across four games. France had a resurgent regular season for the Padres as well, slashing .295/.363/.502 with 21 home runs, 72 RBI, 59 runs scored, and one stolen base across 500 plate appearances. While San Diego has now dropped each of the first two games of the NLDS, France has done his job. If the Padres are going to mount a comeback against the Brewers, they will likely need France to stay locked in.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 4, 2026, 10:19 PM ET
San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller had a rare off outing in his team's 4-3 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday. The 28-year-old was asked to get a six-out save and came up just short, allowing a hit, three walks, and two earned runs across 1 2/3 innings. Miller cruised through the eighth inning, but he walked three of the first four batters he faced in the ninth before allowing the game-winning two-run single to Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio. Miller was arguably the best relief pitcher in baseball this season, recording a 1.67 ERA and 0.90 WHIP with 129 strikeouts and 38 saves across 70 innings (66 games). However, the flame-throwing right-hander looked more mortal in the second half of the season, recording a 2.67 ERA with a 10.6% walk rate after the All-Star break. If San Diego is going to come back from down two games to zero against Milwaukee, it will need Miller to bounce back.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 4, 2026, 10:08 PM ET
Milwaukee Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio was the hero of his team's 4-3 win over the San Diego Padres in Game 2 of the National League Division Series on Sunday, recording a walk-off two-run single off Padres closer Mason Miller. It was Chourio's lone hit in his four at-bats, but it came at the biggest possible time. Chourio has played a key role in both of Milwaukee's wins in the series, as he hit a game-tying two-run home run in the third inning of Game 1 after San Diego jumped out to a quick 2-0 lead. Across 573 plate appearances in the regular season, the 22-year-old hit .291/.351/.487 with 25 home runs, 75 RBI, 96 runs scored, and 23 stolen bases. If the Brewers are going to make a deep postseason run, having Chourio at his best will likely be crucial.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 3, 2026, 9:58 PM ET
Chicago White Sox right-hander Grant Taylor was electric out of the bullpen in his team's 3-0 win over the Cleveland Guardians in Game 1 of the American League Division Series on Saturday. The 24-year-old entered the game in the sixth inning and shut the door on the Guardians, allowing just two hits while striking out six across four scoreless frames. Taylor was one of the best relievers in baseball during the regular season, recording a 2.25 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 106 strikeouts and 10 saves across 84 innings (60 games). Taylor's ability to work multiple innings makes him a unique weapon for the White Sox to deploy out of the bullpen. Taylor threw 42 pitches on Saturday, so he may not be available for Game 2 on Monday. However, the White Sox could try to get multiple innings out of him at least one more time in their series against the Guardians.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 3, 2026, 9:46 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Kyle Tucker had a big game in his team's 5-3 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 1 of the National League Division Series on Saturday, going two-for-four with a two-run home run and a stolen base. It was a highly underwhelming first season in Los Angeles for Tucker in 2026, as he hit .233/.330/.385 with 17 home runs, 70 RBI, 90 runs scored, and 12 stolen bases across 627 plate appearances. Tucker's barrel rate fell from 10.8% in 2025 to 6.3% this season, and his 36.3% hard-hit rate was the worst of his career. However, the 29-year-old has a chance to wipe the slate clean at the start of the postseason. Tucker also has plenty of experience in October, as he's now logged 283 plate appearances across seven career trips to the playoffs. If he can rediscover his old form, Tucker could help drive a deep postseason push for Los Angeles.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 3, 2026, 9:35 PM ET
Tampa Bay Rays first baseman Jonathan Aranda had the biggest hit of his team's 1-0 victory over the New York Yankees in Game 1 of the American League Division Series on Saturday, slugging a solo home run off Yankees right-hander Gerrit Cole in the third inning. It was Aranda's lone hit of the night, but it proved to be the difference in a pitcher's duel. The 28-year-old was a steady presence at the top of the Rays' order during the regular season, hitting .274/.358/.434 with 22 home runs, 92 RBI, and 73 runs scored across 668 plate appearances. He had one of his better power months to close the year, hitting five home runs in just 85 plate appearances in September. If Aranda can stay hot in October, he could be an X-factor for Tampa Bay.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 3, 2026, 9:26 PM ET
Tampa Bay Rays starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen dominated the New York Yankees in his team's 1-0 victory in Game 1 of the American League Division Series. Rasmussen took a no-hitter into the eighth inning and finished his night by allowing just one hit and two walks while recording 10 strikeouts across eight shutout frames. Rasmussen was one of the best pitchers in baseball in the regular season, recording a 16-5 record with a 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, and 174 strikeouts across 172 innings (30 starts). He also pitched extremely well against the Yankees, recording a 2.86 ERA and 0.82 WHIP with 26 strikeouts across 22 innings (four starts). Rasmussen would likely get the ball for a second time in the series in Game 4 if the Yankees can take one of the next two games.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 3, 2026, 9:18 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Teoscar Hernandez was one of the stars of his team's 5-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves in Game 1 of the National League Division Series on Saturday. The 33-year-old got the scoring started with a two-run home run in the fourth inning and finished the game with two hits and an additional run scored in four at-bats. Hernandez had an up-and-down regular season in 2026, hitting .267/.334/.425 with 16 home runs, 64 RBI, 66 runs scored, and five stolen bases across 491 plate appearances. The veteran slugger posted a middling .706 OPS across 251 plate appearances before the All-Star break, but he closed the season by hitting .341 with four home runs and 18 RBI across 100 trips to the plate in September. If Hernandez can carry his recent hot streak into the postseason, he could be a major difference-maker for Los Angeles.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 3, 2026, 9:09 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers starting pitcher Tarik Skubal picked up his first win of the postseason on Saturday in his team's 5-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves in Game 1 of the National League Division Series. The 29-year-old allowed just one earned run on two hits and two walks while striking out seven across six innings of work. Skubal was excellent in the regular season after being acquired by the Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers at this summer's trade deadline, recording a 5-2 record with a 2.61 ERA, 1.05 WHIP, and 70 strikeouts across 62 innings (10 starts). The hard-throwing lefty also has an impressive resume in the postseason, allowing just 10 earned runs while logging 63 strikeouts across 45 2/3 career playoff innings (seven starts). Skubal's next scheduled start will be in Game 5 of the NLDS, if the series goes that far.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 3, 2026, 10:54 AM ET
Left-handed pitcher Parker Messick will take the ball for Game 1 for the Cleveland Guardians as they take on the Chicago White Sox in the ALDS. Messick was 12-9 during the regular season with a 2.56 ERA and 1.06 WHIP with 193 strikeouts in 186 1/3 innings. Messick will look to shut down a talented White Sox lineup that is very deep and can do damage from all thirds of the lineup. Messick will take the ball as the Guardians' ace and face an opener in Hagen Smith. The Guardians will hope to get some length from Messick to set up what is a good bullpen backed by quality closer in Cade Smith. Messick has good career numbers against the White Sox and will look to get settled in right from the start in Game 1 on Saturday afternoon.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Zack Meisel, The Athletic

Question 2: If not, can the Yankees win without them?
As for the second question, it certainly hurts not to have them at full strength (Stanton) or at all for now (Judge). item.content:encoded:
Aaron Boone's in a true no-win situation. He's had a largely effective year, transitioning the Yankees through injury after injury to collect 93 wins (better than most best-case projections). He defeated - no, destroyed - the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series. But after being shut down in Game 1 by Drew Rasmussen of the Tampa Bay Rays, the boo birds are back anyway - and they won't be changing their tune unless things flip on a dime.
One specific area where Boone will never be able to win his haters over is lineup construction. For years, certainly folks have dug their heels in that if only Boone could keep his lineup consistent, his Yankees would finally be able to get in an offensive rhythm. Now, after Boone's announcement of his Game 2 lineup ahead of Yankees-Rays, the same people are almost certainly yelling, "No, not consistent like THAT, you clown!" blaming Boone for allowing the Rays' righty starter to get in a comfortable lane with the same eight lefty batters.
Yup, you heard that right. It's the same starting nine from Game 2 against Boston (massive blowout win) and Game 1 against the Rays (depressing, dispiriting loss). What's on the horizon for Boone's Yankees? Dunno. Probably one of the two.
Remember when Heliot Ramos was going to be huge for the Yankees with Aaron Judge out? Anyway...
It's on Yankees players to step up and learn changeup recognition in Game 2 vs. Rays
There's something to be said for a little bit of variance. If I made the lineups - I don't, but... - I would've started Jose Caballero, who is on record as wanting to make the Rays "suffer," and benched Trent Grisham. Seven lefties, two righties. Caballero has a two-homer game against his old team at The Trop this year. It's not much, but it's a little something.
That said, there weren't many different overly creative directions for Boone to go here - and, of course, he gets guff whether he keeps the lineup consistent (stubborn!) or switches it up (panic!). The onus is on the players, who must work the count early against Peralta, drive up his pitch count, and lay off the changeup.
Otherwise, it's going to be a true "Run it Back" scenario, where both Kevin Gausman and Trey Yesavage were able to dominate the Yankees with the exact same gameplan back-to-back nights to start off last year's ALDS in Toronto. And if Boone's players have another negligent game, he'll be blamed instead of them for doing what the fans regularly ask him to.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] Brian Cashman and Dave Dombrowski: A comparison on how to build a contender

item.content:encoded:
The Wild Card Series came and went this year without much intrigue. The Yankees blew the Red Sox out of the water, the White Sox stuck the final stake into the dying heart of the Astros, and the Padres embarrassed the Cubs. None of those series were competitive, but there was one that at least reached a Game 3: the divisional battle between the Braves and Phillies.
For one side, it was a mental block that had to be erased. The Braves hadn’t won a playoff series since winning the World Series in 2021, and had lost to the Phillies in consecutive NLDS in 2022 and 2023 to springboard their latest contention window. It’s a win-now core, and even though they had a lot of issues, they weren’t a team that can accept a loss this early.
The other side couldn’t really accept that either: the Phillies had been eliminated earlier and earlier since a heartbreaking loss in the 2022 World Series. Their core was much older, with much less young talent to supplement it. They had stumbled into the playoffs with a disastrous final week that messed up their pitching. They had reached the point where most teams are at the end of their contention window. If you don’t show reason to believe in this core, it’s going to be dismantled.
The Braves won that grudge match in Game 3, sending the Phillies home with another disastrous season and ensuring no October baseball in the City of Brotherly Love for the first time in five years. It’s a sobering defeat for a team whose best players are past their prime, which has an interim manager, and which faces an extremely bleak outlook. Such a bleak outlook is solely because of one man and his ideas of roster construction: Dave Dombrowski.
At the same time that the Phillies and their brass were openly wondering what was next for the franchise, the Yankees were preparing to play Game 1 of the ALDS at Tropicana Field, which they lost last night in St. Petersburg. It came in the team’s 34th consecutive winning season and their ninth playoff appearance in the last 10 years.
Despite having a core of older veterans who do have a gradually closing window, like the Phillies, the Yankees found a lifeline in the development of two little-known prospects into the likely AL Cy Young and a slugging first baseman/DH who will get down-ballot MVP votes in his second full season. The much-maligned architect of this entire core, and several before it, is Brian Cashman.
Cashman and Dombrowski have spent a long time as adversaries. While he was no longer in charge, a roster full of players acquired under Dombrowski beat the dynasty Yankees in the 2003 World Series. His next team, the Tigers, beat the Yankees in the postseason in 2006, 2011, and 2012. His Red Sox took out the Yankees in 2018 en route to a World Series. You’d think the guy who has won all these head-to-head battles would be heads and shoulders above, but then you must wonder why he’s had to bounce around so much.
Here, what we really get is two entirely different executives with entirely different philosophies about how to build a contender. Neither has much experience overseeing failure, so the large part of their careers has been defined by their climb toward the top of the mountain.
With Cashman, as we’ve seen for essentially three decades, it’s an approach that is more focused on long-term sustainability. He’s been blessed with the power of working with one of the league’s deepest pockets in the biggest market in baseball, which usually allows him the bandwidth to fill crippling holes. His approach in the offseason is predicated on getting high-end talent on big deals in free agency to flex their financial muscle, but also making shrewd, under-the-radar trades to fill much of the roster.
While he’s willing to shell out for big contracts both via trade and in free agency and absorb the financial risk that he knows ownership can deal with, he’s more measured when it comes to truly taking that next step. You’ll see him balk at an additional year in a free-agent deal or hold onto a top prospect in trade discussions for a top-level talent. There are times this works, but there are also times he’s left at the altar and burned for it. Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s free agency and trade discussions for Gerrit Cole in the winter of 2017 ring a bell for that.
That restraint is based on his belief in long-term sustainability. The Yankees rarely have a great farm system, but if they can produce an era-defining superstar (hello, Aaron Judge), it makes everything drastically different for roster construction. By that note, he’ll always leave holes on the roster to allow for a cheap, homegrown player to fill them. From here, it can go two ways. You can get a Judge and some great complementary pieces on rookie contracts like Gleyber Torres and Gary Sánchez, but you can also get burned by hoarding a prospect in trade talks (Chance Adams, Clint Frazier, Deivi Garcia).
This mentality is completely different than the one you’ll see Dombrowski employ. His approach to roster building, while similarly predicated on a very generous owner with deep pockets, is more based on taking risks in both free agency and the trade market, pursuing as much proven talent as possible. This approach narrows a contention window, but it’s something he’s able to work off of. It’s a lot easier to do your job when you identify a five-year window to win and disregard anything that comes after it.
Looking at how he’s managed this throughout his tenure, he made some gigantic trades and signings to turn Detroit into a perennial AL contender, acquiring Miguel Cabrera from his old stomping grounds in Miami in 2007 and David Price in 2014, while also inking Prince Fielder to a ridiculous nine-year contract. In Boston, he made blockbuster signings in Price and J.D. Martinez while swinging a franchise-altering deal for White Sox ace Chris Sale. In Philly, he’s been more muted, but gave a massive 11-year deal to Trea Turner to solidify the shortstop position. You’re never bored in an offseason under Dombrowski.
This approach is predicated on doing whatever it takes to climb to the mountaintop, looking to increase the team’s chances of raising the Commissioner’s Trophy at least one time by enough that it offsets the losses that will come down the road. It’s risky in a sport that has so much randomness in the postseason, but if it pays off, it’s genius. Just ask the 2018 Red Sox, who proceeded to bottom out in the ensuing two seasons and only make one playoff appearance over the next six seasons, if they’d trade that title for more wins in those lost seasons.
When it doesn’t work? It leads to a lot of resentment. The Tigers won a pair of pennants in 2006 and 2012, but in an extended, decade-long run with the same core of Cabrera and Verlander at the forefront, the Tigers imploded, missing the playoffs in four consecutive years between those pennants and ultimately wound up spending over a billion and burning up the farm system for no World Series. After Dombrowski was dismissed after a terrible 2015 season, the Tigers wouldn’t make the playoffs again until 2024.
The Phillies hired him to be their President of Baseball Operations in 2020, and he did what he does best. He got Turner; he got Kyle Schwarber; he extended Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola. In lieu of blockbusters, he elected to slowly chip away at the farm depth by making a mountain of smaller moves every winter and summer. It was, honestly, his least all-in job as an executive since he was in Miami, but it’s still leading to the same place as Detroit. He was hailed as a savior in 2022 when the Phils won the pennant, but is now on the verge of being driven out of town as they stare down an unbelievably bleak future without a title to show for it.
The strengths and weaknesses of Cashman and Dombrowski are directly opposite of each other. They show the two ways you can run a perpetual contender. Cashman’s philosophy allows him to keep his job for decades and decades, while Dombrowski often gets canned after the contention window slams shut. You might think Cashman’s job security is a byproduct of organizational complacency, but there’s a reason he’s universally revered for his work in baseball circles.
The two rarely go head-to-head for big signings or trades, but you can imagine how they would go. Dombrowski might give a guy an extra year or two in a deal that Cashman is apprehensive about doing. It could either end up like Yamamoto, where his prime wins you multiple championships, or like Turner, who’s turning into one of the worst contracts in the sport just four years in. In the trade market, Cashman might balk at the asking price for a big-time player, while Dombrowski would go for it. That could lead to a massive success like Sale, or a massive failure like what the Mets did with PCA.
If Dombrowski ran the Yankees over the last 15 years, do we see a World Series? I’m not sure. I’d imagine he’d be much more interested in that mega-deal the Braves proposed in 2014 that would’ve sent Luis Severino, Sanchez, and Judge to Atlanta for a box full of proven talent. He’d also be much more likely to pull the trigger on a Kyle Tucker trade that included Ben Rice in the winter of 2024 or a Eugenio Suarez/Merrill Kelly deal with the D-Backs that would’ve sent Cam Schlittler to the desert.
All in all, as the Phillies enter an offseason where they must consider firmly shutting their contention window, the Yankees not only still have a chance to win this year, but seem to have enough young talent left over to win down the road when Judge and Gerrit Cole hang up their cleats. It’s the latest chapter evolving in the several decades that Dombrowski and Cashman have spent as two of the league’s most famous executives, a chess match to truly decide which is the better style of building a contender.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What's Aaron Judge's Legacy if Ben Rice Leads Yankees to World Series
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
One scenario that might give the trolls some joy. What if the New York Yankees win a World Series without Aaron Judge, and Ben Rice puts up the kind of postseason numbers Judge has never been able to?
For anyone who still posts that video of Judge dropping a fly ball in the World Series, this situation might give them a little more ammunition, even if the Yankees are the last team standing.
It shouldn't matter, but at some point in the dead of winter, when baseball is months away — or if a lockout makes MLB's start date a complete unknown — a conversation about this might spark on WFAN. Shaun Morash might bring it up to Tiki Barber and Evan Roberts, and if things are going well for the Rangers and Knicks, it could be one of the few things to grumble about.
Indeed, Judge has wildly underperformed in his career when the lights are brightest, but if there's one way to think about a Judge-less championship, the Yankees carried their captain after years of him carrying them. They may not have won anything in decades, but the only reason they've had a puncher's chance at a title since Judge took off in 2017 is because of their captain.
Taking turns carrying each other
Think of that roster in 2022. Without Judge chasing down Maris, they would have missed the playoffs. That notion proved true the next year when Judge crashed into a Dodger Stadium wall, and the Yankees' postseason chances followed him to the IL.
In 2024, Judge had Juan Soto to back him up, but for a while, it did seem like their hold on the division could slip at any time. Their two sluggers pulled them out of a Summer funk and led them to the World Series. The 2025 team was a bit more balanced and had one of the best offenses in baseball, but another MVP effort helped push the Yankees over, even though they ultimately lost to the Toronto Blue Jays in the ALDS.
This year, with a healthy Judge, the Yankees might win the division, or it's closer than it was.
The fact is, it would only be fitting if the Yankees won without Judge and delivered their captain a World Series ring — his first. After years of him dragging them across the finish line, his teammates are finally doing something for him.
Judge's legacy is still that of a three-time MVP and one of the all-time great right-handers in the sport's history. Albert Pujols, Hank Aaron, Willie Mays, and Judge will be on that right-handed Mount Rushmore. Judge will find his way to the Hall of Fame, and if he's getting the loudest pops every time the Yankees are introduced, then rightfully so.
Bruce Wayne is still the one true Batman of Gotham, even though he's incapacitated for a time and Dick Grayson needs to take up the cape and cowl. In this case, Rice is the Robin.
The most important thing to remember, if this happens, is that the Yankees did win a World Series, and if they do, it's the only thing worth mentioning. No one should rain on that parade. Just look at the Atlanta Braves. They won without their star Ronald Acuña Jr., but nobody would nullify his impact on the Braves or think less of that championship.
The only reason it would be a conversation is that it's New York, and the biggest stars around here will always have a target on their back. Tyrese Haliburton is a great player, but a good portion of his allure is tied to what he did against the New York Knicks.
All that potential noise won't matter, though. At least the Yankees will have won, and it would be their first championship since 2009.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [fansided.com] Four reasons the white-hot Yankees could derail a Dodgers three-peat

item.content:encoded:
For the second time in three years, we have a shot at seeing the New York Yankees and Los Angeles Dodgers battle it out in the World Series. Both teams continue the postseason this weekend, with the Yankees facing the Rays in the ALDS and the Dodgers welcoming the Braves for an NLDS clash.
Only seven wins separate those four teams — and the other four still alive — from the pennant, and the Yankees looked sharp in their Wild Card Series sweep of the rival Red Sox. Even with Aaron Judge still on the mend, the 27-time World Series champions are built to capture only their third pennant since the start of 2004.
And while casual fans may think Shohei and the Dodgers are guaranteed a third consecutive title, don’t rule out the Yankees just yet.
Welcome to the Yankees’ George Lombard Jr. experience
Somewhere out there is a baseball fan feeling old because they’re watching George Lombard Sr.’s son play for the Yankees. If it’s any consolation, the 2023 first-round pick began his playoff career with four hits — three coming in Game 1 — and three runs scored against the Red Sox. Yep, he belongs, and he clearly can handle the New York spotlight.
Although Lombard’s defensive issues were a significant talking point down the stretch, he handled all seven chances without an error. He also became the youngest Yankees shortstop to start a playoff game at 21 years and 119 days old.
“It’s really cool,” Lombard said following the Wild Card Round. “There’s been a lot of countless legends that have come and played in the pinstripes so it’s really cool.”
How can you complain when you have Cam Schlittler and Max Fried?
No, we’re not forgetting Carlos Rodón or Gerrit Cole, the latter of whom is expected to start Game 1. But Schlittler showed why he’s the presumptive AL Cy Young winner by dominating the Red Sox yet again, allowing only two runs and one walk over 20.2 career postseason innings.
Elbow injuries limited Fried to 20 starts, though his 2.80 ERA and 24.0 percent strikeout rate were both in line with last year’s 2.86 ERA and 23.6 percent strikeout marks. Schlittler is expected to start Game 2, with Fried, Rodón, or Cole likely to follow in Game 3 (depending on who starts the ALDS opener).
The Jazz Chisholm and Austin Wells comeback trains are back on
Wednesday’s Game 2 showed exactly why Chisholm, who reached base three times and recorded two steals, could still command a multi-year deal this offseason. Injuries and a sharp reduction in power make it easy to forget how electrifying the two-time All-Star second baseman is, both as a player and an energetic personality. He marches to the beat of his own drum, and the Yankees need that balance of power, speed, and enthusiasm.
As for Wells, look who finally won back Yankees fans’ support. The embattled catcher quietly hit .229 with a .787 OPS in the second half, drastically up from his .155 and .504 marks over his first 66 games. Any concerns about that being a flash in the pan ended — or at least temporarily paused — after the fourth-year backstop went 3-for-6 with four RBIs in the Wild Card Series.
Imagine telling someone immediately following the trade deadline that Wells and Chisholm are among the Yankees’ most intimidating bats entering the ALDS.
We don’t talk enough about David Bednar and the Yankees’ bullpen
Not only did the Yankees bullpen’s 3.13 ERA lead baseball, but it ranked considerably above the second-place Brewers’ 3.22 mark. Bednar was fantastic in his first full Yankees season, racking up 35 saves — the most by a Yankees closer since Arolis Chapman’s 37 in 2019 — and a 2.47 ERA in 69.1 innings. He’s a pending free agent who has set himself up to cash in, and we’ll see whether the Yankees pay up.
Keep your eyes on Paul Blackburn, who pitched to a career-best 1.69 ERA — nearly three full runs fewer than his lifetime 4.46 ERA — in 85 innings. Although his 9.8 percent walk rate is concerning, he’s carved out a Luke Weaver-type role as a reliable swingman.

item.content:encoded:
Los New York Yankees están a horas de conocer si podrán contar con su capitán para la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana. Aaron Judge continúa trabajando para recuperarse de una distensión en el sóleo de la pantorrilla derecha, pero el equipo todavía no ha tomado una decisión definitiva sobre su inclusión en el roster para enfrentar a los Tampa Bay Rays.
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: Dodgers vs Braves: revancha, poder y alto voltaje en la NLDS
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: Las claves de los cuatro Juegos 1 de las Series Divisionales de la MLB
Suscríbete al Newsletter de Unanimo y recibe gratis las últimas noticias. Dale click aquí
Judge no juega desde el 16 de septiembre, cuando sufrió la lesión durante el encuentro ante los Minnesota Twins. El problema llegó poco después de que el jardinero regresara de una fractura en la costilla derecha que lo mantuvo fuera durante buena parte de la temporada. En total, disputó apenas 66 partidos de temporada regular y bateó para .241, con 18 jonrones, 41 carreras producidas y .871 de OPS.
Sin embargo, el tres veces MVP de la Liga Americana ha acelerado su recuperación durante los últimos días. El jueves tomó turnos ante lanzadores en vivo en Yankee Stadium y este viernes volvió a realizar trabajo de bateo durante la práctica del equipo en Tampa Bay. También ha comenzado a correr sobre el terreno después de trabajar previamente en una caminadora antigravedad.
El principal interrogante está precisamente en la exigencia física que implica jugar en el jardín derecho. Judge todavía no ha corrido las bases desde que sufrió la lesión, aunque el manager Aaron Boone explicó que eso no necesariamente significa que el jugador deba completar esa prueba para ser incluido en el roster. El cuerpo médico tendrá un papel importante en la decisión.
El escenario también tiene una particularidad: el Juego 1 de la ALDS se disputará este sábado en el Tropicana Field, cuya superficie artificial es otro elemento que los Yankees deben considerar al evaluar el estado de la pantorrilla de Judge. Boone reconoció que el terreno entra en la valoración, especialmente por tratarse de una lesión muscular.
Nueva York, además, tendrá que decidir cómo utilizarlo en caso de que esté disponible. Judge ha señalado que su intención es regresar como jardinero derecho, mientras que una alternativa sería emplearlo como bateador designado o emergente. El problema es que los Yankees ya tienen competencia por el puesto de DH, con Ben Rice, Paul Goldschmidt y Luis García Jr. entre las opciones.
Ver esta publicación en Instagram
La incertidumbre llega después de que los Yankees demostraran que pueden producir sin su principal estrella. Nueva York barrió a los Boston Red Sox en la Serie de Comodines y los superó 18-2 en los dos encuentros, avanzando a una ALDS en la que enfrentará al equipo con el mejor récord de la Liga Americana durante la temporada regular.
Los Yankees deben entregar su roster de 26 jugadores antes de las 10:00 de la mañana del sábado, aproximadamente diez horas antes del primer lanzamiento. Para entonces tendrá que estar resuelta la gran pregunta que ha acompañado a Nueva York desde mediados de septiembre: si Aaron Judge estará listo para volver al terreno o tendrá que esperar una oportunidad más adelante en octubre.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Gerrit Cole set for first postseason start since Tommy John, Yankees mulling Aarond Judge decison
item.dc:creator: Abbey Mastracco; New York Daily News
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — For all of the noise that has been made about the Yankees' use of analytics in recent years, their postseason decisions show the feel the club has for the game, something numbers can't quantify. Calling on Gerrit Cole to start Game 1 of the ALDS is one of those decisions. The Yankees may have four aces in their rotation, and the Rays have struggled against left-handers. But Cole, a right-hander, is the quintessential big-game pitcher. He's the guy who can set the tone for
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — For all of the noise that has been made about the Yankees' use of analytics in recent years, their postseason decisions show the feel the club has for the game, something numbers can't quantify.
Calling on Gerrit Cole to start Game 1 of the ALDS is one of those decisions. The Yankees may have four aces in their rotation, and the Rays have struggled against left-handers. But Cole, a right-hander, is the quintessential big-game pitcher. He's the guy who can set the tone for his team in a meaningful way, and this start against the Tampa Bay Rays has extra meaning, being the first postseason appearance for Cole since his 2025 Tommy John surgery.
"It's incredibly special," Cole said Friday at Tropicana Field. "Coming back from surgery, I mean there's not much more I could ask for. I feel tremendously blessed. I feel that the people in the clubhouse that have contributed to the success this year deserve a lot of the credit. It's been a team effort overall, and so excited to go out and compete again."
Whether Cole competes with Aaron Judge is yet to be determined.
Judge could be active for this next round, even if he isn't ready for Game 1. The Yankees could include him on the roster to utilize him as a pinch hitter. The winner of the last three MVP Awards, Judge hit at Yankee Stadium on Thursday, and spent Friday working out nearby at GMS Field before joining the team for the workout day in St. Petersburg.
Judge took batting practice on the field, but did not run the bases. He declined to take questions from the media.
Manager Aaron Boone was non-committal on the status of his captain's strained right calf. Boone has not seen Judge run the bases, but did confirm that he has started running. The turf at the Trop could be reason enough to hold him out of action in this round, but if they can use him in New York, it might be advantageous to include him on the roster.
"[The turf] plays into it a little bit; it's just as far as him and the field, potentially," Boone said. "But we're looking at the days, so it's more, is he going to be available at some point in this series, potentially, as a player? That's what we're kind of weighing, and then seeing where he's at now these last few days having taken live BP. We'll see how today goes."
Whether the Yankees have Aaron Judge or not, Cole provides a presence.
It's been a learning experience for the 36-year-old as he progressed through rehab and through the season. The elbow injury that started with edema in 2024 and culminated in ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction in 2025 was the first major injury of a career that has spanned nearly 13 years. One of the more durable aces in the game, Cole is one of the few starters who still regularly throws 200 or more innings and makes 30 or more starts.
He edited and updated his routine this season as needed, ultimately going back to what has always worked for him in the past. Cole wanted to stay flexible and open to anything that could keep his elbow healthy, while also maintaining his effectiveness on the mound.
"Humans, we don't progress in a linear fashion, or there are times where we have to adapt," Cole said. "I spoke about just staying curious about the process earlier in the season; I thought that really carried us a long way in terms of making some of the adaptations."
Limited to 95 innings in 2024, and 127 this season, Cole is coming into the postseason with a well-rested arm. He last pitched 10 days ago against Tampa Bay in a 5 2/3-inning effort for his 10th win of the season. He knows the lineup, and he's pitching in a place he enjoys.
The Trop might be the target of ridicule from fans around the league, but if it's good enough for Cole, it can't be all that bad. He's also had success in Tampa, with a 3.32 ERA at Tropicana Field in 10 starts. The Rays have hit .218 off Cole in their home park.
Still, Cole said his arm doesn't feel any different than it usually does at this time of year, probably because he's gotten a lot of mileage out of it throughout the years, and he's coming off a 22-start season.
"I do feel just to an extent I've been pitching all year, and I feel that you know I've had opportunities to settle into the season and settle into the routine, so that there's really nothing new approaching me at this point," Cole said. "So in that regard, it's pretty much the same."
While he may have more excitement for this start given that it's his first in the postseason since the 2024 World Series, his mentality isn't any different either, because postseason starts are always special. Judge or not, Cole provides an intangible presence that can't be measured by any analytical formula.

item.dc:creator: Jon Conahan

The Rays, who have arguably been not only the best team in the American League for much of the campaign, but also in all of Major League Baseball, always find ways to win. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will have their toughest test yet against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
The Rays, who have arguably been not only the best team in the American League for much of the campaign, but also in all of Major League Baseball, always find ways to win.
While the Yankees are much more talented than the Rays in terms of payroll, on paper, and in other ways, this is not a series the Yankees are going to just walk away with. There's a reason why Tampa Bay won the division, and it is going to show that in this series.
Keeping everybody healthy for the Yankees is a top priority, but unfortunately, that doesn't look guaranteed.
For Yankees slugger Aaron Judge, it remains uncertain whether he'll play.
There's a lot of hope that Judge might eventually be activated in this series, but the latest reports suggest it will take time, if the Yankees decide to do so.
"Judge's status for the Yankees' AL Division Series matchup against the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays remains up in the air and is unlikely to be decided until shortly before the series begins Saturday, sources familiar with the deliberations told ESPN.
"Some in the organization want him to play. Others, wary of him further aggravating the injury and imperiling him for the remainder of the postseason, would prefer to wait another week. Further complicating matters is the likelihood that Judge could be resigned to designated hitter duties, potentially taking at-bats from Luis Garcia Jr," Jeff Passan of ESPN wrote.
There's unfortunately so much that has to happen for the Yankees over the next 24 hours for this to be a reality, and the biggest one is that even if Judge does return, there's going to be a big question about whether he's the same type of player that everybody expects him to be.
Regardless, the Yankees have to feel somewhat confident that he's going to be good to go, as Judge is the best hitter in Major League Baseball, and having him in the lineup, even if he's not fully healthy, completely changes the dynamic of this lineup.

item.content:encoded:
Will Aaron Judge Be Available For Yankees' ALDS Series vs. Rays?
The New York Yankees surged its way to the American League Division Series after its two-game sweep over the Boston Red Sox. And yet, the Yankees' dominant series win came without star Aaron Judge.
Judge has been out with a calf strain injury since Sept. 19, when the Yankees originally moved him to the 10-day injured list. Especially as the Yankees creep towards its next postseason series against the Tampa Bay Rays, Judge's timeline and likeliness of making the 26-man roster this weekend is still unknown.
The Yankees have until Saturday morning to submit their final rosters ahead of Game 1 at 6:30 p.m. in St. Petersburg, Florida. If Judge were to be added to the roster, it would be his first roster appearance this postseason run for New York.
Manager Aaron Boone provided clarity on Judge ahead of submitting the roster, and gave a status update on Judge’s health.
"The trainers will obviously play a big part in this. As the day unfolds, we'll see where we're at and what it potentially looks like for the series," Boone said.
Although Judge has been a part of live batting practice, Boone is still weighing in how, and when, Judge can be utilized against the Rays.
"It's just as far as him and the field, potentially," Boone said. "But we're looking at the days and so it's more, 'Is he going to be available at some point in this series, potentially, as a player?' That's what we're kind of weighing and then seeing where he's at now these last few days having taken live [batting practice]."
The Yankees' postseason run continues tomorrow at 6:30 p.m. in a three-game divisional series against the Rays.

"We'll see," Boone said when asked about Judge's availability. "He'll be working out [Friday]. He hit again live [Thursday] at Yankee Stadium. He's doing more today over at [Steinbrenner Field in Tampa] and [Tropicana Field]. So we'll probably make those calls later tonight." Asked if Judge had run the bases during his wo
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge's status for the New York Yankees' American League Division Series matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays is still uncertain, manager Aaron Boone told reporters on Friday.
"We'll see," Boone said when asked about Judge's availability. "He'll be working out [Friday]. He hit again live [Thursday] at Yankee Stadium. He's doing more today over at [Steinbrenner Field in Tampa] and [Tropicana Field]. So we'll probably make those calls later tonight."
Asked if Judge had run the bases during his workouts, Boone said he wasn't sure but knew that Judge had been running.
The Yankees have until 10 a.m. ET Saturday morning to submit their 26-player roster for Game 1, which is scheduled for 6:30 p.m. ET in Tampa Bay.
Aaron Boone gives an update on Aaron Judge's status for the ALDS: "We'll see. He'll be working out today, hit again live yesterday."
Boone is not sure if Judge has run the bases but knows that Judge has started running pic.twitter.com/RItnaCMlAj
— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) October 2, 2026
Judge hasn't played since suffering a calf injury on Sept. 16 and was placed on the injured list two days later. He was left off the Yankees' roster during their wild-card series versus the Boston Red Sox — though the Yankees didn't need Judge in their two-game sweep, winning by scores of 9-0 and 9-2.
One consideration in playing Judge at Tropicana Field is the ballpark's artificial turf. That could preclude him from playing the outfield if he's on the roster.
"It plays into it a little bit," Boone said, via the Associated Press. "But we're looking at the days and so it's more is he going to be available at some point in this series, potentially, as a player? That's what we're kind of weighing and then seeing where he's at now these last few days having taken live BP."
Games 1 and 2 at Tropicana Field are scheduled for Saturday and Monday. The series shifts to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday and Game 4, if necessary, on Thursday, if the preference was to save Judge for the grass field in New York. Game 5 at Tampa Bay is scheduled for Oct. 10.
The Yankees could decide to have Judge on the ALDS roster even if he's only available to pinch-hit. If he can't play in right field, Ben Rice will likely remain at designated hitter. He batted 5-for-9 with 2 home runs and 6 RBI in the two wild-card games.
However, Rays manager Kevin Cash is proceeding as if Judge will be in the Yankees' lineup.
"I expect him playing right field, hitting third," Cash said, via the AP.
Gerrit Cole (3.61 ERA) will be the Yankees' starting pitcher for Game 1, while Drew Rasmussen (2.67 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays.

item.content:encoded:
New Aaron Judge Rumors, Updated Injury Status for Yankees vs. Rays in 2026 MLB Playoffs
The Tampa Bay Rays may have to wait until closer to Saturday's first pitch of the ALDS to find out if Game 1 starter Drew Rasmussen will be facing Aaron Judge at the plate.
ESPN's Jeff Passan reported earlier on Friday that Judge's status "remains up in the air and is unlikely to be decided until shortly before the series begins Saturday, sources familiar with the deliberations told ESPN."
"Some in the organization want him to play," Passan reported. "Others, wary of him further aggravating the injury and imperiling him for the remainder of the postseason, would prefer to wait another week."
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters that Judge could be included on the roster even if he is not in the lineup for Game 1:
Passan noted the decision is also impacted by the fact Judge could be returning as a designated hitter. Notably, DH Luis García Jr. just helped the Yankees close out their Wild Card sweep of the Boston Red Sox by opening Game 2 scoring with a home run.
Judge initially said he hoped to return for the beginning of the postseason before he was left off the Yankees' Wild Card roster amid his recovery from the right calf strain that resulted in a trip to the injured list on Sept. 19.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said at the time the decision was made because the club didn't feel Judge was "all the way back."
Judge has appeared in just seven games for the Yankees since he was shut down with a right rib injury May 31. Following his return Sept. 8, he was held to a batting average of .174 with one home run in 24 plate appearances before suffering the calf injury.
The Yankees will hope giving Judge more time to recover from his latest injury will result in a more productive return from the slugger. Should he sit out the divisional series, he would gain an additional week to recover in the event the Yankees advance to the ALCS.
Gerrit Cole will start Game 1 for the Yankees when the ALDS begins Saturday at 6:30 p.m. ET in St. Petersburg. He will be facing a more rested lineup given that the Rays sat out the Wild Card round after clinching the AL's top seed.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will play the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series.
Game 1 of the series will begin at 6:30 p.m. EDT on Friday at Tropicana Field.
The Yankees were without star outfielder Aaron Judge in the American League Wild Card Series due to a calf strain.
Despite Judge's absence, the Yankees swept the Boston Red Sox 2-0 in the Wild Card Series. New York outscored Boston 18-2.
Before the ALDS, Yankees manager Aaron Boone announced an update on Judge.
New York Yankees' Aaron Boone Announces Aaron Judge News Before ALDS vs. Rays
Aaron Boone gives an update on Aaron Judge's status for the ALDS: "We'll see. He'll be working out today, hit again live yesterday."
Boone is not sure if Judge has run the bases but knows that Judge has started running
Aaron Boone gives an update on Aaron Judge's status for the ALDS: "We'll see. He'll be working out today, hit again live yesterday."Boone is not sure if Judge has run the bases but knows that Judge has started running pic.twitter.com/RItnaCMlAj— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) October 2, 2026
Looking at Aaron Judge
The Yankees placed Judge on the injured list on Sept. 19 with a right calf strain.
Judge missed most of the season with a right rib stress fracture, landing him on the IL on June 2. New York activated him on Sept. 7.
Before being placed on the IL in June, Judge hit .248/.375/.533 with 17 home runs and 38 RBI over 59 games this season.
Judge struggled after returning from the IL in Sept., hitting just .190/.227/.333 with one home run and three RBI over six games before landing on the IL again.
Since making his MLB debut in 2016, Judge has slashed 291/.410/.610 with 386 home runs and 871 RBI.
Judge has won three AL MVP Awards throughout his career.
Looking at the Yankees-Rays ALDS
Here is the Yankees-Rays ALDS schedule:
- Game 1: 6:30 p.m. EDT on Saturday, Oct. 3, @ Tropicana Field
- Game 2: 8:00 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 5, @ Tropicana Field
- Game 3: 8:00 p.m. EDT on Wednesday, Oct. 7, @ Yankee Stadium
- Game 4 (if necessary): 8:00 p.m. EDT on Thursday, Oct. 8, @ Yankee Stadium
- Game 5 (if necessary): 8:00 p.m. EDT on Saturday, Oct. 10, @ Tropicana Field
All of the games will be available to watch on TBS and HBO Max.
The winner of the Yankees-Rays series will play the winner of the ALDS between the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians in the American League Championship Series.
The Rays finished the season with the best record in the American League at 98-64.
The Yankees ended the regular season 4 1/2 games behind the Rays for first place in the division.
The Rays won seven of 13 games against the Yankees this season. However, the Yankees won three of four games in their last series with the Rays.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] 5 Reasons Why the Yankees Shouldn't Keep Aaron Judge off the ALDS Roster
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown

For anyone who watched this team all year—or even the past few years—the best version of this team has Judge in the lineup. Who knows what would've happened to the division this year if Judge were healthy, or, in the case of the 2023 season, their postseason chances if Dodger Stadium hadn't taken him out. The Texas Rangers won the World Series by com
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees may have blown the doors off the Boston Red Sox without Aaron Judge, but that doesn't mean that they don't need their captain. For anyone who watched this team all year—or even the past few years—the best version of this team has Judge in the lineup.
Who knows what would've happened to the division this year if Judge were healthy, or, in the case of the 2023 season, their postseason chances if Dodger Stadium hadn't taken him out. The Texas Rangers won the World Series by coming out of the American League, but the Yankees took a series from them without Judge that summer.
Heading into the division series against Tampa Bay, the Yankees should activate him if he's healthy enough to play. Here are five reasons why.
Lineup protection
The Yankees' lineup outscored the Red Sox 18-2 in two games. It's hard to find a bigger mismatch in the postseason than that with the remaining teams.
As great as Ben Rice performed, imagine a world where a pitcher is staring at who is coming up, and the part of the lineup he has to navigate is Judge, Rice, and Cody Bellinger. They'll be extra careful and may be forced to pitch to these guys because, as Bellinger proved in Game 2, if you put runners on in front of him, he has a shot at taking a pitcher deep.
Still a homer threat even if he struggles
Judge struggled throughout the 2024 postseason. However, one of the memorable home runs during that series came off him, taking Emmanuel Clase deep. The Yankees still lost that game, but it showed that as long as Judge is in that lineup, he can change the complexion of any game.
At that point, Clase was one of baseball's best closers. Judge still sent a triple-digit pitch into the seats.
Flexibility proved to be a little overrated in the Wild Card Series
Aaron Boone mixed and matched his roster a bit in the Wild Card Series, but not everyone performed despite the run parade. Amed Rosario and Heliot Ramos, specifically, provided next to nothing. Ramos is essentially Judge's replacement on the roster when the Yankees face lefties, and the southpaw Payton Tolle overpowered him in Game 1.
Judge may not have fared much better than Ramos, but there's a difference between a bench bat and a three-time MVP. Pitchers are looking at that matchup a little differently.
The best defensive roster has Judge in right field
Judge has a calf strain, and playing on it could be detrimental. But if a doctor says he's healthy enough to get out there, he should be in right field. With Judge in the outfield, that opens up the DH slot so Ben Rice and Luis Garcia Jr. can play at the same time. The best Yankee lineup has those three in there at the same time.
No "what ifs"
The 2026 season has been one big "What if?" What if the Yankees were healthy? What if the rotation didn't deal with as many IL stints as it did? What if Judge stayed on the field?
There's no remedying what happened in the regular season, but if Judge is healthy and can go up against the Rays, the Yankees can put a lot of those questions to rest — especially if they beat Tampa with Judge's help.
Anyone who thought the Yankees would have won the AL East if Judge had stayed on the field would be somewhat redeemed. Granted, the stakes are a little higher than what happens between April and September.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

Yankees' Aaron Judge reveals early injury status for ALDS against Rays originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees did exactly what they had to do on both sides of the baseball against the Boston Red Sox in the American League Wild Card series.
As the Yankees prepare for the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays, there's reason to believe this roster will be even better than it was during the Wild Card.
As of now, it remains uncertain what the Yankees want to do with Aaron Judge, or whether he can even play, but there's hope around the fan base that he might come back.
Speaking to reporters while celebrating his team advancing, Judge said that he feels good, but he doesn't have an answer as to whether he's eventually playing.
"We just finished the Wild Card," Judge said in the middle of a clubhouse celebration, per NJ.com. "We'll get into that as we get close. I got nothing for you yet, but I have an opportunity to get ready. That's what I've been doing every day."
"I'm feeling good," he said.
Getting Judge back has to be the biggest priority for the Yankees over this postseason.
While the Yankees played very well against the Red Sox and there was a lot to like, things are only going to get more difficult.
Not having the best hitter in Major League Baseball doesn't help, and the Yankees will have to work around it if he's not ready to go.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Aaron Judge says quiet part out loud about Rays appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are riding high after defeating the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card series on Thursday. Now they will face their other division rival, the Tampa Bay Rays, in the ALDS beginning on Saturday, Oct. 3, at Tropicana Field.
Going into the series, Aaron Judge was highly complimentary of the Rays, per Gary Phillips of The New York Daily News. Essentially, Judge said that the Rays are a complete team, but that the Yankees are ready to take them on.
"They got everything," Judge said. "We're up for the task."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
The Rays have a vast array of assets working in their favor. They won the AL East Division with a 98-64 record. They also went 55-26 at home and defeated the Yankees 7-6 throughout the season.
The Rays also have power at the plate with Junior Caminero, who hit 42 home runs. They have consistency at the plate in Yandy Díaz, who led the AL in hits with 180. Additionally, Chandler Simpson is a reliable presence on the base paths.
Nevertheless, the Yankees have a lot going for them. They dominated the Red Sox with 9-0 and 9-2 victories in the Wild Card series. Plus, their staff ace Cam Schlittler is on a roll after pitching 6 1/3 scoreless innings against Boston. Their bullpen, led by Carlos Rodón, is also pretty top-notch.
The Yankees also lead the AL with a 3.24 ERA.
Meanwhile, Judge was left off the roster for the Wild Card series because of a recent calf strain. His status for the ALDS remains unknown.

item.title: [Yahoo] Yankees Banking on Track Record By Turning to Gerrit Cole In Game 1 of ALDS
item.dc:creator: Ben Watanabe
item.description: Through all the hand-wringing over the lineup and injury status of Aaron Judge all season, the fact of the matter was that the New York Yankees possess an embarrassment of riches in their starting rotation. It ultimately might be what delivers them another World Series. So the fact that the Yankees could turn to arguably their fourth-best starting pitcher for Game 1 of their American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays, and only prompt minor debate among observers about the move, i
item.content:encoded:
Through all the hand-wringing over the lineup and injury status of Aaron Judge all season, the fact of the matter was that the New York Yankees possess an embarrassment of riches in their starting rotation. It ultimately might be what delivers them another World Series.
So the fact that the Yankees could turn to arguably their fourth-best starting pitcher for Game 1 of their American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays, and only prompt minor debate among observers about the move, is another sign of how stacked the team is on the mound.
Gerrit Cole will start Game 1, the Yankees announced Friday morning, going with the safe choice to open the series. The Rays will counter with All-Star right-hander Drew Rasmussen.
Cole comes into Saturday's game with plenty of rest. He was scheduled to start Game 3 on Thursday against the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series, but that game turned out not to be necessary. The 36-year-old last pitched more than a week ago, giving up two runs in 5 2/3 innings against these same Rays on Sept. 23.
Carlos Rodon also has plenty of rest, however, and even ace Cam Schlittler should be relatively fresh, having not pitched since Game 1 against the Red Sox on Tuesday. Rodon, Schlittler and Max Fried all have better numbers this season than Cole, who missed all of last season after undergoing Tommy John surgery. But Cole has the name and the track record.
Cole has started 12 playoff games in his Yankees career, with a 2.93 ERA. He's started 22 playoff games in total with a 2.77 ERA and 1.020 WHIP that reveal how misleading his 7-8 career postseason record is.
Going solely by this season, the Yankees might have better options. But Cole has the longest resume of success, and on Saturday, he'll have the ball.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] An open letter to Yankees fans who wanted Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone gone | Klapisch

item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — This is an open letter to anyone who's railed against Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone over the years. That's a huge swath of Yankees fans – maybe all of them. So let's call this a mass mailing. The Yankees are a step closer to the World Series for two reasons. The first was the Red Sox's glaring deficits. Scoring just two runs in 18 innings, they just weren't good enough to hang with the Yankees. If the Wild Card Series were replayed 10 times, the Yankees would likely win ni
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — This is an open letter to anyone who's railed against Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone over the years. That's a huge swath of Yankees fans – maybe all of them. So let's call this a mass mailing.
The Yankees are a step closer to the World Series for two reasons. The first was the Red Sox's glaring deficits. Scoring just two runs in 18 innings, they just weren't good enough to hang with the Yankees. If the Wild Card Series were replayed 10 times, the Yankees would likely win nine.
The second reason is why we're here today. Although this isn't the greatest Yankees roster of the last 20 years, it is remarkably well-constructed and well-managed. That's another way of saying Cashman and Boone have done their jobs well. They deserve credit for that.
The question is whether the critics will ever reconsider. I have my doubts. The folks who've been demanding Cashman's and Boone's firing for almost a decade aren't exactly open to reasonable dialogue. They're dug in so deep that one of them, who just happens to be an old college buddy, insisted, "Anyone could've beaten the Red Sox. That's how much they sucked."
My friend isn't entirely wrong — at least about Boston's non-existent offense. It's hard to believe this was the same team that went on a 14-game winning streak this summer.
But to suggest that any manager with Cam Schlittler as their ace and Ben Rice hitting lasers could've taken down the Sox is flat-out wrong. That's like saying all managers are the same. Their only job is to fill out the lineup card and talk to the TV cameras after the game.
Not quite.
Managers have personality traits that can enhance the roster's potential. Joe Torre, laid-back in a streetwise sort of way, was the perfect candidate to replace the hyper-involved Buck Showalter. Torre was never loud, but still tough enough to absorb late owner George Steinbrenner's manic behavior.
When Torre's enthusiasm for managing waned by 2006, Joe Girardi — ultra-prepared, obsessed with process — represented the pendulum swinging in the other direction. And when the next generation of Yankees decided Girardi was just too uptight and disconnected from the clubhouse, Boone won over Cashman because he was smart, calm and relatable.
I realize fans no longer care about Boone's personality. Not even his .582 winning percentage — second only to the Dodgers' Dave Roberts among active managers — gets the credit it deserves. What matters are championships. Boone has none since he replaced Girardi in 2018. In the Bronx, that's 0-for-forever.
That doesn't mean Boone is a bad manager. He checks so many other boxes that have kept the Yankees competitive. The players like Boone, but more importantly, they trust his instincts. In fact, Boone had a terrific series against Boston, embarrassing Chad Tracy, his counterpart in the other dugout.
Boone didn't make any significant mistakes against the Sox. His most important decision of the series came in Game 1.
After allowing Schlittler to throw 117 pitches, Boone summoned Paul Blackburn in the seventh inning to protect a 2-0 lead. Facing Ceddanne Rafaela with the tying run at the plate, Blackburn induced an inning-ending double play. The Yankees went on to score seven runs in the next two innings.
Tracy, on the other hand, made two decisions that doomed Boston. In both games, he pulled his starter in the fifth inning with two outs and the Sox trailing 1-0 — first Payton Tolle, then Sonny Gray. The Yankees promptly destroyed reliever Erik Miller on both occasions.
Several Sox players, including Gray and Willson Contreras, have since second-guessed Tracy's strategy and the team's overall direction.
You don't hear that kind of anti-Boone sniping in the Yankees' clubhouse. Even Boone's handling of Aaron Judge's irritation at being left off the Wild Card roster showed finesse. Boone demonstrated he was in control without making a show of pulling rank.
One former Yankee texted me the other day about the back-and-forth between Boone and Judge. He believes the episode showed how much Boone has grown on the job.
"All (Boone) said was, 'We don't expect Judge to be back,'" the former Yankee said. "That's Boone's way of telling the rest of the players, 'It's time for you to step up. Don't sit here waiting for Judge to rescue you.' It was a positive message."
Of course, it takes the right kind of players to understand that. The Yankees are a stable group. Even Jose Caballero, who came to the Yankees with the reputation of being a rogue element, has fallen into line.
That's where Cashman comes in. He made one right call after another in assembling this 93-win roster. The bullpen is airtight; the gamble on trading for closer David Bednar has worked to perfection. The GM made the smart move by promoting George Lombard Jr. this summer instead of waiting until September or 2027. And the rotation, finally healthy, is the Yankees' best since 2009.
MORE BY BOB KLAPISCH
All it took was one more piece — Max Fried. His signing in free agency in 2025 had Cashman's fingerprints all over it.
Beat the Rays, and the Yankees are back in the AL Championship Series. Win there, and they're back in the World Series for the second time in three years. At that point, those haters just might admit Cashman and Boone had something to do with it.
I'm such a nice guy that I'll give my friend a chance to admit he was wrong all along.
Read the original article on NJ.com. Add NJ.com as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
