item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees beat the Boston Red Sox by a score of 9-2.
With the victory, they swept the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series.
Bob Nightengale of USA Today wrote: “The New York Yankees sweep the Boston Red Sox out of the Bronx in humiliating fashion. They outscored the Red Sox 18-2 in the wild-card series. They are off to Tampa Bay for a best-of-five AL Division Series beginning Saturday”
Judge Makes Bellinger Statement After Sweep
Cody Bellinger finished the win with two hits, including one home run and four RBIs.
After the game, Aaron Judge was asked about Bellinger when he spoke to YES Network.
Meredith Marakovits: “Last night it was Ben Rice. Tonight it was Cody Bellinger with some big hits. Those two bats in the lineup. Just how valuable are they?”
Judge: “It’s amazing. We saw Ben Rice make a lot of strides last year. I knew coming into this year he’s going to have a great year for us. And then that’s why we signed back Cody Bellinger, man. He’s built for this. He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment. And he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Looking At Bellinger
Bellinger is in the middle of his second season with the Yankees.
He has also spent time with the Los Angeles Dodgers and Chicago Cubs over 10 seasons at the MLB level.
As Judge alluded to, Bellinger signed a big deal with the Yankees over the offseason.
Looking At The Yankees
The Yankees finished the regular season as the second-place team in the American League East with a 93-68 record in 161 games.
They are looking to win their first World Series title since the 2009 season.

item.content:encoded:
Having bashed Boston without Judge, Yankees turn attention to AL Division Series vs. pesky Rays
NEW YORK (AP) — Having bashed Boston without Aaron Judge, the New York Yankees face a far different task when they face the pesky Tampa Bay Rays in an AL Division Series starting Saturday,
Riding powerful pitching led by Cam Schlitter and Max Fried, Yankees batters broke though just enough against Red Sox starters and beat up Boston’s bullpen in sweeping their rival in the Wild Card Series.
“We’re going to continue to rely on amazing starting pitching like we have all year,” Ben Rice said after Wednesday night’s 9-2 win. ”Especially in the postseason, that’s what you need.”
Schlittler and Fried combined to go 2-0 with a 0.73 ERA against the Red Sox with 16 strikeouts and two walks in 12 1/3 innings.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone must decide whether to open against the Rays with Gerrit Cole, who was set to start a Game 3 against Boston, or Carlos Rodón.
“Obviously, Gerrit’s lined up for that. Carlos is very much in play for that,” Boone said. “We have a ton of confidence in both guys. I think they’re both throwing the ball really well.”
Boone said it was possible Schlittler, Fried, Cole and Rodón all will start against the Rays. New York’s starters led the major leagues with a 3.30 ERA.
“That’s been the biggest strength for us throughout the year,” Boone said. “It sustained us. It got us through some difficult times. And I feel like they’re all in a good place right now.”
New York’s best-of-five series against the Rays has an extra off day between Games 1 and 2, allowing Schlittler to start the second game and come back on normal rest for a Game 5.
Whether Judge will return to the lineup remains unclear.
Sidelined since Sept. 16 by a strained right calf, Judge has resumed hitting.
“Saturday’s a long ways away, but I’m doing everything I can, all morning, night, during the game, everything to prepare myself to be ready to go,” Judge said. “So I want to be in there. So we’ll see what happens.”
Tampa Bay won the season series 7-6 en route to an AL-best 98-64 record, their runners often spinning around the bases like a roulette ball going around the wheel. The Rays were sixth in the major leagues with a .326 on-base percentage and tied for second with 164 stolen bases.
Rays batters struck out the fewest times in the major leagues at 1,145, an average of about two per game fewer than the Yankees.
Because they won the AL East and had a bye, the Rays will enter the series with five days’ rest — which some in baseball is convinced causes rust.
“The alternative is playing three must-win games or two out of three. I’ll take where we’re at,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said.
Rays left-handed pitchers held lefty batters to a .205 average during the regular season. Yankees lefty batters hit .500 (11 for 22) against Boston southpaws.
“They faced so many guys for months there where we were very left-handed, where in the fifth inning every day it was one lefty and then another one because that’s how they attack us,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “So I’d like to think some of that familiarity and reps and all that prepared us well.”
New York was second in the majors with 223 home runs, three behind Houston. What was often a home-run-or-bust batting order diversified in the Wild Card Series.
Homegrown players — Rice, Spencer Jones, George Lombard Jr., Anthony Volpe and Austin Wells — combined for 11 RBIs.
“The young guys have done a tremendous job,” outfielder Cody Bellinger said. “It’s been fun to watch. It’s fun to watch them grow and they’ve been a huge part of our success.”

item.title: [whec.com] Aaron Judge remains unsure for ALDS after missing Yankees' first-round win over Red Sox

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge remains unsure for ALDS after missing Yankees’ first-round win over Red Sox
NEW YORK (AP) — Yankees captain Aaron Judge remained unsure of his Division Series status following New York’s Wild Card Series sweep of the Boston Red Sox.
Sidelined since Sept. 16 by a strained right calf, Judge went to the Yankees’ Double-A ballpark in Somerset, New Jersey, for live batting practice Wednesday as he tries to work his way back from a leg injury to be available later in the postseason.
“Saturday’s a long ways away, but I’m doing everything I can, all morning, night, during the game, everything to prepare myself to be ready to go,” Judge said after Wednesday night’s 9-2 win. “So I want to be in there. So we’ll see what happens.”
Judge did not join teammates along the first-base line for introductions before the Yankees’ 9-0 win in Tuesday’s opener of the best-of-three series.
“I think he was getting treatment,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Judge ran in the outfield before Tuesday night’s game and on Wednesday went to Somerset to hit. He returned to the Bronx in time to watch Game 2.
A three-time AL MVP, Judge was limited to 66 games this season. The 34-year-old slugger hit .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs in September.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers, sidelined with a left forearm flexor strain since Aug. 22, was to throw a bullpen at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday.
Boone said right-hander Clarke Schmidt won’t pitch again this year. The 30-year-old relieved on Sept. 16 at Minnesota in his first big league appearance since Tommy John surgery on July 11, 2025, then was put on the injured list with right biceps inflammation.

item.content:encoded:
Regardless of how his career turns out, Chicago Cubs superstar Pete Crow-Armstrong may already have Mike Trout beat in one key category: playoff games.
Both are still seeking their first Championship Series appearance, but at least PCA had another opportunity this week. Any hopes the Cubs had of advancing beyond the Wild Card Round ended fairly quickly, though, with the presumptive NL MVP being held hitless in eight at-bats against the Padres.
Crow-Armstrong’s dreadful two-game performance follows him hitting .184 with 12 strikeouts over eight playoff games last year.
“You can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn’t contribute,” he told reporters. “None of it feels good. Pretty disappointed in myself, but that’s for me to work on.”
Given the current state of baseball’s labor crisis, he’ll likely have plenty of additional time to reflect on what went wrong.
Should Chicago Cubs fans be concerned by Pete Crow-Armstrong’s playoff struggles?
Some of the more generous PCA-related social media posts have involved questioning his MVP status or accusing him of being overrated. Right, because someone who just put up nearly 10 bWAR and joined the 40-40 club is overrated.
This will sound crazy, but Crow-Armstrong is still only 24. He’s already become one of the sport’s premier faces to the point that we wouldn’t be shocked if he’s on the cover of next year’s MLB The Show game. We talk so much about New York and Los Angeles that we forget he’s thrived in the Chicago media market, which isn’t exactly a bunch of villages and huts in the middle of nowhere.
Anyone who blames Crow-Armstrong for the Cubs’ playoff loss is deliberately being lazy. Alex Bregman, Dansby Swanson and Ian Happ all went hitless in the series themselves. They managed one run over 18 innings.
Credit to the Padres for keeping Crow-Armstrong off the basepaths, which should sound obvious enough. But he drew walks in nearly 12 percent of his plate appearances during the regular season yet only managed a single free pass this week.
Analysts constantly referenced Trout’s 1-for-12 showing in the 2014 ALDS — still his lone postseason appearance — because he and the Angels still haven’t returned to the playoffs. That’s why no one even bothers bringing it up anymore; we’ve just collectively gotten used to the Angels finishing in or near last place.
Do you remember who else had a reputation as a poor postseason performer? Alex Rodriguez, a narrative that vanished when the Yankees won the 2009 World Series. The talk surrounding Aaron Judge’s October struggles will vanish if he catches the final out of the Fall Classic.
Let’s give Crow-Armstrong some more time. Besides, the Cubs are only 10 years into a title drought rather than 108. Things could be far worse.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Yankees’ Spencer Jones Makes MLB History With Incredible Feat
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: New York Yankees outfielder Spencer Jones already looked like an outlier before he stepped into the batter’s box in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series. The Yankees rookie is 6-foot-7, plays center field, runs better than a frame that size usually allows, and carries a batting stance that draws comparisons to Shohei Ohtani. On Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, he added a line to the record book that no one else has occupied in more than a century of searchable pla
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees outfielder Spencer Jones already looked like an outlier before he stepped into the batter’s box in the sixth inning of Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series.
The Yankees rookie is 6-foot-7, plays center field, runs better than a frame that size usually allows, and carries a batting stance that draws comparisons to Shohei Ohtani.
On Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, he added a line to the record book that no one else has occupied in more than a century of searchable play-by-play.
Jones led off the sixth against Garrett Crochet, the Red Sox ace working in relief for the first time in months. The at-bat ended with a swing and a miss on a pitch in the dirt.
A third strike that the catcher does not hold is not automatically an out, and Adley Rutschman could not keep the ball. Jones took off for first. The call on the field went against him. Replay did not. The out was overturned, and a strikeout that should have ended the plate appearance instead put the tallest man in the Yankees lineup on base.
From there the inning got stranger. Jones stole second, tacking a stolen base onto a strikeout that had not counted as an out. He later came around to score. New York kept hitting.
The Yankees batted all the way around, and Jones found himself in the box again before the sixth was over. This time the strikeout stuck. There was no wild pitch, no errant throw, no second life. He was out.
The combination is what makes the sequence historic.
According to Baseball Reference researcher Katie Sharp, Jones is the first player in major-league history, regular season or postseason, to record two strikeouts and a stolen base in the same inning.
The play-by-play record used for that search reaches back to 1910. In more than a hundred years of games, including every October series that has been logged the same way, nobody had done it.
The oddity landed inside a series New York has controlled without its captain. Aaron Judge has been unavailable, and the Yankees still won the first two games against Boston by scores of 9-0 and 9-2. Jones is not Judge, and nobody in the organization is pretending otherwise.
He is, though, another 6-foot-7 outfielder with real power, and he just turned a pair of strikeouts into a run and a stolen base in a playoff inning.
That does not decide a series against the Tampa Bay Rays, the American League’s top seed, if New York advances. It does suggest a club that has found ways to convert messy moments into something useful.
The franchise has not won a World Series since 2009. An inning that had never happened before is not a championship. It is a reminder that this October, even the failures have not stayed failures for long.

item.content:encoded:
Colin Cowherd's Aaron Judge take will catch Yankees fans' attention appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees recently punched their ticket to the ALDS with a comfortable home win over the rival Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card series, sweeping that matchup and moving on to the next round. The Yankees won this series without superstar Aaron Judge, who is still recovering from an injury suffered toward the end of the regular season.
Recently, sports media personality Colin Cowherd of FS1 weighed in on Judge with a hot take.
"Aaron Judge didn't play. Stanton didn't play. None of it mattered when you have two phenomenal pitching performances. They're not just Aaron Judge reliant anymore," said Cowherd, via Herd w/Colin Cowherd on X, formerly Twitter.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
While the Yankees certainly didn't need Judge to make quick work of the Red Sox this week, or stay afloat in the AL standings overall this year, they will more than likely need him back in order to have any realistic chance of making a run at the World Series this year, starting with their upcoming matchup against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Judge missed the majority of this season due to a ribcage injury and had only recently returned from that issue when he went down with a separate ailment, sidelining him for the Red Sox matchup and having some fans wondering if the season would crash and burn before the traditional playoffs even got underway.
However, now that the team has punched its ticket to the ALDS, fans will be scouring the internet for positive injury updates on Judge prior to Game 1.
In any case, the Rays and Yankees are set to get their series underway on Saturday at 6:30 pm ET from Tampa Bay.
Related: Why Red Sox fan Dave Portnoy called out Yankees after AL Wild Card Series

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Aaron Judge Gives Personal Injury Update Ahead of ALDS vs. Rays
item.dc:creator: Cole Sullivan
item.description: The New York Yankees have punched their ticket to the ALDS after defeating the Boston Red Sox 9-2 in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series on Wednesday night. They outscored Boston 18-2 across the two games they played, and both of the Red Sox runs came off solo home runs. Now, the Yankees are set for another real challenge as they'll begin a best-of-five series against the No. 1-seeded Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on Saturday. Aaron Judge Gives Personal Update on Injury Following the Yankees' win
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have punched their ticket to the ALDS after defeating the Boston Red Sox 9-2 in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series on Wednesday night.
They outscored Boston 18-2 across the two games they played, and both of the Red Sox runs came off solo home runs.
Now, the Yankees are set for another real challenge as they'll begin a best-of-five series against the No. 1-seeded Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on Saturday.
Aaron Judge Gives Personal Update on Injury
Following the Yankees' win, superstar Aaron Judge spoke to the media and gave a brief update on the calf injury that ultimately kept him off the 26-man roster for the Wild Card Series.
Now that the series is over, the Yankees can submit an entirely new roster for the ALDS, which could include Judge if they deem him healthy enough to play.
Judge, however, said that he did not run the bases at Somerset on Wednesday and hasn't run the bases yet, which is likely one of the major steps in his rehab. He noted that he's working every day toward a return.
"My job is to continue to get ready. That's what I've been doing every day," Judge said postgame.
Aaron Judge, while dodging champagne spritzes, said that he did not run the bases in Somerset today.
He didn’t have anything to say about his potential availability for the ALDS, other than, “My job is to continue to get ready. That’s what I’ve been doing every day.” #Yankees https://t.co/5GhWIRVrd3
— Gary Phillips (@GaryHPhillips) October 1, 2026
How Can Judge Play in ALDS?
For Judge to be eligible to play in the ALDS, the Yankees would obviously need to activate him and then add him to the 26-man roster before Saturday's game.
However, doing that would mean removing another player. Given that New York already went hitter-heavy with its pitcher-to-batter ratio for the Wild Card roster, it would likely be one of its bench bats, such as Amed Rosario or Jose Caballero. If they choose to keep the infield depth, it would have to be one of the outfielders, such as Heliot Ramos, Trent Grisham, or Spencer Jones.
The team added Giancarlo Stanton to the Wild Card roster, but he made no appearances. So, it's possible they could add Judge and let him continue rehabbing for Games 1 and 2 before bringing him back when the series heads to New York.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are moving on!!
They will face the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series, beginning this weekend.
As Aaron Judge's status is still in limbo, other players will need to step up. If manager Aaron Boone pencils Anthony Volpe in the lineup during the ALDS, he could be a difference-maker.
Recently, FanSided.com contributors made a bold Anthony Volpe prediction, and it's pretty positive.
More MLB on Heavy: Toronto Blue Jays Trade Prediction Lands 2X MLB All-Star Infielder
Anthony Volpe Predicted to Have Impact at 3B for Yankees
With George Lombard Jr. manning the reins at shortstop, if Anthony Volpe sees himself in the lineup, it will either be at third base or second.
Volpe's arm doesn't play well at third base, but that didn't stop the speculation, as the Yankees would also look much better on paper with Volpe at 3B over Ryan McMahon.
FanSided MLB director Adam Weinrib recently made the bold prediction that Volpe will be an impact player at 3B:
"The Yankees turned to Volpe out of sheer desperation, due to both Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s injury and Ryan McMahon's ineffectiveness, and the one-time punching bag was actually … pretty good in September? The offense is unremarkable but still worlds better than McMahon, and his defense has been fine at third base. New York is going to need him in October."
Anthony Volpe was in the lineup for game one against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round, but that was with a left-hander on the mound. Manager Boone has had a clear strategy when it comes to stacking the lineup with favorite hitting matchups, according to whoever the opposing starter is.
More MLB on Heavy: Houston Astros Predicted to Cut Ties with Manager Joe Espada After Quick White Sox Series
Anthony Volpe's 2026 Season At a Glance
You have to give Anthony Volpe a lot of credit for the way he's handled the 2026 season.
He started the year on the IL, which led to him not really having a starting spot in the infield, and Volpe was eventually demoted to the minors for a long stretch of the season.
After an injury to Jazz Chisholm Jr., Volpe stepped up in a few clutch moments in September for the Yankees, and he's now back in the fold, with Chisholm and Volpe platooning at 2B.
However, New York Yankees fans would be very pleased if this Anthony Volpe prediction could come to life over the next few weeks.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Announce Ben Rice Change During Red Sox Series

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees were able to complete a two-game sweep of the Boston Red Sox without Aaron Judge, but in order to make a World Series run, you can bet they'll need their captain back in the lineup.
But when could that happen?
Judge suffered a calf strain on Sept. 16, an injury that was ruled "moderate." The injury also occurred in the soleus muscle, which is connected to the Achilles tendon. Understandably, the Yankees are being extra cautious.
Just over two weeks have passed since Judge was first injured, and typically, moderate strains can take a month-and-a-half to two months to heal.
New York doesn't have that much time.
So could Judge actually return as soon as the Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays?
The Yankees will open up Game 1 of the ALDS this Saturday, and considering Judge hasn't even run the bases yet, a return in the opener seems slim to none.
However, former New York manager Joe Girardi has proposed a scenario in which the Yanks could put Judge on the ALDS roster, sit him for the first couple of games and then potentially play him later on in the series.
The Yankees did something similar with Giancarlo Stanton in the Wild Card Series. Stanton was healthy enough to make the roster, but New York didn't actually have to use him as it outscored the Red Sox 18-2 over the course of the two-game sweep.
Of course, that concept becomes a bit riskier over the course of a longer series where you might need some more pitching.
Unlike the Wild Card Series, which is a best-of-3, the Division Series is a best-of-5, so the Yankees have to be careful in how they go about constructing their roster.
Stanton will certainly be on the roster again. He has been transitioned into a pinch-hitting role for New York for his lethal October bat alone. So can the Yankees find room for Judge?
In the Wild Card Series, New York employed 16 position players and 10 pitchers. It remains to be seen how Aaron Boone goes about allocating his 26-man group for the ALDS, but there is absolutely a chance he features more pitching.
One thing is for sure: even if Judge does play, he won't be in right field. He would DH, which would move Ben Rice into a full-time role at first base and send Luis Garcia Jr. to the bench. Not a bad bat to have off the pine.
All that being said, we'll see what Boone ultimately decides ahead of Game 1. If he feels Judge isn't even close, he might not even put him on the roster.

item.title: [bolavip.com] Brian Cashman, NY Yankees’ front office earn shoutout from Gerrit Cole after eliminating Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Federico O'donnell
item.description: Much was said about the New York Yankees and the way the front office, led by general manager Brian Cashman, went about its business at the trade deadline. Many believed the Bronx Bombers didn’t do enough to truly compete in the 2026 MLB Postseason, but that was proven wrong in the AL Wild Card against the Boston Red Sox—despite Aaron Judge’s absence. Amid the champagne celebration, starting pitcher Gerrit Cole voiced an honest assessment of the work done behind closed doors by the front office.
item.content:encoded:
Much was said about the New York Yankees and the way the front office, led by general manager Brian Cashman, went about its business at the trade deadline. Many believed the Bronx Bombers didn’t do enough to truly compete in the 2026 MLB Postseason, but that was proven wrong in the AL Wild Card against the Boston Red Sox—despite Aaron Judge’s absence. Amid the champagne celebration, starting pitcher Gerrit Cole voiced an honest assessment of the work done behind closed doors by the front office.
Although the true test will come when the Yankees play the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS next, the way the squad in The Bronx has been assembled clearly didn’t go unnoticed by Cole, who praised Cashman and the Yankees’ brass after the 2-0 series win over the Red Sox.
“You’ve got to go out and buy the tools. The roster looks really good at this point. We’re very competitive, and we have a lot of different ways that we can beat you. A lot of credit goes to a lot of people in this building,” Cole stated, via Chris Kirschner of The Athletic.
NY Yankees’ lineup depth proves decisive
It’s a new day in New York, more specifically in The Bronx. Indeed, the Yankees would love to have Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton back at the plate, but they have figured things out even without those two power bats.
Gerrit Cole #45 of the New York Yankees at Yankee Stadium.
New York is no longer a home-run-dependent creature in the MLB Playoffs. The Yankees are now a depth monster, ready to drown out opponents with lengthy, grueling innings, especially when playing at home at Yankee Stadium.
Yankees’ perfect 6th inning in Game 2
It remains to be seen how this strategy stacks up against the AL East-winning Rays, but it wreaked havoc against the Red Sox. The bottom of the sixth inning in Game 2 was Aaron Boone’s team’s magnum opus so far in the postseason. The Yankees made the most of every single thing the Red Sox gave them.
A wild pitch? Spencer Jones would run his way to first. Another bad throw, and he stole two bases, setting up shop at third. From there on, the Yankees’ batters simply kept the base hits coming until it was Cody Bellinger’s turn at the plate.
The Red Sox picked their poison: They intentionally walked Ben Rice to first base. Bellinger needed just one changeup from Garrett Whitlock to decipher the code. On the second pitch, he went yard, calling game in the process as New York jumped to a game-sealing, series-ending 8-1 lead.
NY Yankees are for real in 2026 postseason
It was the perfect demonstration of how the entire lineup can come together to decide postseason games for the Pinstripers. If they could, the Yankees would hang it up on a wall at Yankee Stadium, but they don’t do that in The Bronx.
All they care about is winning the World Series, and this Yankees team, with a different recipe from years past, confirmed it can be a serious contender for the Commissioner’s Trophy in 2026. And that’s even without Judge.
Lastly, Brian Cashman, who’s been through the wringer and at the receiving end of fans’ criticism time and again, deserves credit. It’s still early for victory laps, but Cole’s shoutout to the front office’s work was well deserved.
Key takeaways
- Brian Cashman received praise from Gerrit Cole after New York eliminated Boston.
- The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-0 in the AL Wild Card series.
- Cody Bellinger hit a game-sealing home run in the sixth inning of Game 2.

item.title: [The Big Lead] Cam Schlittler names best player in MLB after Yankees sweep Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Tate Mosher

New York will next meet their division winner Tampa Bay Rays in the best-of-five ALDS. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have gotten off to an incredibly fast start to the 2026 MLB postseason. They made quick work of their arch rival Boston Red Sox in the best-of-three Wild Card series, outscoring them 18-2 in a 2-0 series win.
New York will next meet their division winner Tampa Bay Rays in the best-of-five ALDS. That series begins Saturday in Tampa Bay and continues there on Monday before coming back to the Bronx next Wednesday.
Once again, the Yankees will head into the division series on the heels of a lights-out performance from their ace right-hander Cam Schlittler. In Game 1 against Boston, he hurled 6 ⅓ scoreless innings while racking up 10 strikeouts.
Potential reinforcements
Following Wednesday’s series conclusion in Game 2, Schlittler spoke on currently injured outfielder Aaron Judge. Per Greg Joyce of the New York Post, the ace said that he believes Judge is the best player in baseball and that the club will only get stronger upon his return.
The 34-year-old appeared in just 66 games this season, missing a huge chunk of time through the summer before briefly returning in September. He unfortunately suffered a moderate calf strain Sept. 16 and has been on the injured list since.
When he was on the field, Judge admittedly was not quite playing like himself. Across 285 plate appearances, he slashed .241/.360/.511 (.871 OPS) with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs.
With the ALDS versus the Rays beginning Saturday, that will mark 17 days since Judge suffered the calf strain. Only time will tell whether he will be healthy enough to play, though there is some serious doubt on that.
Series outlook
For the Yankees side of things, it will be either righty Gerrit Cole or lefty Carlos Rodón on the mound for Game 1 of the ALDS. That choice from the club will come out in the next couple of days.
Schlittler will be on five days’ rest to pitch Game 2 on Monday, before lefty Max Fried gets the ball in Game 3 back in the Bronx. Beyond that, a prospective Games 4 and 5 do not have pitching probables.
Surprisingly enough, despite the two teams’ competitiveness over the last several years, they have yet to meet in the postseason following a normal 162-game season. It will be the first time each club has headed to the other’s venue for playoff baseball in their histories.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Cody Bellinger takes Chad Tracy's gift, ends Red Sox season in Yankees legacy moment
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows. Payton To
item.content:encoded:
Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows.
Payton Tolle getting the 83-pitch early hook in Game 1 was somewhat defensible. He was losing grip. He's past a career high in innings. They have the horses. Removing Sonny Gray from this do-or-die game before the end of the fifth inning, midway through a masterpiece, was one of the silliest bits of overmanaging you'll see. Bringing in Erik Miller, who was victimized with two outs in the fifth in Game 1 to get victimized again was even sillier.
Bellinger smoked a two-out RBI single off Miller to add a second run to the Yankees' lead. The next time he strode to the plate, he made a much larger impact.
Cody Bellinger cements Yankees' ownership of the Boston Red Sox
Gone. Very gone. In a snap, the Yankees turned two productive outs and a three-run mash into an 8-1 ballgame. Losing Garrett Whitlock, who surrendered the bomb, might've been the Yankees' most prudent Rule 5 Draft move in franchise history. It's called the long game.
For those keeping track at home, the 2026 Red Sox rode a 32-5 midsummer stretch to the postseason, reached within a half-game of the Yankees and got high on their own supply. From that point forward, they were much closer to .500, losing impact role players and stars alike by the bowlful. Sox fans were undeterred. They continued to crow. They loved to laugh at Aaron Judge's injury troubles. They purported to be inside Cam Schlittler's head. If they truly were in there, they might've been able to pick up some knowledge on what it takes for a pitcher to go deep into games in the postseason and dominate.
And so, for the second season in a row, the Yankees have flushed the Sox out of the postseason - Boston actually doesn't even reach October this year, which begins tomorrow. Last year, it was Schlittler, the Massachusetts native, growing up on the big stage. He helped this year, too.
But this time around, it ended with Tracy hooking Gray for no apparent reason and Bellinger, a son of pinstripes, delivering the crushing blow. Maybe, just maybe, order has returned to the universe and karma has begun to punish the brashness of Bostonians in new and unique ways. Whitlock gagging, Garrett Crochet disintegrating after an Adley Rutschman slow play (the trade target the Sox outbid the Yankees for, by the way), and Caleb Durbin making the final out ... in a game Gray should've owned ... was a pretty clever way to get it done.
Thanks, Belli.

item.content:encoded:
Not even the bubbly and suds that dripped down his 6-foot-7 frame late Wednesday emboldened Aaron Judge enough to make any proclamations about his chances of being on the Yankees ALDS roster.
But his teammates are at least giving him a chance.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
On a day that began with Judge going to Somerset to get another round of live at-bats and continue his running progression as he rehabs a right calf strain, the Yankees finished off a sweep of the Red Sox with a 9-2 win in Game 2 of the AL wild-card series in The Bronx.
“Saturday’s a long ways away,” Judge said, referring to Game 1 of the ALDS against the Rays. “But I’m doing everything I can, all morning, night, during the game, everything to prepare myself to be ready to go. Yeah, I want to be in there. But we’ll see what happens.”
Wednesday marked two weeks since Judge sustained the calf injury, and while he tried to defy the odds and make a late push to be on the roster for the wild-card series, the Yankees ultimately left him off because he was not ready.
Whether he can be ready to go by Saturday remains to be seen, especially with the complicating factor of having to play on the turf at Tropicana Field, which can be troublesome for players dealing with soft-tissue leg injuries.
“We just finished the wild-card [series]. We’ll get into that as we get closer,” Judge said amid the champagne celebration. “I got nothing for you on that yet, but my job is to continue to get ready. That’s what I’ve been doing every day.”
Judge’s around-the-clock treatment is apparently what kept him missing from Tuesday’s pregame player introductions ahead of Game 1. He arrived in the dugout by first pitch, and then Wednesday, pulled up a seat around the sixth inning to watch his teammates finish the win.
The three-time AL MVP said he did not run the bases Wednesday afternoon in Somerset, which is a hurdle he will likely have to clear to prove he can be a right fielder for the ALDS.
“I think it’s been encouraging that a couple nights ago [Monday] for the workout he was able to get out there for live BP,” manager Aaron Boone said before Game 2. “Again, that wasn’t just, he’s just going out for live BP. He had to check a lot of boxes for the trainers and the strength guys to say, ‘OK, you’re ready for that, you can go do that.’
Go beyond the box score with the Bombers

Thank you
“So I feel like in the couple weeks since the injury, he’s made real strides and significant improvements. And hopefully we’re in a position to make another decision in a couple of days.”
It is possible the Yankees could carry Judge on their ALDS roster to serve as a DH, but even he has acknowledged that it would be best for the team if he can return as a right fielder because of the logjam at DH/first base involving Game 1 hero Ben Rice, Luis García Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt.

item.title: [wral.com] Fried, Bellinger and García lead Yankees over Red Sox 9-2 for 2-game Wild Card Series sweep
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM
item.description: NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston. Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep. Other WRAL Top Stories “We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said. New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series start
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston.
Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep.
Other WRAL Top Stories
“We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
“The fans were electric from the first pitch and the boys were hungry. We got a young, hungry team here," Yankees captain Aaron Judge said as teammates sprayed him with bubbly during the clubhouse celebration. “This makes me feel young every single time.”
Judge missed this series because of a calf injury and isn't sure whether he will play against the Rays, who beat New York 7-6 in the season series.
“Saturday’s a long ways away," he said.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston's 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke open the game with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.
“Step one,” said Bellinger, who caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay, a 2000 Yankees World Series champion. “Now we got to go into Tampa and play against a tough team."
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, lost last year's wild-card matchup after defeating the Yankees in the opener.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series and that ended for us tonight, so it’s frustrating,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “There’s a lot of things you can say, but in the moment right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it’s going to take some time to get over that.”
Boston, which also got a seventh-inning homer from Nick Sogard off Will Warren, was missing leadoff hitter Roman Anthony because of a hand injury. The Red Sox were held to a .117 average in the series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and outscored 18-2.
New York hit .382 in the series. Boston's bullpen had a 20.25 ERA.
“We played great baseball in a lot of ways here, obviously anchored by our two great starters," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Yankees batters hit .450 (9 for 20) with runners in scoring position after finishing 19th among the 30 teams with a .246 RISP during the regular season.
“I feel like it’s a whole new level from regular season to these last two days,” Austin Wells said.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García's fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved.
Gray was disappointed he wasn't allowed to face Bellinger.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. "I would’ve liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. So I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted.”
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger's homer.
"I can’t believe they were willing to face a guy like Belli with men on base there," Rice said.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year's Wild Card Series opener, hadn't pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off Adley Rutschman's chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled that Jones was out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner's office.
“I couldn’t believe he was there,” Boone said. "I saw the ball squirt away a little bit. I didn’t think that much of it, and looked up and I was, like, 'Oh, he’s safe.'''
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Wells' sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“Definitely wasn’t sharp from the get-go but just wanted to challenge them, not try to give any free passes, especially in the first inning," Fried said.
After a night of celebration and a day off, the Yankees will head to Florida on Friday.
“There’s just so much more to do,” Bellinger said after the big night with his father on hand. “So obviously enjoy the moment, understand how cool it is, but keep on going.”
Up Next
New York RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.
___

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are hoping to advance to the ALDS (obviously) and return the services of star outfielder Aaron Judge.
Judge was left off the Yankees' Wild Card roster against the Red Sox as he continues to battle a calf injury.
If the Yankees are to advance, it's possible that Aaron Judge will return to the roster, but how long will he last?
In a recent bold prediction, FanSided.com believes that if Judge is activated to the Yankees playoff roster, it will be a short-lived move.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 3 Sudden Roster Moves Amid MLB Playoffs
Aaron Judge Handed Cryptic Prediction
In a recent piece for FanSided.com, the contributors came up with 30 bold predictions, and one of them involved Aaron Judge, per Chris Landers:
Here is the headline for the cryptic prediction:
"Aaron Judge forces his way onto the Yankees roster — but doesn't last more than a game"
"This just has disaster written all over it. Judge suffered a Grade 2 calf strain on Sept. 16; less than two weeks later, he's publicly turning up the heat on his own team to let him on the Wild Card roster anyway. I doubt New York says no to its foundational star. I also doubt Judge is ready to be an impactful player."
Landers does have a point: if Judge does return, and he even swings the wrong way, his status could be in jeopardy.
It certainly would be something if the Yankees are able to advance to the Fall Classic without their megastar in Judge, which at this particular junction, feels entirely possible.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] The New York Yankees did not need Aaron Judge to sweep the Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — For about 10 minutes, there was a ballgame.
The window opened around 9:56 p.m. ET on Wednesday. Boston first baseman Willson Contreras sliced a Max Fried fastball through the crisp Bronx air into the first row in right for a solo home run. That cut New York's lead in half. For the first time in this best-of-three wild-card series between longtime rivals, a Red Sox hitter touched home plate. And so, a glimmer of hope flickered in the visiting dugout as Game 2 flipped to the bottom of the sixth.
By 10:06 p.m., when rookie George Lombard Jr. laced an RBI single over the second baseman's head, that flame had already begun to falter. By the end of the inning, it was thoroughly extinguished.
Ten Yankees hitters came to the plate in the bottom of the sixth; six scored. Last year's AL Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, injured for nearly the entire regular season, entered as a reliever and did not record an out (though he did strike out a batter). Boston's most trusted setup man, Garrett Whitlock, then entered the ballgame to serve up the final blow: a moon-scraping, three-run homer via Cody Bellinger that pushed New York's lead to seven.
Yankee Stadium rumbled as Bellinger's ball returned to Earth. Libations sprung into the sky like a Bellagio fountain of booze. Popcorn rained from the heavens. Bellinger rounded the sacks and entered the dugout to a tunnel of high-fives and atta-boys. The rest of this lopsided laugher was merely epilogue. By the ninth inning, Yankee fans were serenading the defeated Sox with "na, na, na, na, hey, hey, hey, goodbye." A few minutes later, they were hollering Sinatra's "New York, New York" as the Yankees strolled onto the diamond in a casual celebration.
No doubt — not a crumb — was left as to which is the better team.
"Total domination," a Yankees employee could be heard saying to a colleague in the champagne-soaked afterparty.
Predictably, New York skipper Aaron Boone offered Boston its flowers, but it was incredibly telling that the first question asked to him at his postgame media conference was: "Were you surprised by the margins of victory?"
"Yes," Boone, ever the politician, replied. "As I said, kind of all year, but even going into this series, that was a scary team to us, especially as well as they pitch. So for us to have the offensive outbreaks that we had here these last two nights and late, credit to those guys."
No more than 30 minutes later, Boone could be seen stampeding past the Yankees' clubhouse with neither a shirt nor a worry in the world. Nothing about this wild-card matchup provided any reason for him or any other Yankees employee to view the Red Sox as a scary team. No, this was a drubbing.
The Yankees outscored the Red Sox 18-2 across the two games. Boston mustered seven total hits, the fewest ever in a wild-card series (this format was implemented in 2022). It was a damning, telling offensive performance by a lineup that lacked both the impact and the depth of a legitimate championship contender. And while the Sox certainly felt the absence of Roman Anthony — the young slugger was scratched from the roster after suffering a wrist injury in Game 1 — not even a resuscitated, cryogenically unfrozen Ted Williams could've helped this Boston ballclub.
"You're thinking we're going to play closer games," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy admitted postgame. "They swung the bats extremely well. You've got to give them credit. It was frustrating."
Also frustrating, for Tracy, must have been the noticeable chasm in talent between the two clubs. The Red Sox drew deserved plaudits ahead of the series for their run-prevention prowess. And yet, on paper, the Yankees' rotation looked far more dangerous. And that's how it played out, with soon-to-be Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler dicing in Game 1 and Fried cruising in Game 2.
New York's decision to roster just 10 pitchers for this series was also an indication of the organization's immense level of confidence in its staff, particularly its starters. Why enter the battle with an army when a small special-ops unit can do the job?
"That's been the biggest strength for us throughout the year," Boone said of his team's rotation. "It sustained us. It got us through some difficult times. And I feel like they're all in a good place right now."
The Yankees' lineup is also clearly in a very good place. With captain Aaron Judge off the roster and watching from the dugout in a hoodie, New York's offense impressed. In both games, the Bombers needed a few innings to get revved up but eventually bludgeoned Boston's bullpen into submission. They tallied 26 total hits, the most by the Yanks in a two-game playoff span since 2004.
Judge's status for the ALDS against Tampa Bay remains a mystery. Fellow injured large man Giancarlo Stanton was on the roster for the wild-card round but wasn't called upon for a plate appearance. The Rays will likely present a stiffer challenge than whatever this was, but New York's lineup is humming at the perfect time.
Boston, meanwhile, didn't even get to play October baseball. When closer David Bednar punched out Caleb Durbin to conclude the proceedings, the clock read 11:14 p.m. ET.
September lived on. The Red Sox did not.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Yankees set sights on tougher Rays team after embarrassing Red Sox with Wild Card sweep
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips

He talked about it with his new teammates, many of whom spoke from experience that he did not have. The New York native got his first taste on Tuesday, going 0-for-1 off the bench in the Yankees’ easy 9-0 win over the Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series. But on Wednesday, he made his mark in his first postseason start, hammering a Sonny Gray sweeper in
item.content:encoded:
Ever since the Yankees acquired Luis García Jr. on Aug. 3, the former National pictured what postseason baseball would look and feel like. He talked about it with his new teammates, many of whom spoke from experience that he did not have.
The New York native got his first taste on Tuesday, going 0-for-1 off the bench in the Yankees’ easy 9-0 win over the Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series. But on Wednesday, he made his mark in his first postseason start, hammering a Sonny Gray sweeper in the fourth inning of Game 2.
The solo shot jumpstarted an offense that ensured there would not be a Game 3, as the Yankees cruised to a 9-2 victory after García got them on the board. Complete with an animated bat flip, he sparked the dugout’s first celebration of the night.
“It’s unforgettable to be in the middle of all that,” said García, draped in a towel. “I’m sure it’s something I’m not gonna forget.”
With Cody Bellinger adding a three-run homer in the sixth and Max Fried holding Boston to one earned run over six innings, the party eventually moved to the mound and then the home clubhouse at Yankee Stadium. There, the boozy Bombers celebrated a rather smooth sweep of their embarrassed archrivals with bubbly and beers.
“That was a scary team to us, especially as well as they pitch. So for us to have the offensive outbreaks that we had here these last two nights and late, credit to those guys,” Aaron Boone said. “That was very satisfying to play that well in these two games.”
Now another division foe awaits in the ALDS, and a tougher one at that.
The Yankees already know how formidable the Rays, their next playoff opponent, are, as the pinstripers failed to win the American League East for the second straight season because of Tampa Bay. Despite a luxury tax payroll that fell $228.9 million short of the Yankees’, the Rays finished the season with the AL’s best record at 98-64 and earned a first-round bye in the postseason.
The Yankees’ meanwhile, ended up 93-68, settling for the top Wild Card spot and a rematch with the overmatched Red Sox.
Cam Schlittler, who shoved in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, said it was “frustrating” to lose the AL East to the Rays, but he tipped his hat to them, too.
“They’ve been great all year,” said Schlittler, who is expected to start Game 2 of the ALDS. “We had opportunities to take the [division] lead, and we couldn’t get that done.”
But, he said, “We’re on a roll at the right time.”
While the Yankees are hot after beating up on Boston, the rested Rays, who celebrated their division crown in the Bronx on Sept. 22, have home field advantage in the best-of-five ALDS. Carried by its quickness, pitching staff and Junior Caminero’s rising star, Tampa also has the comfort of knowing that it won the season series against the Yankees, 7-6.
“They bring speed to the game,” said Carlos Rodón, a candidate to start Game 1 of the ALDS alongside Gerrit Cole. “They have some good pitching. They play good defense. They’ll take the extra bag. They’re gonna be running. They’re gonna be bunting. You don’t see that in the game much anymore, but it’s worked for them. They’re a solid club. They play well, so it should be a good series.”
“It’s going to be a tough series,” Bellinger added.
If the Yankees are lucky, a reinforcement or two will join them in Florida for the showdown. Ryan Weathers, working his way back from a flexor strain as a reliever, could be one of them.
Getting Aaron Judge back would be a much bigger deal, however, after the back-to-back MVP watched the Wild Card Series from the bench in a jacket and a hoodie.
The Yankees managed to take Boston down without the captain after a right calf strain kept Judge off their Wild Card roster. On Wednesday, Boone said it’s “too early to tell” if Judge will be available for Game 1 of the ALDS, which begins on Saturday.
The manager added that Tampa Bay’s turfed Tropicana Field “could” factor into the Yankees’ decision with Judge having yet to run the bases. That call, however, is still a few days away from being made after the Yankees bought themselves some time with a quick Wild Card Series.
Judge, who lobbied to be on the Wild Card roster, declined to talk about his potential availability for the ALDS. But the slugger, who also missed 99 days with a fractured rib this season, did take a moment to praise what his peers have accomplished thus far.
“I’ve been so proud of these guys,” Judge said as he dodged champagne spritzes. “I’ve been out for quite a long time this season, and they never wavered. They never took a step back. They just kept going forward.”
“When the Yankees win, we all win. So it doesn’t matter if you played, didn’t play, hit the game-winning hit, pitched a shutout. We’re all wearing ‘NY’ in this room. That’s why we’re all celebrating together.”

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Luis Garcia Jr. has first Yankees moment in series-clinching win vs. Red Sox
item.dc:creator: James O'Connell

Never thought I was going to be part of [the Red Sox-Yankees rivalry in the postseason],” Garcia said before Game 2. “But my mom has a
item.content:encoded:
If you would’ve told Luis Garcia Jr. before this season what he’d be doing on Sept. 30, he probably wouldn’t believe you.
That’s because the 26-year-old was slated to bat in the middle of the order for the lowly Washington Nationals, who had virtually no aspirations of competing, with October as a good target month for a postseason vacation.
“No, no, not at all. Never thought I was going to be part of [the Red Sox-Yankees rivalry in the postseason],” Garcia said before Game 2. “But my mom has a good saying, and she’s always telling me never stop dreaming.”
Garcia delivered one of the biggest swings of the night for the Yankees in their Game 2 victory on Wednesday to eliminate the Boston Red Sox and advance from the Wild Card series to the ALDS to take on the Tampa Bay Rays.
The slugger launched a solo shot in the bottom of the fourth off of Red Sox starter Sonny Gray — who was cruising early — to jumpstart the Bombers offense that delivered another strong performance in their 9-2 victory, and hand them a much-needed early lead against an opponent that was on the ropes.
Garcia tossed his bat into the air and celebrated his first postseason moonshot.
“Not a lot is going through my mind in that moment. It’s just a reaction,” said Garcia. “But I could tell you what’s going through my body is just pure happiness. Being able to come through for the team, being able to put this team ahead in that moment, you’re just feeling joy as you’re running.”
It was Garcia’s first career homer in his first postseason start. He did get a taste of the playoffs during Tuesday’s victory, however, he was limited to just one pinch hit appearance.
On Wednesday, Garcia was one of the main reasons for the fans excitement in the Bronx. The left-handed hitter went 3-for-5 with a homer and two singles.
“It’s unforgettable, to be in the middle of all of that,” Garcia said. “Like I mentioned before the game, fans are standing from the first pitch until the last. Being in the middle of it and just taking it all in, I’m sure it’s something I’m not going to forget.”
The first baseman entered the postseason struggling mightily as he slashed .229/.250/.343 in 19 games during September. However, it was largely a solid run for Garcia during his first stint with the Yankees as he posted a .736 OPS in 43 games with the team.
Garcia is expected to pick up a bulk of the offensive load left behind by the injured Aaron Judge, who’s status remains uncertain heading into the upcoming series against the Rays.
Aaron Boone will almost certainly continue to pencil Garcia’s name into the third spot in the order, especially against right-handed pitching, for as long as this postseason run continues for the Yankees.

item.title: [New York Post] Spencer Jones’ unheralded speed at center of game-altering Yankees inning
item.dc:creator: Dan Martin
item.description:
The Yankees have always insisted Spencer Jones was more than just a power hitter. They also praised his quickness and athleticism.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees have always insisted Spencer Jones was more than just a power hitter.
They also praised his quickness and athleticism.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
It was that latter part that was on display in Wednesday’s Game 2 wild-card-clinching 9-2 win in The Bronx.
With the Yankees clinging to a two-run lead, Jones led off the bottom of the sixth against Garrett Crochet, one of the game’s premier lefty pitchers, just coming back from a five-month absence because of a shoulder injury.
Jones whiffed, but Crochet badly bounced the third strike, and it got away from Adley Rutschman.
Jones hustled down the line, and after initially being ruled out, reached first when the call was overturned.
“When he gets it going, he can really go,’’ Aaron Boone said.
The 6-foot-7 Jones then attempted to steal second, and Rutschman’s throw went into center, allowing Jones to get to third.
With the infield in, fellow rookie George Lombard Jr. drove in Jones with a single to spark a six-run inning.
“Speed is something I’ve always had,’’ Jones said. “I’m glad it worked out. It was a fun night.”
There have been a few of those lately for the 25-year-old, who has contributed in numerous ways down the stretch after getting off to a 4-for-24 start with 12 strikeouts in his first 10 games in the majors.
When Jones returned to The Bronx later in the season, he had improved his approach at the plate and showed he could hit in the majors.
Jim Hendry, special assistant to GM Brian Cashman — who was among the Yankee scouts who evaluated Jones while he was at Vanderbilt — said the fast development shouldn’t come as much of a surprise.
“Big guys like that, it takes them longer to adjust,’’ Hendry said prior to the game. “Sure, they’re gonna strike out a lot. They’ve got more holes to figure out how to fix. But you know when they do, they can be special.”
As Hendry noted, the Yankees “have always liked big players.”
Still, there aren’t many examples of players Jones’ size hitting well, with Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton being two exceptions.
Jones is trying to become another, and the Yankees have seen some promising signs in the second half of the season.
As they’ve dealt with the lengthy absence of Judge because of rib and calf injuries, multiple injuries to Trent Grisham, as well as another disappointing season from Jasson Domínguez, Jones has been thrust into an important role.
In Game 1, the Yankees went with the lefty-swinging Jones against left-hander Payton Tolle.
Shop Yankees Merch
He had a pair of solid at-bats against Tolle, and Aaron Boone said Wednesday that he considered having Giancarlo Stanton pinch hit for Jones to lead off the bottom of the seventh against another southpaw, Alec Gamboa.
Instead, Boone stayed with Jones, who singled.
Among the reasons Boone stuck with Jones was the success he’d had versus lefties in the majors — just part of what’s developing into a well-rounded game for the former first-round pick.
“It’s hard in the modern game to hit when you’re 6-foot-7,’’ Hendry said. “But when you do it well, you don’t have to worry about launch and other things. When you’re that big, the ball lifts itself. He’s still got a lot of work to do, but he’s becoming a good player already.”

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Cody Bellinger hit a three-run homer during a six-run sixth inning and finished with four RBIs as the New York Yankees pulled away for a 9-2 rout of the Boston Red Sox on Wednesday and a two-game sweep of an American League wild-card series.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox in the wild-card round for the second straight year and were significantly more prolific at the plate than last year, when they needed three games to advance.
Despite the absence of Aaron Judge, who has a strained right calf, New York scored 18 runs and totaled 26 hits in the series to advance to the AL Division Series against the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays. The best-of-five ALDS begins Saturday in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Bellinger capped New York’s big inning by hitting a 1-0 changeup from Garrett Whitlock into the right-center-field seats after the Red Sox opted to intentionally walk Ben Rice. The blast pushed New York’s lead to 8-1.
In the fifth, Bellinger chopped an RBI single against left-hander Erik Miller over second baseman Nick Sogard’s head to give the Yankees a 2-0 lead.
New York’s Max Fried (1-0) followed Cam Schlittler’s dominance in the series opener by allowing one run on three hits in six innings on Wednesday. Fried struck out six and walked one.
Luis Garcia Jr. also homered for the Yankees, connecting against Sonny Gray’s 1-2 sweeper while leading off the fourth to open the scoring.
The Yankees sent 10 to the plate against Garrett Crochet and Whitlock in their big inning, getting things started with rookie Spencer Jones hustling around the bases.
Jones started things by reaching on a wild-pitch strikeout when he beat catcher Adley Rutschman’s throw by a step on a call that was overturned on replay after the Yankees challenged. Jones then stole second, advanced to third on Rutschman’s throwing error and scored on George Lombard Jr.’s single.
After singles by Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham loaded the bases, Whitlock replaced Crochet. Austin Wells lifted a sacrifice fly, and Ryan McMahon followed with a soft RBI groundout for a 5-1 lead.
Willson Contreras homered off Fried in the sixth, and Nick Sogard homered off Will Warren in the seventh.
Wells added an RBI single in the bottom of the seventh.
Gray (0-1) allowed two runs on six hits in 4 2/3 innings, with five strikeouts and no walks. Crochet made his first appearance since April 25, having recovered from a shoulder ailment, and was charged with four runs without recording an out.
The Red Sox finished with seven hits in the series and experienced a disappointing end to a season where they overcame firing their manager in April and having a 32-46 record in late June. Boston vaulted into playoff contention with a 32-5 surge that included a 15-game winning streak but struggled at the plate in the final month.

item.title: [bolavip.com] NY Yankees clear up confusion around Aaron Judge with reassuring update
item.dc:creator: Federico O'donnell
item.description: The New York Yankees sparked confusion around Aaron Judge during player introductions ahead of Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox. While several non-roster players were announced to the fans at Yankee Stadium, Judge, the franchise player, wasn’t. Immediately, the fanbase in The Bronx started panicking over what it might mean not only for the 2026 MLB Postseason but looking ahead to the offseason, too. However, before Yankees fans could run away with all sorts of theorie
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees sparked confusion around Aaron Judge during player introductions ahead of Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox. While several non-roster players were announced to the fans at Yankee Stadium, Judge, the franchise player, wasn’t.
Immediately, the fanbase in The Bronx started panicking over what it might mean not only for the 2026 MLB Postseason but looking ahead to the offseason, too. However, before Yankees fans could run away with all sorts of theories, manager Aaron Boone explained the real reason Judge wasn’t introduced along with the rest of his clubhouse teammates.
“Aaron Judge missed the pregame intros because he was receiving treatment, Aaron Boone said,” as reported by Bryan Hoch of MLB.com on X. “Judge is in Somerset today taking live at-bats.“
Positive news for NY Yankees
Although every fan in The Bronx will agree Judge should take any chance he can to get treatment and rehab for his calf strain, some didn’t appreciate the fact that Judge wasn’t out on the field with the rest of the team for player introductions before the series against Boston. “He couldn’t take a break, pause or start it later?” a fan replied to the update.
Manager Aaron Boone #17 of the New York Yankees walks back to the dugout.
Still, the majority of the fanbase was pleased to learn there were no sketchy things happening inside the clubhouse and that it was simply a bad-timing issue. Many feared Judge missing the player introductions was related to Boone’s explanation of Judge’s absence for the Wild Card against the Red Sox and that there might be some sort of rift inside the locker room. That appears to be out of the question.
Judge prioritizes his return
Instead, it’s an encouraging sign to learn Judge is still making progress and getting himself ready to return at some point in the 2026 MLB Postseason. In order to do so, however, the Yankees must defeat the Red Sox, and they already know what will happen if they win, tie, or lose in Game 2 of the Wild Card.
Any buzz of a divide between Judge and the rest of the team should be put to rest. In fact, Judge was in the dugout to watch the action and cheer on his teammates during Game 1’s statement 9-0 victory for the home team.
Key takeaways
- Aaron Judge missed pregame intros because he was receiving treatment for a calf strain.
- The franchise player was in Somerset taking live at-bats to prepare his return.
- He remained in the dugout to support the Yankees during their 9-0 victory in Game 1.

item.title: [New York Daily News] It’s ‘too early’ to know if Yankees will have Aaron Judge for potential ALDS
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: With the Yankees one win away from advancing to the ALDS, Aaron Boone wasn’t sure if he would have Aaron Judge for the potential showdown with the Rays. “Probably too early to tell,” Boone said Wednesday when asked if Judge could return should the Yankees pick up another Wild Card win over the Red Sox. Judge, recovering from a moderate right calf strain that he suffered on Sept. 16, went to Double-A Somerset to face live pitching on Tuesday. Boone, speaking before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series,
item.content:encoded:
With the Yankees one win away from advancing to the ALDS, Aaron Boone wasn’t sure if he would have Aaron Judge for the potential showdown with the Rays.
“Probably too early to tell,” Boone said Wednesday when asked if Judge could return should the Yankees pick up another Wild Card win over the Red Sox.
Judge, recovering from a moderate right calf strain that he suffered on Sept. 16, went to Double-A Somerset to face live pitching on Tuesday. Boone, speaking before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, wasn’t sure who threw to Judge. The manager said the potential options included Luis Gil, Eli Morgan and Justin Topa.
Boone also wasn’t sure what, if any, running Judge did on Wednesday. On Tuesday, the skipper said that Judge would have to run the bases before he could be “a full player” for the Yankees.
On Wednesday, Boone also didn’t rule out the idea that the Rays’ home could impact whether the Yankees roster Judge for the ALDS. Tropicana Field has a turf field, the type of surface that isn’t kind to lower-body and leg injuries. Even when Judge is healthy, Boone tries to get him a DH day or two at The Trop when possible.
“I guess that could [make an impact],” Boone said, “but we’ll see where we are in hopefully making that decision in a couple days.”
In addition to baserunning — Judge did do some light running and agility work in the outfield at Yankee Stadium on Tuesday — the back-to-back MVP still needs to do defensive work. Judge did face live pitching during Monday’s pre-postseason workout, too.
“He had to check a lot of boxes for the trainers and the strength guys to say, ‘OK, you’re ready for that, you can go do that,’” Boone said. “I feel like in the couple weeks since the injury, he’s made real strides and significant improvements. Hopefully, we’re in a position to make another decision in a couple of days.”
Aside from Judge’s rehab plans, Boone also addressed the slugger’s absence from pregame introductions on Tuesday. Judge’s name noticeably wasn’t called as the Yankees took to the first base line — others left off the Wild Card roster participated — but Boone indicated he was getting treatment.
“I didn’t even know until it happened,” Boone said. “But I think a couple of the injured guys weren’t involved in it. But I think he was getting treatment stuff.”

He did not join teammates along the first-base line for introductions b
item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Aaron Judge Takes Swings in Double-A Park, Eyes Postseason Return
Yankees captain Aaron Judge went to Somerset, New Jersey, for live batting practice Wednesday as he tries to work his way back from a leg injury to be available later in the postseason should New York advance.
Sidelined since Sept. 16 by a strained right calf, Judge was not included on the roster for the AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox. He did not join teammates along the first-base line for introductions before the Yankees' 9-0 win in Tuesday's opener of the best-of-three series.
"I think he was getting treatment," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Judge ran in the outfield before Tuesday night's game and on Wednesday went to the ballpark of the Yankees' Double-A farm team to hit. He was due back at Yankee Stadium to watch Game 2 on Wednesday night.
Aaron Judge has been sidelined since Sept. 16 with a strained right calf, Judge was not included on the roster for the AL Wild Card Series against the Boston Red Sox. (Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
If New York advances to a best-of-five Division Series against Tampa Bay, it would start Saturday.
"Probably too early to tell," Boone said of Judge's potential availability.
A three-time AL MVP, Judge was limited to 66 games this season. The 34-year-old slugger hit .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs in September.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers, sidelined with a left forearm flexor strain since Aug. 22, was to throw a bullpen at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday.
Boone said right-hander Clarke Schmidt won't pitch again this year. The 30-year-old relieved on Sept. 16 at Minnesota in his first big league appearance since Tommy John surgery on July 11, 2025, then was put on the injured list with right biceps inflammation.
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Yankees flex homegrown muscle in Game 1 win vs. Red Sox: ‘All of us came up with one another in a way’
item.dc:creator: James O'Connell
item.description: The Yankees’ domestic scouting department is certainly giving itself a pat on the back after Tuesday night. The Bombers defeated the Boston Red Sox 9-0 in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card series, and it was a homegrown victory in every sense. On top of Cam Schlittler’s continued dominance, the Yankees offense was carried by five of their own draft picks, one of which enters the postseason as the engine of their offense. Ben Rice continued his superb season into the playoffs, going 4-for-5
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ domestic scouting department is certainly giving itself a pat on the back after Tuesday night.
The Bombers defeated the Boston Red Sox 9-0 in Game 1 of the American League Wild Card series, and it was a homegrown victory in every sense.
On top of Cam Schlittler’s continued dominance, the Yankees offense was carried by five of their own draft picks, one of which enters the postseason as the engine of their offense.
Ben Rice continued his superb season into the playoffs, going 4-for-5 with two homers and six RBIs. Rice’s first homer of the night came in the sixth inning off of reliever Erik Miller into Monument Park to extend the Bombers’ lead to 2-0 — although it felt much larger with the way Schlittler was dealing. His second shot sealed the deal with a grand slam in the bottom of the eighth to put the finishing touches on the Bo Sox.
“He pummeled pitches all night,” said manager Aaron Boone. “They went after him a little bit and he made them pay. I mean, some great left-on-left at-bats, the double to right-center smoke, the homer out the front door in Monument Park. And an exclamation point there at the end. Just a big-time night by a great hitter.”
It was the 27th multi-homer game in Yankees postseason history and in the absence of Aaron Judge, they’ll need more performances just like that. Rice slashed .264/.363/.534 with 41 homers and 97 RBI during the regular season, so offensive output was somewhat expected and crucial this postseason.
However, the same can’t be said for his fellow homegrown Yankees who ignited their offense in the second inning off of Red Sox starter Payton Tolle.
George Lombard Jr., Anthony Volpe and Austin Wells — all three being former first-round picks of the club — were at the center of a crucial rally to get the Yanks on the board in a game where offense was a premium.
Lombard started off the frame with a bloop single to center and was followed up by a bullet line drive into left-center by Anthony Volpe to set up first and second with one out.
While another of their former first-rounders, Spencer Jones, popped out, it set up Wells for a clutch two-out RBI single to give the Yanks a 1-0 lead that they carried all the way through to being just one win away from advancing to the ALDS.
“Yeah, it’s super fun,” said Rice about the homegrown guys’ contributions. “All of us came up with one another in a way. There was some overlap. Maybe a couple guys were ahead of others. But now we’re all here in the big leagues. And it’s been so cool seeing each guy have success and carve out their own role.
“Definitely a tight-knit group, and we take pride in that.”
It wasn’t exactly the smoothest season for any of the three players. Lombard. had a tough transition to the bigs, committing seven errors at shortstop and posting a .696 OPS, Volpe was up-and-down between Triple-A after losing his job as the Yankees shortstop and Wells had a brutal year batting .186 with a .624 OPS.
As they say, nothing matters when the playoff starts, and it seems the unexpected contributors took that as a fresh slate.
Lombard collected three singles while Volpe’s lone hit came in the second. Jones added a single of his own to leadoff the seventh that led to yet another rally that included a single from Wells and an RBI single from Rice to take a 3-0 lead.
All in all, their homegrown kids combined for 11 of their 12 hits on Tuesday night and the Bombers will need plenty of more contributions from their kids throughout the postseason, especially from Rice, Lombard, Wells and Jones, who are expected to start most games throughout their run.
Volpe, who started at second base, will likely take a seat for Jazz Chisholm Jr. in Game 2 with right-hander Sonny Gray on the mound, but still figures to have a vital role for this team in the postseason — especially against left-handed pitching.

item.title: [New York Post] Ben Rice delivers otherworldly night to carry Yankees’ offense in Game 1 win
item.dc:creator: Dan Martin
item.description:
For so much of this season that’s seen Aaron Judge sidelined with injuries, Ben Rice was the driving force of the Yankees lineup. So why should the first game of the playoffs, with Judge still out with a strained calf, be any different?
