item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are nearing the end of the 2026 MLB regular season as they await their postseason debut. The matchup against the Boston Red Sox could be more challenging than many expect, especially with Aaron Boone not viewing Aaron Judge as fully ready for his return.
According to what The New York Post Sports’ Greg Joyce revealed on X, the manager said that Judge has been doing some plyos and has been on the treadmill, but “not a whole lot yet.” It appears that No. 99 still does not have a guaranteed return in the near future.
The Bronx Bombers face a tough Wild Card matchup against the Red Sox, a historic rival who the Yankees know very well from their battles in the AL East. Having Judge back on the field could potentially tip the scales in Boone’s favor, but not at any cost.
Judge’s injury struggles this season
It’s been a brutal, injury-plagued 2026 campaign for Aaron Judge. After missing more than three months with a fractured right rib that kept him sidelined from late May until early September, he barely got seven games under his belt before getting bit by the injury bug again.
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees looks on.
This time, a moderate right calf strain landed him right back on the injured list, requiring a plasma injection and leaving Aaron Boone uncertain about whether he will be able to count on his star player at the start of the playoffs.
The Yankees have their eyes on the playoffs
The Yankees are closing out the 2026 regular season today, September 27, hosting the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium. Once Game 162 is in the books, all eyes turn directly to October baseball: New York secured the #4 seed and will host the rival Boston Red Sox in a high-stakes, best-of-three Wild Card clash right in the Bronx.
That series kicks off on Tuesday, September 29, with Game 2 on Wednesday, September 30, and a deciding Game 3 on Thursday, October 1 if necessary. If Aaron Boone’s men manage to advance past Boston, they’ll move on to the American League Division Series to square off against the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays.
Key takeaways
- Aaron Boone indicated Aaron Judge is doing treadmill work but is not fully ready.
- The star slugger missed more than three months with a fractured right rib.
- The Yankees secured the #4 seed and will host the Red Sox on Tuesday, September 29.

item.title: [amNewYork] Yankees-Red Sox Wild Card preview: Big questions looming for both NY, Boston | amNewYork
item.dc:creator: Joe Pantorno; Amnewyork
item.description: Another October begins with baseball’s greatest rivalry clashing in the Bronx, as the Yankees host the Boston Red Sox for a second straight year in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series, beginning on Tuesday night. Taking advantage of a significantly subpar American League, the Yankees managed to tread water without Aaron Judge for more than half of the season, finishing second in the East behind the Tampa Bay Rays. Behind them in third were the Red Sox, who fired their manager, Ale
item.content:encoded:
Another October begins with baseball’s greatest rivalry clashing in the Bronx, as the Yankees host the Boston Red Sox for a second straight year in the best-of-three American League Wild Card Series, beginning on Tuesday night.
Taking advantage of a significantly subpar American League, the Yankees managed to tread water without Aaron Judge for more than half of the season, finishing second in the East behind the Tampa Bay Rays. Behind them in third were the Red Sox, who fired their manager, Alex Cora, in April following a miserable start, then caught fire in the summer behind a historic 15-game winning streak to grasp onto the No. 2 Wild Card spot and never let go.
The Yankees will hope that history repeats itself in 2026 and that they can find a way to get past their bitter rivals at home, but there are a remarkable number of huge questions looming over this series for both teams that can turn the tide before a single pitch is even thrown.
Let’s take a look.
Will the Judge preside over his court?
The Yankees’ captain and two-time-defending American League MVP missed three months earlier this summer due to a fractured rib, then lasted just seven days before suffering a “moderate” calf strain, as described by manager Aaron Boone.
All signs point to Judge not being a part of New York’s Wild Card roster, which in part was fueled by Boone last week when he said that the team was not planning on the 34-year-old slugger being available. But Judge pushed back on that, saying, “I’m doing everything I can every single day I show up here to get back and be ready to go.”
Boone disclosed on Sunday that Judge has been doing plyometrics and treadmill work, but other than that, “not a whole lot yet.” That certainly does not bode well for his availability, as he would likely be significantly compromised even if he was available.
Who starts Game 1?
In a short, best-of-three series, it’s usually a no-brainer to go with your ace in an attempt to do everything possible to get the quickest advantage possible. That, in turn, would mean Cam Schlittler, who posted one of the greatest single-season stat lines ever by a Yankees pitcher (1.95 ERA, 239 strikeouts), would get the ball for Game 1 on Tuesday, right?
Not so fast, says Boone.
The Yankees’ skipper is considering starting southpaw Max Fried for Game 1, meaning Schlittler would start Game 2 to either clinch or keep his team’s season alive.
In fairness, Fried has been great since returning from the IL in late July. Over his last 10 starts, he has a 2.29 ERA with 54 strikeouts in 51 innings. He has also allowed just one earned run in 11.2 innings against the Red Sox this season.
Schlittler has had mixed results against Boston this year, but most recently went 5.2 shutout frames on Aug. 28 despite walking five. Still, it was his heroics in Game 3 of the Wild Card Series last year that put the young righty on the map, going eight scoreless innings and striking out 12 in what was a 4-0 win.
Carlos Rodon, who has been red-hot to end the season, to the tune of a 1.89 ERA over the last five weeks, should get the ball for a potential Game 3, meaning the struggling Gerrit Cole might not be in the Yankees’ equation until a possible ALDS matchup with the Rays.
Will the Sox be without their biggest bat?
Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras’ career-best season was cut short on Sept. 17 when he was hit on the right hand by a pitch. Not only has he not appeared in a game since, but he recently experienced a setback while taking swings, then divulged that he still cannot grip a bat.
“It’s really concerning,” Contreras told reporters on Thursday. “But at the same time, I’m putting all my effort, and everything I can do, I’m doing it. I don’t know what else to say. I’m working hard with the trainers; the hand is slowly getting better, but I haven’t been able to swing the last two days. I’ll be honest with the team. I know Tuesday is a really important game. It’s a really important series, and I’ll be completely honest with the team.”
The Red Sox are already going to be without Mickey Gasper, who suffered what Red Sox manager Chad Tracy described as a “significant biceps injury” on Friday. The 30-year-old first baseman/catcher/DH had been red-hot as of late, coming out of nowhere to hit 10 home runs with a 1.082 OPS over his last 33 games before the injury. He would have been the obvious Wild Card replacement for Contreras, who owned a .905 OPS with 27 home runs and 81 RBI in 129 games this season.
For more on the Yankees, visit AMNY.com

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Brian Cashman is once again learning the hard way about Yankees' annual trade deadline failures
item.dc:creator: Colin Keane
item.description: New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent the 2026 trade deadline adding offense. With Aaron Judge still out and Giancarlo Stanton permanently MIA, it made some sense on paper to add bats like Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos. You know what didn't make sense? Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankee
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent the 2026 trade deadline adding offense. With Aaron Judge still out and Giancarlo Stanton permanently MIA, it made some sense on paper to add bats like Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos.
You know what didn't make sense? Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankees have been running arms like Brent Headrick and Fernando Cruz into the ground all season long.
Not surprisingly, Headrick is beginning to show signs of fatigue (he is human, after all), and Cruz is now injured. The Yankees are signing no-name arms to stay afloat, and Cashman deserves blame for this situation. At least New York Post's Joel Sherman is seeing things clearly.
Brian Cashman thought he could get away with Yankees current bullpen
Are Yankees really still hoping that arms like the untrustworthy Luis Gil or the recovering Clarke Schmidt will help make this crisis go away? That's where we're at entering October, and it's sad.
This roster has a ton of talent, and the American League is decidedly weak this season. But since Cashman ignored the pitching staff at the deadline, their World Series chances have no doubt taken a hit.
While the overachieving Tampa Bay Rays held off the Yankees and Red Sox, and New York deserves credit for emerging from the "grave danger zone" of losing ground to Boston, this front office oversight still doomed them to the Wild Card. Cruz's injury alone doesn't prove this, by the way — he'd been awful since the All-Star break. Anyone watching the Yankees has been able to see that their bullpen has slowly been breaking down. It was happening way before the deadline! It's a miracle things aren't much worse.
Fans can't be too shocked at Cashman's performance (or lack thereof). This has become an annual tradition. He makes false assumptions that the Yankees have enough depth in a certain area (oftentimes the pitching staff), and they never do. He hates purchasing insurance, despite evidence to the contrary that this team underachieves in August (almost every year) and enters the playoffs wounded and tired.
Getting to the postseason has never been a problem for the Yankees during the Cashman era. It's the whole advancing once they get there that's been consistently disappointing, and you can trace that back to Cashman's deadline every season.
Max Fried came back earlier than expected. Great! Schmidt vacillated between being close and injured. Splendid! None of that changes the fact that Cashman should have added reinforcements at the deadline and failed to do so. The script is so familiar at this point. Fans just want something different for once.

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge playing isn't just about Aaron Judge. It's about making the whole roster work around him.
Judge is most effective in right field, and since he's dealing with a calf strain, that could be problematic if the New York Yankees toss him out there. Whether he plays or not, that leaves Aaron Boone with one of his tougher decisions, and since it feels more likely that Judge won't play unless he can somehow force his way in, right field could get a little messy.
Right field is a major Yankees concern ahead of first playoff series
Lately, Boone's best option in right field has been Heliot Ramos, who's mostly been a bust since the trade deadline, aside from a few moments. For the last two nights, his glove has been an adventure—not in a good way—and it's clear outfield depth is needed right about now.
Unfortunately, there aren't many remedies unless Ramos suddenly turns it around defensively. Based on this week, though, it probably isn't happening.
On Wednesday night, Ramos was late to a ball, and not only did it fall in front of him, but he also bobbled it. This allowed the runner Jonny DeLuca to reach second base on a ball that went all of 202 feet.
Ramos had another gaffe on Thursday night. Taylor Walls was rounding second after a Yandy Diaz single, and when Ramos got to it, he attempted to gun Walls down at third. Instead, the ball sailed on him, went past Amed Rosario, and Walls scored.
Right field at Yankee Stadium isn't the most complex outfield situation. Hence why, when they acquired Juan Soto, who has never been a good outfielder by any defensive metric, they stuck him out there.
If Ramos can't handle it, they have a problem, and since they probably don't want to hinder Judge's calf any more than it already is, they might have to go with somebody out of position.
José Caballero is one name. He has had experience in right field, too.
Last season he had 2 Outs Above Average and 6 Defensive Runs Saved in right in 210.2 innings. This year, he's played just 60.1 innings and has been a neutral defender there, with 0 OAA and 0 DRS. A neutral defender feels like they're sporting Judge's defensive prowess out there, seeing as Ramos has a -4 OAA and -1 DRS in right.
Another name they can go with is Trent Grisham. Grisham, unfortunately, has been compromised due to a hamstring issue, but at this point, he might not have the mobility for center, so right field could be the way to go for him. It's much less ground for him to cover, and if he plays right, that could let Caballero play more of a position of need, like third base.
In this case, it's a matter of who they trust to hit against Boston's lefties more: Ryan McMahon or Grisham, who is fresh off the IL without a rehab assignment. This one, of course, is more outside the box, and the Caballero one feels more likely than Grisham covering right.
That isn't even something Boone has broached in his daily meetings with reporters. At the same time, Caballero has had some outfield experience over the last week, playing center field against the Diamondbacks.
In a perfect world, it would just be Judge out there in right field. Since they're thin on outfielders, and Ramos hasn't been any good out there, they might have to get resourceful defensively as they head into the Wild Card round. These are things you wish the Yankees had figured out earlier, but Boone will have to navigate what's happening.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

They had Volpe start at the hot corner Friday for the first time in his big league career, and by the end of the 10-2 loss to the Orioles in the opener of a doubleheader, he was still waiting for his first real chance.

item.content:encoded:
If the Yankees want to ensure they do not have a ball hit to third base against them in the playoffs, perhaps they should just put Anthony Volpe there.
They had Volpe start at the hot corner Friday for the first time in his big league career, and by the end of the 10-2 loss to the Orioles in the opener of a doubleheader, he was still waiting for his first real chance.

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
A ball was finally hit to third base in the ninth inning, except it hit the bag and flew over Volpe’s head, giving him no shot to make a play.
Otherwise, nothing came his way, and while he could start there again Sunday if the Yankees are not washed out, Aaron Boone still considered the game valuable for Volpe.
“Not a lot of action over there, but there’s something to be said for being in there and thinking through the situations and moving and setting up how you’re supposed to,” said Boone, who started Volpe at shortstop in the nightcap.
Volpe seems unlikely to start at third base in the playoffs, but he played there Friday so he could at least have it in his back pocket, which would give him even more positional flexibility after making the transition from shortstop to second base at Triple-A.
Having that versatility could allow the Yankees to get more aggressive in using pinch hitters and pinch runners in the AL Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“I felt comfortable,” said Volpe, who credited third baseman Ryan McMahon, infield coach Dan Fiorito, Triple-A infield coach Gil Velasquez and former teammate Oswaldo Cabrera for helping him get up to speed at the position.
“No matter where you play, you got to anticipate and know where you got to be. I feel like I’ve picked it up.”
Before Friday’s doubleheader, the Yankees held the equivalent of postseason tryouts — or perhaps prove-its — as Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham faced Ryan Weathers, with all three trying to show they are healthy enough and ready to be on the wild-card roster.
Weathers, throwing one inning and about 20 pitches, was facing hitters for the first time suffering a left forearm flexor strain last month. Doing so Friday leaves the door open for him to be on the roster next week, which would give the bullpen a power lefty.
“He looks healthy, that’s what I took away,” Boone said. “Looks like Ryan stuff-wise. He was up to 96 [mph] with the velo[city]. A little scattered there in his inning, but just from my vantage point on the side, stuff looked good. … Whether [he’s an option for the] first round or not, that’ll be the conversation we have here in the next day or two.”
Stanton and Grisham, meanwhile, were facing live pitching for the second time in three days (and faced minor league lefty Xavier Rivas for more at-bats around Weathers’ inning). Despite not having played in a game for five months because of three calf strains, Stanton is in consideration to make the roster as a pinch hitter depending on how many position players the Yankees carry.
“Obviously we’ll talk to G, see where he’s at, mentally, physically, all that,” Boone said. “But having the threat there is real, and if we feel like he’s up to it and ready for it, the threat that we all know G is, we got to weigh that.”
Grisham has been sidelined for three weeks with a hamstring strain but could make the roster as a fourth outfielder (and potentially start in center against righties, with Spencer Jones moving to right).
- CHECK OUT THE LATEST MLB STANDINGS AND YANKEES STATS
“He’s knocking on that door too,” Boone said. “He’s checked a lot of the boxes and gone through his running progressions and things like that. So he’s very much in play and in the conversation too.”
The Yankees had 18 innings to cover Friday, but Carlos Lagrange was not called up to throw any of them. Across the two games, they promoted Brendan Beck, Yerry de los Santos and Alexander Cornielle to eat innings (Beck starting Game 1), allowing them to protect the rest of their pitching staff ahead of the postseason.
Lagrange, meanwhile, was not going to be available to pitch Friday after throwing live on Wednesday in Somerset, N.J., as part of the Yankees’ stay-ready group. The hard-throwing 23-year-old is still not far removed from a shoulder sprain, so the Yankees are being cautious with him even while keeping him in play to potentially be an option for a postseason roster.
“He had an injury, and he’s just started throwing lives again,” Boone said. “He threw live two days ago, so he’s not in play right now. Could be down the road, but he’s not in play yet.”
With Sunday’s regular-season finale in jeopardy because of the nor’easter — and the Yankees planning to call up Elmer Rodríguez for length if they play that game — Lagrange seems doubtful to appear in a regular-season game.
Fernando Cruz (partially torn UCL) was transferred to the 60-day injured list Friday (to make room on the 40-man roster for Cornielle), essentially ruling him out for the entire postseason despite his attempt to make a late-season comeback. … Boone said he did not know what Aaron Judge (calf strain) was doing Friday “as far as baseball goes

item.content:encoded:
With the New York Yankees locked into an American League Wild Card berth, anticipation is building around who will make the final postseason roster—especially after former AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
Gil was optioned alongside fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner, leaving one final roster spot up for grabs, as the Yankees announced on Thursday. While Gil had an opportunity to pitch his way onto the October roster, a rocky, walk-heavy outing against the Tampa Bay Rays sealed his fate.
In addition to bullpen decisions, the Yankees are closely monitoring their key injured stars as October approaches. On that front, manager Aaron Boone addressed the media to clear the air regarding conflicting reports about Aaron Judge’s status.
Boone also remains hopeful that slugger Giancarlo Stanton can return in time for the postseason, as the organization continues evaluating his physical readiness through live drills and simulated games.
Luis Gil #81 of the New York Yankees throws a pitch.
Yankees’ potential postseason roster
While the front office awaits definitive health updates on Judge, Stanton, and outfielder Trent Grisham, the baseline roster is coming into focus for their Wild Card showdown against the archrival Boston Red Sox, who are facing injury concerns of their own regarding catcher Willson Contreras.
Here is how the Yankees’ postseason roster is projecting:
- Starting Rotation: Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Cam Schlittler, Will Warren
- Relief Pitchers: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Michael Fulmer, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, John Schreiber, Ryan Yarbrough
- Catchers: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
- Infielders: Jazz Chisholm Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Ryan McMahon, Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Amed Rosario, George Lombard Jr., Ben Rice (1B/DH)
- Outfielders: Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones
As New York prepares for October baseball, fans are eager to watch the latest chapter in the game’s greatest rivalry unfold, with a spot in the ALDS against the division-champion Tampa Bay Rays hanging in the balance.
Key takeaways
- Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
- Aaron Boone addressed conflicting media reports regarding Aaron Judge’s status.
- New York projects Gerrit Cole to lead its postseason starting rotation.

Since Opening Day back in late March, Judge's jersey sales have surpassed every other player in the American League, based on sales of Nike jerseys from the Fanatics network of sites, including MLBShop.com. They even surpassed former Y
item.content:encoded:
To some, 99 is just a number. To others, it identifies one of the most well-known Major League Baseball players in 2026.
Aaron Judge's jersey, sporting No. 99, is the MLB's second-most popular jersey this year, only behind Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers. Since Opening Day back in late March, Judge's jersey sales have surpassed every other player in the American League, based on sales of Nike jerseys from the Fanatics network of sites, including MLBShop.com.
They even surpassed former Yankee and now crosstown rival Juan Soto, whose jersey was the 10th top-selling this year.
Judge has worn No. 99 since he was assigned the number in spring training when he first joined the team in 2016. The only other players in franchise history to share Judge's number were 2009 relief pitcher Brian Bruney, and outfielder Charlie Keller, otherwise known as "King Kong," who became the first MLB player to wear the number during his final season in 1952.
With Judge's availability for the upcoming Wild Card Series in question, sales are sure to spike to support the Yankees captain. Postseason baseball will begin next week, and if you find yourself wandering around the Bronx or stopping by Billy's Sports Bar, there's no doubt you'll find folks in No. 99 throughout a sea of pinstripes.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] MLB insider strongly cautions Yankees' Aaron Judge to change his rehab strategy after latest injury
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski

Not only does it hurt physically, but it’s a bit of an emotional wound to feel like you could be letting your team down. Even for stars like Aaron Judge, the frustration is very real. But according to one MLB insider, the star’s preferred rehab strategy likely cost the New York Yankees dearly. In fact, it cost them a chance to have their best player during their Wild Card Series matchup against th
item.content:encoded:
If you’re an athlete, the last thing you ever want to do is miss playing time because of an injury. Not only does it hurt physically, but it’s a bit of an emotional wound to feel like you could be letting your team down. Even for stars like Aaron Judge, the frustration is very real.
But according to one MLB insider, the star’s preferred rehab strategy likely cost the New York Yankees dearly. In fact, it cost them a chance to have their best player during their Wild Card Series matchup against the Boston Red Sox.
While speaking on the The Baseball Insiders podcast, FanSided’s Robert Murray offered up his take on what led to Judge suffering a calf strain just days after returning to the Yankees lineup. And it’s something so simple that it may frustrate fans.
According to Murray, Judge will have to “change up his strategy” when it comes to returning from injury. He noted that the Yankees star has been resistant to rehab assignments throughout his career. That preference could have led to some unintended consequences this season.
“And I would definitely imagine that not having a rehab assignment and working his way back up is what contributed to this injury ultimately end up happening,” Murray said of Judge’s most recent injury setback.
Now that the Yankees are without their best player once again this season, it is probably time to change things up.
How can the Yankees best manage Aaron Judge's injury rehab process moving forward?
You could argue that a player could get injured just as easily playing in a minor league rehab assignment as they could in the majors. That might be true to a certain extent. But rehab assignments in minor league parks simply lack the same energy as a big league game.
There’s less of an incentive to stretch a single into a double or dive for a bloop single in front of you. For a player like Judge who always gives it his all, learning how to dial it down in the minor leagues could go a long way in preserving himself in the majors. Rehab assignments are thought of as essential to the ramp-up process for a reason. They help get a recovering body ready for the spotlight.
In his 11-year big league career, Judge has been placed on the IL nearly a dozen times. However, he’s only been on one rehab assignment during that time. In June 2019, the Yankees outfielder played five games with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre before rejoining the team. He remained healthy that season until missing a game in September due to a sore shoulder.
Was that rehab assignment solely responsible for his long-term health? Probably not. But it may have helped Judge get back in the swing of things more effectively. Despite going 0-10 in his first three games back from that rehab assignment, he then went 8-14 over his next four games, including two home runs.
After missing three entire months this season, Judge jumped straight into the Yankees lineup and struggled through seven games. Judge collected just four hits in his 23 at-bats after returning from his IL stint. There was certainly a decent amount of rust for Judge to shake off from his prolonged layoff.
Although he struck out in more than half of those at-bats, there were also some promising signs that showed that he was starting to find his rhythm at the plate again. He smacked a three-run home run off of reliever A.J. Minter during the Yankees 8-3 win over the Minnesota Twins on September 14. It looked like he could potentially be gearing up for a major hot streak exactly when the Yankees could really use the help.
That hot streak obviously never happened, and Judge may not be able to return to the Yankees in the postseason.
As we’ve seen with the Los Angeles Dodgers and their lackluster approach to Shohei Ohtani’s injury, players can sometimes be unreliable when it comes to reporting discomfort or adhering to the best rehab practices. Ball players want to play ball. Everyone can understand that. But taking a conservative approach to injuries for players that have long histories with the IL could actually allow them to play when it matters the most. Judge wanted to rejoin the Yankees as quickly as possible, but it likely led to him missing even more games. Now the team’s offense may suffer for it.
They may not always like it, but players like Judge should be required to go on a rehab assignment moving forward. If they can't slowly ramp up their level of play, they may jump straight back into another injury.

item.dc:creator: Cole Shelton

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could be a team to watch this offseason to add another impact bat to the lineup.
New York is heading back to the playoffs and will host the AL Wild Card series as the Yankees look to get over the hump finally.
The Yankees will begin a three-game road series against the Baltimore Orioles on Friday.
New York Yankees Urged to Acquire Bo Bichette
The Yankees haven’t gotten much production from Ryan McMahon at third base, so New York should look to add an impact bat to replace him.
McMahon’s defense has been solid. But his bat is an issue, and he’s been considered a trade chip or DFA candidate this offseason. With that, Yankees analyst Stephen Parello of FanSided urges the team to acquire Bo Bichette this offseason.
“It might sound strange, but Bo Bichette could be a sneaky-good solution for the Yankees. While he got off to a frigid start in Queens that has depressed his overall line, he’s hit .291/.335/.440 since June 1. There’s also some reason to believe that getting away from the Mets’ dysfunction could help him rebound even more,” Parello wrote.
“What’s more, he could actually provide some things the Yankees need. Having another contact-forward bat would be nice, and he’d add some much-needed right-handed balance to the lineup. It seemed for a while that he was a shoo-in to opt in to his contract, but now, after a return to form, it’s thought to be a 50-50 chance that he tests the free-agent market again this winter. If he does, he deserves a long look.”
Bichette is in the first year of a three-year, $126 million deal but could opt out. If he does opt out, Bichette will have some suitors, and he could fit in nicely with the Yankees.
The slugger showed he can hit in the AL East with the Toronto Blue Jays, and his defense at third base is good enough. He’s hitting .259 with 17 home runs and 76 RBIs this season.
New York Right Now
The Yankees are set to play their final series of the season before the focus shifts to the playoffs.
New York will likely play the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round. However, the team has dealt with a plethora of injuries, including to slugger Aaron Judge.
“I’m proud of the guys,” Judge said. “I’ve been proud of what they’ve done, proud of the young guys coming up and filling some holes for us. You know, seeing Spencer, how he’s really evolved every single time he got called up, gotten a little bit better, a little bit better. Our starting pitching doing what it’s done. You call up a guy like George Lombard [Jr.], 21 years old, to be the shortstop for the Yankees, and he’s just fit right in with this group. I’m just proud of the guys.”
The Yankees will play a doubleheader on Friday before ending the season on Sunday.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] 4 Ryan McMahon replacements Yankees should already be dreaming about for 2027
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello

item.content:encoded:
It's far too late to do anything about it this season, but the New York Yankees officially have a Ryan McMahon problem. It's been a year and a half now that he's been in pinstripes, and his performance with the bat has been worse than notorious frustrations like Joey Gallo, late-career DJ LeMahieu, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa, among others.
With a .208/.274/.344 line over 119 games this season, he has struggled against righties, is even more useless against lefties, and has arrived at a point where his good-but-not-great defense can no longer save his subpar bat.
Now that the case for an offseason DFA is clear, it's time to start thinking about potential 2027 replacements. There might not be a ton of high-end options, but there are a few that we can dream on.
Four dream Ryan McMahon replacements for 2027 if the Yankees shoot for the stars
Rafael Devers
Rafael Devers has been gaining buzz as a trade target for New York since the lead-up to the trade deadline. This would be a 180 in philosophy, as the whole reason things deteriorated between Devers and the Red Sox was growing concerns over his defense, and since arriving in San Francisco, he's primarily been a first baseman and DH. There's a school of thought, though, that George Lombard Jr.'s athleticism and defensive potential could help mitigate the defensive issues.
Devers hit 38 homers this year, and even a slow first half from him was light-years better than what McMahon has put up at any point in his career. Admittedly, this has become a bit more complicated due to questions about his status for Opening Day after undergoing core muscle surgery, and the Yankees would have to assume the vast majority of the nearly $200 million that the 29-year-old is owed, but his bat would be a perfect fit, and this would have the added benefit of tormenting Boston with a Raffy Revenge Tour.
Isaac Paredes
Another trade candidate, Isaac Paredes, could be an interesting option. The 27-year-old has long been on the Yankees' radar, and this winter could be their opportunity to get a deal done. The Houston Astros are never ones to help the Yankees out, but this could be a case where need aligns well enough for both squads that they have no other choice but to come to an agreement.
Houston is in a tough spot. Their horrid start put them behind the eight ball, and they're in a dogfight with the Texas Rangers for the AL West crown. The loser of the division chase might find themselves out of the Wild Card picture, and if that were to happen, it would mark the Astros' second consecutive playoff-less season. They've also fired general manager Dana Brown this summer, so changes are coming.
Paredes was subject to a slew of trade rumors last offseason because Houston has an infield logjam. Carlos Correa's injury cleared that up in 2026, but he'll be back next year and is under contract through at least 2028 (and possibly through 2032, depending on a series of vesting options). Meanwhile, they're also stuck with Christian Walker for another season, and Jose Altuve isn't going anywhere. Houston desperately needs pitching, and doesn't have a lot of room in their budget. Perhaps an Elmer Rodriguez-centric package could sway them.
Bo Bichette
It might sound strange, but Bo Bichette could be a sneaky-good solution for the Yankees. While he got off to a frigid start in Queens that has depressed his overall line, he's hit .291/.335/.440 since June 1. There's also some reason to believe that getting away from the Mets' dysfunction could help him rebound even more.
What's more, he could actually provide some things the Yankees need. Having another contact-forward bat would be nice, and he'd add some much-needed right-handed balance to the lineup. It seemed for a while that he was a shoo-in to opt in to his contract, but now, after a return to form, it's thought to be a 50-50 chance that he tests the free-agent market again this winter. If he does, he deserves a long look.
Zach Neto
This one requires some creativity, but there's a chance that New York could make this work. Zach Neto was the subject of a wave of trade rumors at the deadline, and according to Angels insider Jeff Fletcher of the OC Register, Los Angeles is expected to shop him again this offseason. The Red Sox and Rays were both rumored to be sniffing around the 25-year-old at the deadline, so making a deal for him could also be a defensive move.
Neto is a shortstop by trade, but if there's one knock on his game, it's that his range at the position is lacking. He does have a cannon for an arm, with his throwing power checking in at an 85th-percentile mark per Baseball Savant, so a move to the hot corner could maximize his defensive skill set.
The hiccup here will be the price. Neto is a perennial 30-30 candidate and doesn't hit free agency until 2030, so he won't be cheap to acquire. For this to work for the Yankees, they'd need to be able to hold onto Lombard Jr.; otherwise, they're simply trading one shortstop for another. That might not be possible on either team's end. Los Angeles acquired top prospect Arjun Nimmala from the Blue Jays for Jose Soriano, and the soon-to-be 21-year-old is tearing up Double-A. He could soon be ready to step in and take Neto's job.
This is the longest shot of them all, but it could help the Yankees extend their window well into Aaron Judge's decline. A core of Neto, Lombard Jr., Spencer Jones, Ben Rice, and Cam Schlittler could eventually usher in a new era without the club having to go through any sort of reset.

item.title: [New York Post] Aaron Boone defends Aaron Judge’s ‘passion’ to make quick Yankees playoff return
item.dc:creator: Mark W Sanchez
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge and Aaron Boone agree that the Yankees captain is doing everything he can to get back on the field as soon as he can.
They spoke “a little bit,” the manager said Thursday, about the two things they apparently disagreed on:




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
First, Boone saying Tuesday he did not expect Judge to return in time for the wild-card series before Judge said Wednesday his goal is to be ready for Game 1 of that series; and second, the manager publicly conceding Judge’s calf strain is “moderate,” while the notoriously private — at least on the subject of injuries — Judge said he didn’t “know why [Boone] used those words.”
“I don’t want to get too much into that [conversation with Judge],” Boone said Thursday when asked about the two seemingly not being on the same page. “At the end of the day, we’re all in this together. And in his case, trying to get him right and get him healthy so he can be an option for us here at some point.
“But we’re also going to listen to the injury. I see it as just a passionate player that’s doing all he can to get back for his teammates.”
What others might interpret as annoyance or anger from Judge, Boone said was “passion.”
Boone — who all along has said he is not ruling out Judge returning in time for the postseason (even if it seemed and seems unlikely) — also said the roster decisions for a round that will begin Tuesday may not be made until Tuesday morning.
Thus, the Yankees will give Judge as much time as possible to recover from a calf strain suffered Sept. 16 — which was just seven games after he returned from a rib fracture that cost him more than three months — before declaring him in or out.
“The bottom line is Aaron and I have always had an amazing relationship and still do and will,” Boone said before finishing the series against the Rays in The Bronx. “This is about a player that, again, is pouring everything he possibly can into being ready, and we’re going to support that.
“And when he’s ready, we’ll make a call of when that is based on how he’s doing.”
Both superstar and manager have emphasized this week that Judge is doing everything in his power to build up quickly and be ready for a three-game series that almost certainly will be against the Red Sox, but Judge — who received a platelet-poor plasma injection Monday — is still limited barely a week after suffering the injury.
Notably, he is not swinging yet.
“He’s doing all the things in the training room, all the modalities, that you can take advantage of,” Boone said of Judge, who plans to return as a right fielder and not a DH. “He’s moving on the treadmill, things like that, doing the different exercises to get the calf healed.
“Doing everything he can to make that as speedy as possible.”

item.title: [marca usa] Aaron Judge vs. Aaron Boone: Crece la tensión en los Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jose Rodriguez

La grave lesión de Alex Bregman podría obligar a la MLB a romper una tradición de larga data: "No tenemos por qué seguir haciendo eso" Con apenas tres juegos restantes en la temporada regular y los New York Yankees enfocados en su debut en los playoffs, el estado de Aaron Judge sigue rodeado de incertidumbre. Lo que parecía una actualización médica rutinaria ahora se ha convertido
item.content:encoded:
- MLB. Aaron Judge desafía la postura de Aaron Boone y planea superar su lesión para estar listo en playoffs
- MLB. La grave lesión de Alex Bregman podría obligar a la MLB a romper una tradición de larga data: "No tenemos por qué seguir haciendo eso"
Con apenas tres juegos restantes en la temporada regular y los New York Yankees enfocados en su debut en los playoffs, el estado de Aaron Judge sigue rodeado de incertidumbre. Lo que parecía una actualización médica rutinaria ahora se ha convertido en un debate público, después de que el estelar bateador contradijera abiertamente al manager Aaron Boone, una situación que ya llamó la atención de un reconocido analista de MLB.
Judge cuestiona la postura de Aaron Boone
Mientras Judge continúa fuera de acción por una lesión en la pantorrilla, Boone aseguró que el equipo no espera contar con su capitán para la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana y describió la molestia como una distensión de grado moderado.
Sin embargo, Judge rechazó esa evaluación y dejó claro que su objetivo sigue siendo estar listo para el Juego 1 de la postemporada, lo que llevó al veterano periodista Ken Rosenthal a señalar en Foul Territory que este tipo de desacuerdos públicos son poco habituales dentro de la organización de los Yankees.
"La historia de anoche fue Aaron Judge insistiendo en que quiere jugar. Su plan es jugar y, aunque fue sutil, sí contradijo a Boone. Las palabras importan. No me importa cuánto estuviera sonriendo cuando lo dijo", comentó Rosenthal.
El reconocido analista de MLB también destacó otro punto en el que Judge pareció discrepar con su manager: la gravedad de la lesión.
"Judge también pareció cuestionar que Boone calificara la distensión como moderada. Dijo: 'Una distensión moderada para una persona no es igual que para otra'. Entonces, ¿qué está pasando aquí? Porque con los Yankees rara vez se ve este tipo de desacuerdo hacerse público", agregó Rosenthal.
Una situación poco común dentro de los Yankees
Rosenthal considera que no hay duda de que Judge está haciendo todo lo posible por regresar lo antes posible y cree que sus declaraciones reflejan la mentalidad de una superestrella que no quiere perderse el béisbol de octubre. Sin embargo, advirtió que las lesiones en la pantorrilla suelen ser impredecibles.
"Quizá Aaron Judge se recupere de repente, pero las lesiones en la pantorrilla son notoriamente complicadas. No sé cómo terminará esto. Lo que sí sé es que es muy inusual ver a los Yankees mostrando este nivel de desacuerdo públicamente", concluyó Rosenthal.
A pocos días del inicio de la Serie de Comodines, la situación de Judge sigue sin resolverse. Mientras Boone prepara a los Yankees como si no fuera a contar con su máxima figura, Judge mantiene un mensaje firme: su intención es estar en el terreno de juego para el Juego 1 de los playoffs.

item.title: [amsterdamnews.com] Can the Yankees take down the Red Sox without Aaron Judge?
item.dc:creator: JAIME C HARRIS AmNews Sports Editor
item.description: This was supposed to be the year the Yankees would win the franchise’s first World Series since 2009. A roster that included all-time greats Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera and Alex Rodriguez, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, and Series MVP Hideki Matsui, one of the best players Japan has ever produced. Yet, as the Yankees look towards Tuesday, when they open the playoffs at home against what is virtually certain to be the Boston Red Sox, their longtime nemesis, in a best-of-three wildcard series, the pro
item.content:encoded:
This was supposed to be the year the Yankees would win the franchise’s first World Series since 2009. A roster that included all-time greats Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera and Alex Rodriguez, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, and Series MVP Hideki Matsui, one of the best players Japan has ever produced.
Yet, as the Yankees look towards Tuesday, when they open the playoffs at home against what is virtually certain to be the Boston Red Sox, their longtime nemesis, in a best-of-three wildcard series, the prospects of them navigating an always perilous path to the World Series were reduced when Yankees manager Aaron Boone said this past Tuesday that the reigning American League MVP likely won’t play in the series due to a right calf strain.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone revealed to reporters.
Judge, who has only appeared in 66 games this season, primarily recovering from a right rib stress fracture, which caused him to sit out 84 games from May 31 to Sept. 8, is now on the 10-day injured list, placed there last Friday. The 34-year-old Judge, arguably the best player in the sport over the last decade, isn’t expected back for the divisional round if the Yankees get by the Red Sox.
Last weekend, Boone informed the media the team didn’t have a firm estimate as to when Judge, a three-time AL MVP, three-time AL home run leader, two-time MLB RBI king and last season’s MLB batting champion, would return to the lineup.
“I mean, I have no idea, we’re in the early stages,” expressed Boone, now in his ninth season as the Yankees manager. “We’ll just obviously treat it and see what transpires.”
The Yankees watched Tampa Bay clinch the AL East title on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium when they won the second game of a double-header on Tuesday 6-1. The Yankees shut out the Rays in the opener. Tampa Bay 96-61 going into the third game of the four-game series last night with the finale scheduled for 7:05 tonight. The Yankees were second in the division at 90-67 and the 84-73 Red Sox third.
With Judge unavailable, the Yankees offense will have to be multifaceted — both power and small ball will be required to make a deep postseason run. Designated hitter Ben Rice, who as of Wednesday had 39 home runs and 95 RBIs, both team highs, was the only Yankee with more than 20 homers and 80 runs batted in, so timely power will have to come from sources such as second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (19 home runs), first baseman Paul Goldschmidt (18), and left fielder Cody Bellinger (17).
But it is pitching that must advance the Yankees, led by leading AL Cy Young Award candidate Cam Schlittler, who is 14-6 with a 1.94 ERA and 234 strikeouts. Schlittler is scheduled to start tonight before taking the mound next week in the wildcard series.
But the prevailing question is: Can the Yankees win without Judge?

He allowed two earned runs (with eight strikeouts) in 5.2 innings. After the gam
item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday night, the New York Yankees beat the Tampa Bay Rays (at home) by a score of 9-3.
They were led by Ben Rice, as he hit two home runs.
The Yankees wrote (via X): “Last night, Ben Rice became the third Yankee in franchise history to hit at least 40 HR within his first three Major League seasons, joining Aaron Judge and Joe DiMaggio 🙌”
Gerrit Cole Makes Rice Statement
Gerrit Cole got the start on Wednesday.
He allowed two earned runs (with eight strikeouts) in 5.2 innings.
After the game, Cole was asked about Rice (via YES Network).
Reporter: “We’ve seen a lot from Ben Rice over the last year-plus. But 40 and 41 now. What does it say about his continued development and what he really means to this lineup?”
Cole: “Super proud of him. Really exciting season for him. Deserves it too. He works really hard and puts in a lot of work behind the scenes. And had a great night tonight along with Mac. That was great to see along with George. Just keep plugging along. Those homers were huge for us. The offense played well. And we played pretty good defense in a tough environment tonight too. So overall really great, and a nice night for Ben.”
Looking At Rice
Rice was picked in the 12th round of the 2021 MLB Draft.
He is currently batting .263 with 148 hits, 41 home runs, 97 RBIs, 103 runs and three stolen bases in 151 games.
The 27-year-old has spent all three seasons of his MLB career with the Yankees.
Looking At Cole
Cole is in the middle of his 13th MLB season.
He has also had stops with the Pittsburgh Pirates and Houston Astros.
Right now, Cole is 10-9 with a 3.61 ERA in 22 starts.

item.content:encoded:
Judge hopes to be ready for playoffs and Stanton could return for Yankees after 5 1/2-month absence
NEW YORK (AP) — Yankees slugger Aaron Judge hopes to return from a strained right calf for the playoffs next week and Giancarlo Stanton could be back after a 5 1/2-month absence.
New York manager Aaron Boone repeated he’s not counting on Judge to play in the AL Wild Card Series opener Tuesday. Judge, sidelined since Sept. 16, said he’s trying to do all he can to be in the lineup.
“The Bronx is a magical place in October,” Judge said after Wednesday night’s 9-2 win over AL East champion Tampa Bay. “I don’t want to miss out on that opportunity.”
Judge had a platelet-poor plasma injection Monday. He was sidelined by a fractured rib from May 31 to Sept. 8 and played in just seven games before the latest injury.
“Any injection doesn’t feel too good that day, but I feel a lot better today and we’re going to keep making strides,” he said.
A three-time AL MVP, Judge is hitting .241 with 18 homers, 41 RBIs and an .871 OPS in 66 games this season, including .174 with one homer and three RBIs since coming back from the rib injury.
“We are going to listen to the body and see how he heals,” Boone said. “If he is in a position to do that, obviously we are going to want him. So, no, I haven’t ruled anything out, of course.”
Boone said Tuesday he wasn’t planning on having Judge available for next week’s best-of-three series, likely against Boston.
“Obviously as a player, you don’t want to hear that but that’s out of my control,” Judge said.
Boone said Judge had a moderate strain.
“Everybody’s `moderate’ is a little different,” Judge said.
Stanton, trying to return from injuries to calf muscles in both legs, faced pitchers Wednesday at Double-A Somerset along with center fielder Trent Grisham, sidelined since straining his right hamstring on Sept. 4. Both ran the bases and Stanton homered while taking six or seven at-bats.
“Putting them on the outskirts of the conversation,” Boone, bothered by a cold, said in a raspy voice.
Following the end of the seasons for Yankees farm teams, New York has minor leaguers working out at Somerset in nearby New Jersey.
Stanton hasn’t played since April 24 because of strained calf muscles in both legs after starting the season with a .256 batting average, three homers and 14 RBIs in 24 games. The 36-year-old former NL MVP had 38 homers and 100 RBIs in his first season with New York in 2018 but has missed 500 of 1,194 games since (41.9%), through the end of this regular season.
His other injuries included strains of his right biceps, right knee, left hamstring (three times), left quadriceps and both calf muscles along with right ankle inflammation, left Achilles tendinitis and tendon pain in both elbows.
“You’re looking more at a pinch-hit scenario,” Boone said. “We’ll see if that’s even a realistic option.”
Stanton is owed $25 million next year in the final guaranteed season of a $325 million, 13-year contract that includes a $10 million buyout of a 2028 club option.
Lagrange could be brought up for major league debut
Carlos Lagrange, a 23-year-old right-hander who reached 100 mph with 98 pitches at Triple-A this year, threw to batters at Somerset. He was out between June 28 and Sept. 16 because of a right capsule strain.
Lagrange was shifted to the bullpen at the start of June.
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said.
Clarke Schmidt still out
Right-hander Clarke Schmidt, who returned Sept. 16 following Tommy John surgery in July 2025, played catch but remains sidelined by right biceps cramps. New York had hoped to use him as a reliever in the postseason.
“Today was better than yesterday,” Boone said. “If he’s not a real viable option by tomorrow, then we’ll probably go a different way.”
Postseason rotation
Boone said Cam Schlitter will start Game 1 or 2 of the playoffs. Max Fried appears set to start whichever game Schlittler doesn’t, with Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón available for Game 3.
“Whoever goes 1 or 2 can pitch 2 and 5 in the next series,” Boone said.
Fernando Cruz throws a bullpen
Right-hander Fernando Cruz threw a bullpen this week and is to throw another one Thursday.
He hasn’t pitched in a game since Aug. 25 because of right elbow discomfort caused by a partially torn ulnar collateral ligament.
“I’m in a really good position to be back I will say in the next couple of weeks,” Cruz said.
He took issue with the diagnosis of his injury.
“I had a real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” he said. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart it’s not a partial tear.”
Volpe will see time at the hot corner
With second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. back from a sprained right thumb, Boone said Anthony Volpe will see time at third.
“I’ll probably get him on there a time or two,” Boone said.
Volpe entered Wednesday hitting .263 with one homer, seven RBIs and four stolen bases over 11 games since his recall from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. He played three games at third base for the RailRiders.
“It didn’t feel that bad when I played there, but we’ll see,” Volpe said.

item.title: [Fox News] Why Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is in the AL MVP conversation and could join an exclusive club
item.dc:creator: Ryan Canfield
item.description: If you shoot for the moon, you will land among the stars. In Cam Schlittler’s case, however, he and his blazing fastball may take him past the stars and straight to the moon. The New York Yankees ace has been nothing short of dominant this season. The swashbuckling 25-year-old is all but a lock to win the American League Cy Young Award. But why stop there? He should win the American League MVP too. Schlittler should become just the 12th player in MLB history to win the Cy Young and MVP in the sa
item.content:encoded:
If you shoot for the moon, you will land among the stars. In Cam Schlittler’s case, however, he and his blazing fastball may take him past the stars and straight to the moon.
The New York Yankees ace has been nothing short of dominant this season. The swashbuckling 25-year-old is all but a lock to win the American League Cy Young Award.
But why stop there? He should win the American League MVP too. Schlittler should become just the 12th player in MLB history to win the Cy Young and MVP in the same season.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
Heading into his final start of the year against the Tampa Bay Rays on Thursday, Schlittler leads all American League pitchers in ERA (1.94) and is tied for first in WHIP with Drew Rasmussen (0.91). He has been durable, making all his starts, and is second in the AL in innings pitched (190 2/3).
With a devastating combination of cutters, sinkers and fastballs, the young right-hander has racked up 234 strikeouts, third in the AL behind Cleveland Guardians ace Gavin Williams (244) and likely Cy Young runner-up Dylan Cease (239).
Schlittler has set a Yankees franchise record by allowing one or no runs in 21 starts this year. He became just the third pitcher age 25 or younger in the live-ball era, which began in 1920, to achieve the feat, joining Dean Chance (1964) and Blake Snell (2018).
Schlittler also leads the AL in bWAR with 7.0, ahead of other MVP contenders such as Houston Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez (6.6), Kansas City Royals star Bobby Witt Jr. (6.5) and Rays phenom Junior Caminero (5.6).
The numbers for Schlittler are outstanding, but they don’t tell the full story.
Schlittler has been the pillar of the Yankees' pitching staff, which leads all of baseball with a 3.21 team ERA.
While the pitching staff has been fantastic, it has have dealt with plenty of injuries to the starting rotation.
Gerrit Cole didn’t make his season debut until May 22, as he was recovering from Tommy John surgery. Carlos Rodón began the season on the IL after undergoing surgery to remove a bone spur and loose bodies and didn’t debut until May 10. That was just his first stint on the IL. He returned to the IL on July 3 and didn’t come back until Aug. 18.
Rodón was not the only Yankees ace to land on the IL twice, as Max Fried did as well. Fried first went on the IL with a left elbow bone bruise on May 13, right after Cole returned, and was activated on July 22. He went on the IL for a second time on Aug. 17 with the same injury and returned Aug. 29.
Ryan Weathers, who had been key in stepping up during the absences of Cole, Fried and Rodón, went on the IL on Aug. 23 with a left forearm flexor strain.
For the Yankees, not only was it paramount that Schlittler make every start, but it was also essential that he remain dominant to help keep the rotation afloat.
Adding to the pressure on Schlittler and the pitching staff as a whole, the Yankees’ offense cratered after Aaron Judge was placed on the IL at the beginning of June. Since June 1, the Yankees have hit a paltry .229 with a putrid .297 on-base percentage.
The Yankees’ offensive ineptitude put further pressure on Schlittler and Co. to win games without Judge.
In 2023, the Yankees’ season went off the rails when Judge suffered a torn ligament in his toe. They went 25-31 without the captain and missed the postseason. The Yankees’ pitching staff in 2023, led by Cole, who won the AL Cy Young Award that season, had a 3.97 ERA, which was not enough to save the Yankees from finishing 82-80.
In 2026, the Yankees went 48-41 without Judge in the lineup, buoyed by the pitching staff’s excellence. Carried by the Schlittler-led pitching staff, the Yankees made the postseason and secured home-field advantage in the American League Wild Card Series.
While the Yankees didn’t catch the Tampa Bay Rays and win the American League East, they might have missed the postseason entirely if it weren’t for Schlittler.
By the award’s definition, Schlittler has been the most valuable player on his team.
Alvarez has been dominant in his own right. The hulking left-handed hitter, with a .316 batting average, 41 home runs and 102 RBI made a bid for the Triple Crown, but that seems out of reach.
Alvarez has been primarily a designated hitter, filling that role in 131 of the 154 games he played this season. Shohei Ohtani is the only player to win an MVP as a primary designated hitter, and he did so after becoming the first player to hit 50 home runs and steal 50 bases in a season.
Unless Alvarez surges to win the Triple Crown, nothing he is doing this season is unprecedented or historic.
Alvarez’s Astros, who are 78-80, might miss the postseason despite playing in the American League West, a division that has been historically bad.
Bobby Witt Jr. has been his usual superstar self but missed 11 games due to injury and has also taken a slight step back from last season while playing for the AL Central-worst Kansas City Royals.Caminero, the linchpin of the AL-leading Rays’ lineup, trails Schlittler in bWAR by more than a full win. Still, his .274 average and 41 home runs leave him in the thick of the AL MVP race.
Despite the excellence of Alvarez, Witt and Caminero, Schlittler should become the first pitcher since Justin Verlander in 2011 to win the American League MVP.
Verlander, like Schlittler this year, led the American League in bWAR with 8.6.
Without Schlittler, the Yankees do not survive Judge’s absence. When the Yankees could hardly scrape together three runs a game in the dead of summer, Schlittler made sure it was enough to hold on.
Without Schlittler’s dominance and durability, the Yankees do not have the second-best record in the American League (91-67).
Without Schlittler, Yankees fans are in a complete state of panic because they might still be trying to secure a Wild Card berth in a weak American League.
At the sportsbooks, Schlittler is a long shot to win the American League MVP. But odds be damned, the award should be his. He has landed on the moon.

item.dc:creator: Ariel Velázquez

item.content:encoded:
El número 41 apareció en la pantalla del Yankee Stadium y, por un instante, los Yankees volvieron a mirar hacia 1961.
Ben Rice conectó dos cuadrangulares el miércoles ante Tampa Bay para llegar a 41 en la temporada. El segundo puso al primera base de Nueva York en el mismo escalón de jonrones que Pete Alonso, Junior Caminero y Yordan Álvarez en la Liga Americana.
Pero el verdadero alcance de la noche va más allá de una carrera por el liderato de cuadrangulares. Rice acaba de entrar de lleno en la conversación por el MVP de la Liga Americana en la última semana del calendario. Sus números de temporada, después de 162 partidos para Nueva York, son 41 jonrones, 97 carreras anotadas, 148 hits, .263 de promedio, .362 de porcentaje de embasarse y .899 de OPS.
Al otro lado del clubhouse está Cam Schlittler.
El derecho de 25 años se convirtió en el brazo alrededor del cual gira la conversación por el Cy Young de la Americana. Después de 32 apariciones suma 14-6, 1.94 de ERA, 190.2 innings, 234 ponches y 0.91 de WHIP.
Pareja que entraría a los libros de historia de Yankees
Si Rice terminara conquistando el MVP y Schlittler el Cy Young, los Yankees volverían a tener en una misma temporada a los ganadores de los dos premios individuales más importantes de la Liga Americana. La última vez ocurrió en 1961.
Ninguno de los dos llegó a Nueva York con la etiqueta de fenómeno inevitable.
Rice fue elegido por los Yankees en la ronda 12 del Draft de 2021, con la selección 363, procedente de Dartmouth. Schlittler fue seleccionado en la séptima ronda de 2022, con el pick 220, después de jugar en Northeastern.
No fueron elecciones de primera ronda. No fueron nombres destinados desde el Draft a cargar con el uniforme de los Yankees.
Hoy, sin embargo, Rice es un bateador de 41 jonrones y Schlittler es el líder de una rotación que tiene al resto de la industria hablando del Cy Young. MLB describió recientemente la transformación de Schlittler como la de un séptima ronda convertido en All-Star y candidato al premio.
Y mientras Aaron Judge pasó buena parte de 2026 fuera por lesión, Rice terminó ocupando el espacio ofensivo que quedó abierto. Judge apenas disputó 66 encuentros y bateó .241 con 18 cuadrangulares.
¡Qué sucedió en 1961 para los Yankees!
Roger Maris y Whitey Ford escribieron una de las temporadas más reconocibles en la historia de la franquicia.
Maris bateó 61 cuadrangulares, rompió el récord de 60 que Babe Ruth había establecido en 1927 y terminó como MVP de la Liga Americana. En 161 partidos produjo .269/.372/.620, con 141 carreras impulsadas.
Ford, mientras tanto, tuvo una temporada que parecía diseñada para acompañar semejante hazaña: 25-4, 3.21 de ERA, 283 innings y 209 ponches. Ganó el Cy Young.
Los Yankees ganaron 109 juegos, conquistaron la Liga Americana por ocho juegos y después vencieron a Cincinnati en cinco partidos para ganar la Serie Mundial.
Existe además una precisión histórica importante. En 1961 todavía había un solo Cy Young para toda MLB. El premio comenzó a entregarse por separado en cada liga en 1967. Ford fue, por tanto, el ganador absoluto del Cy Young de 1961.
Rice no necesita batear 61 para entrar en esta conversación. Schlittler tampoco necesita reproducir exactamente los números de Ford.
Lo extraordinario sería que dos Yankees seleccionados fuera de las primeras rondas terminaran colocando sus nombres junto a Maris y Ford en la misma fotografía de premios.
¿Hay otros equipos con Cy Young y MVP en la misma temporada?
Antes de 1967, cuando el Cy Young era único para toda MLB, ocurrió con los Braves de 1957 —Hank Aaron y Warren Spahn—, White Sox de 1959 —Nellie Fox y Early Wynn—, Pirates de 1960 —Dick Groat y Vern Law— y Dodgers de 1962 —Maury Wills y Don Drysdale—.
Después de la división del premio por liga, la lista continuó con casos como Boston en 1986, Milwaukee en 1981, Oakland en 1990, Atlanta en 1991, Chicago White Sox en 1993, Oakland en 2002, St. Louis en 2005 y Minnesota en 2006. MLB registra 18 ocasiones en las que dos jugadores de un mismo equipo consiguieron MVP y Cy Young en la misma temporada hasta ese último caso.
También existe otra variante. Un mismo jugador ganó ambos premios en una temporada. Justin Verlander lo hizo en 2011, mientras Clayton Kershaw lo consiguió en 2014. En total, 11 pitchers han ganado Cy Young y MVP en el mismo año.
Por eso el último tramo de 2026 tiene una particularidad para Nueva York.
Today in 1961, Roger Maris of the @Yankees surpasses Babe Ruth’s record with his 61st homerun of the season. ⚾️
(📽 “61” released in 2001)#TodayInSports #PinstripePride
https://t.co/QJYClMw96G
Ben Rice y Cam Schlittler están en carrera por estos dos prestigiosos premios y también están intentando devolver a los Yankees a una fotografía que no aparece desde que Roger Maris y Whitey Ford hicieron historia hace 65 años.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Could New York shut Clarke Schmidt down amid injury concern? appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
As the New York Yankees prepare for the playoffs, they are also trying to manage some of the injuries they're dealing with. One of those players is Clarke Schmidt, who has been working through a biceps injury. He's been going through testing, and though it seems like he's progressing, there's a chance that the Yankees consider shutting him down, according to MLB.com.
"Sept. 22 was a 'better' day for Schmidt, who felt discomfort while warming up Sept. 20 at Arizona. If Schmidt is unable to pitch Sept. 24, the Yankees may shut him down," MLB.com wrote.
That's not the best news for the Yankees, as Schmidt is an important part of the team. Especially with it being the playoffs, they want to be as healthy as possible. Right now those chances are looking slim, but it all depends on whether he's able to pitch in their final game of the series against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
The Yankees are already going to be without Aaron Judge for their first playoff series as he deals with a calf injury. He is still hoping to come back at some point, but the goal is to be as healthy as possible.
"My goal is to come back as soon as I can," Judge said. "That's what we're doing right now. If [Boone] says I'm not gonna be ready, I've got no control over that. I've got control over what I can do to try to get back."
It'll be interesting to see what the Yankees' lineup looks like by the time they get to the playoffs.

item.title: [The Big Lead] Ben Rice joins list of Yankee legends featuring Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig & Joe DiMaggio
item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: The MLB season has seen Ben Rice etch his name alongside some of the greatest players in New York Yankees history. The 27-year-old slugger reached the 40-home run mark Wednesday during a 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays, putting him in an exclusive group of Yankees who have hit at least 40 home runs in a season at age 27 or younger. That list features legendary names including Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Mickey Mantle, all of whom accomplished the feat twice. Joe DiMaggio, Roger Maris, Aaron Ju
item.content:encoded:
The MLB season has seen Ben Rice etch his name alongside some of the greatest players in New York Yankees history.
The 27-year-old slugger reached the 40-home run mark Wednesday during a 9-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays, putting him in an exclusive group of Yankees who have hit at least 40 home runs in a season at age 27 or younger.
That list features legendary names including Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Mickey Mantle, all of whom accomplished the feat twice. Joe DiMaggio, Roger Maris, Aaron Judge and Juan Soto are also members of the group.
MORE: Blue Jays & Mariners make MLB history in worst way
Rice powers his way into Yankees history
Rice did not stop at one home run Wednesday, launching two against the Rays to reach 41 for the season. Through 151 games, he is batting .263 with 41 home runs and 97 RBI.
His power has been a major part of an impressive season, and reaching 40 home runs places Rice in company with some of the most celebrated sluggers to ever wear the Yankees uniform.
While Rice has already secured his place in the team’s statistical history, the Yankees are now preparing for the postseason.
Yankees prepare for the postseason
New York has clinched the American League’s top Wild Card position, holding a 10-game advantage over the Chicago White Sox, who occupy the final Wild Card spot. However, the Yankees will not be able to catch Tampa Bay for the AL East title.
The Yankees enter the final stretch of the regular season five games behind the Rays with only four games remaining. That leaves New York focused on preparing for the postseason rather than chasing the division crown.
The Yankees will send ace Cam Schlittler to the mound Thursday for the series finale against Tampa Bay. They will then close out the regular season with a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles over the weekend.
For Rice, the final games offer an opportunity to build on a milestone season. At just 27 years old, his 40-home run campaign has already placed him alongside an extraordinary collection of Yankees legends, giving him a notable piece of franchise history heading into the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
Knicks Superfans Wanted for a Paid Commercial in New York
Remember When The New York Knicks Won the NBA Finals?
New York sports fans are having a tough go at it this fall.
The New York Mets are struggling to say the least. An Aaron Judge injury could affect the New York Yankees in the playoff season.
After beating the Dallas Cowboys at home, during the 1st game of the season, the New York Giants were dealt a devastating blow. QB1 Jaxson Dart is out for the season.
In times like these we like to dive back into happier times, like when the New York Knick won the NBA Finals beating the San Antonio Spurs back in June of 2026.
Who could forget Jalen Brunson and the boys coming back from behind every game to take the championship in 5 games?
I still dream about OG tipping the ball in during Game 4. Incredible run.
At least we have the Knicks (and the Bills if you're into that).
With that being said, New York Knick fans...you're needed!
New York Knick Fans Needed for Paid Commercial
Are you a New York Knick super fan? If so, you're needed!
House of Talent put out a casting call looking for a very specific fan group. They write on their website "Seeking massive Knicks Superfans in New York City for a paid commercial for a tech brand."
There is no previous acting experience needed and they add:
We're looking for friends, families, firefighters, nurses, and people engaged with & servicing their community.
It's a paid gig too! Those picked to be in the commercial will be paid $750 for 10 hours. Pretty sweet deal if you ask me.
If You Want to Be in the Knicks Commercial Here's What To Do
So you want to be in the commercial? Here's what you need to do.
Fill out the application on their website knicksfans.castingcrane.com. The applications must be in by September 25th, 2026.
Callbacks will be on Zoom on September 30th.
You also must be available for a fitting on October 5th, and filming on October 6th and 7th.
According to the website, the commercial will be used for the following:
All Media (including industry events such as Meta Connect, Cannes, CES, AdWeek etc. and any events attended by or sponsored by advertisers, etc).
Let us know if you get the job and we'll keep an eye out for ya!

item.title: [Field Level Media] Ben Rice hopes to add to homer total as Yankees battle Rays

Until he does come back, the slugger and the rest of the New York Yankees will be curious to see if slugger Ben Rice can homer again. item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge said he wants to return for next week’s wild-card series. Until he does come back, the slugger and the rest of the New York Yankees will be curious to see if slugger Ben Rice can homer again.
With four games remaining, Rice is among seven MLB players with at least 40 home runs, and he will attempt to continue his late-season surge Thursday night when New York hosts the Tampa Bay Rays, the American League East champion.
The Yankees (91-67) are assured of hosting the wild-card series and probably will face the Boston Red Sox for the second straight year. New York might be without Judge, who is dealing with a strained right calf after playing in seven games following being out with a fractured right rib.
On Monday, manager Aaron Boone described Judge’s strain as moderate and indicated he was not necessarily expecting the three-time American League MVP to be available. After the Yankees improved to 50-42 in games Judge has missed with Wednesday’s 9-2 rout of the Rays, the eight-time All-Star expressed confidence in his ability to return by next week.
“My goal is to come back as soon as I can,” Judge said. “If you ask me if I’m going to be back, I’m gonna tell you, yeah, I’m doing everything I can every single day I show up here to get back and be ready to go.”
Judge expressed confidence in his return after watching Rice hit a pair of solo homers on Wednesday, giving him 41 home runs in his second full season. Rice had three hits and a walk and is batting .349 with five homers in his past 12 games and .333 with seven homers and 17 RBIs in his past 27.
For the season, he is batting .263 with 97 RBIs after finishing with 26 homers, 65 RBIs and a .255 batting average last year.
“Each year, he’s gotten better,” Judge said of the 27-year-old. “Each month he’s gotten better. Even through bad slumps, he’s just making the reads and making the changes he needs to get back to his normal self. So it’s been fun to watch. He’s a complete player.”
Rice is hitting .381 against the Rays (96-62), who clinched the AL East with a 6-1 win over the Yankees on Tuesday night. After clinching, the Rays on Wednesday sat Yandy Diaz, who had a pair of two-run singles in the clincher.
Junior Caminero will be in the lineup to keep his streak of playing each game going but likely will be replaced after a few at-bats. Caminero took two at-bats and was lifted for a pinch hitter in the sixth.
“I just want to see good health and some guys freshened up,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said. “It’s been a long season. They’ve played really hard to get to this point. Let’s find a way to continue to get our work in, and I know and trust that whoever’s on that field, they’re going to do everything they can to win games.”
Whoever is in the lineup for the Rays will face right-hander Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.94 ERA), who will make his final regular-season start before likely starting Game 1 of the wild-card series.
Since lasting 4 1/3 innings in an 8-2 loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers on July 19, Schlittler is 5-0 with a 1.46 ERA in his past 11 starts. The Yankees fell to 20-12 in his starts on Saturday when he allowed one earned run on three hits in six innings in a no-decision during a 5-3 loss at Arizona.
Schlittler is 1-2 with a 2.63 ERA in four career starts against the Rays.
Left-hander Ian Seymour (9-7, 4.38 ERA) originally was slated to start Wednesday but had his start pushed back a day to give Freddy Peralta extra rest to face Philadelphia on Friday.
Seymour is 0-1 with a 5.79 ERA in three starts this month, including Friday’s 4-2 loss to Boston when he allowed four runs on seven hits in five innings. One of his best starts this season occurred July 7 in Tampa Bay when he struck out 12 in 5 1/3 innings during a 6-4 win over the Yankees.
-Field Level Media

item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed
item.description: The New York Yankees start the postseason on Tuesday, and three-time MVP Aaron Judge is on the injured list with a calf strain. Manager Aaron Boone has said the team does not plan to use Judge in the Wild Card Series, but he has not ruled him out. Boone described Judge's calf strain as "moderate" on Tuesday, but Judge is not a fan of him saying that. "I don't know why he used those words," Judge told reporters on Wednesday. Despite details of his injury that are known to the public, Judge is say
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees start the postseason on Tuesday, and three-time MVP Aaron Judge is on the injured list with a calf strain.
Manager Aaron Boone has said the team does not plan to use Judge in the Wild Card Series, but he has not ruled him out. Boone described Judge's calf strain as "moderate" on Tuesday, but Judge is not a fan of him saying that.
"I don't know why he used those words," Judge told reporters on Wednesday.
Despite details of his injury that are known to the public, Judge is saying he plans to be ready for Game 1 of the Wild Card Series. He received a PPP injection on Monday and is working hard to get back in the lineup for the Yankees' first postseason series.
"Everybody's 'moderate' is a little different," Judge said. "I think your moderate is a little different than my moderate."
Whether or not Judge comes back remains to be seen, but as of right now, it does not seem like his manager is expecting him to play when the Yankees begin their quest for a World Series. Still, Judge knows that what Boone says does not impact how hard he works to return.
"Boonie is my guy. I've always got his back," Judge said. "I know he makes the right decisions. Obviously, as a player you don't want to hear that, but that's out of my control. I've got to come back and be ready to go, and that's what I'm focused on right now."
