item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — La respuesta de Aaron Judge ante los cada vez más sólidos argumentos a favor de Cam Schlittler como MVP ha llamado la atención en las filas de los Yankees. Ahora, un lanzador del Salón de la Fama se ha sumado al debate… y está de acuerdo con Judge.
El exas de los Atlanta Braves, John Smoltz, defendió el razonamiento que hay detrás de los comentarios de Judge durante su aparición en el podcast «Flippin’ Bats» de Ben Verlander, sumando así otra voz destacada a un debate que ha acompañado a Schlittler a lo largo de su dominante mes de septiembre.
«Entiendo lo que dice Aaron», dijo Smoltz.
El capitán de los Yankees desató el debate después de que Schlittler arrollara a los Mets el 13 de septiembre en el Yankee Stadium. Cuando le preguntaron si su compañero merecía ser tenido en cuenta para el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana, el tres veces MVP elogió a Schlittler, pero dejó clara la diferencia entre los dos principales premios individuales de la liga.
«Sin duda está lanzando como un MVP, pero el Premio Cy Young existe por algo: es para el mejor lanzador de la liga», dijo Judge. «Así que tiene mi voto, sin duda, para el Cy Young».
La respuesta llamó la atención porque otros Yankees habían llegado más lejos.
El entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, dijo que Schlittler «también podría ser el MVP», mientras que Cody Bellinger mencionó la temporada de Clayton Kershaw en 2014, cuando fue nombrado MVP de la Liga Nacional, como prueba de que un lanzador excepcional puede entrar en esa discusión.
Judge no criticó a Schlittler. De hecho, dijo explícitamente que el lanzador diestro estaba lanzando a un nivel digno de un MVP.
Pero su comentario de que el Premio Cy Young existe para reconocer al mejor lanzador del béisbol desató un debate más amplio sobre si los lanzadores deberían ser considerados seriamente para el MVP.
Smoltz explica por qué la postura de Judge le parece lógica
La defensa de Smoltz se centró menos en las estadísticas y más en el papel diferente que desempeña un jugador de campo a lo largo de una temporada.
El miembro del Salón de la Fama argumentó que los lanzadores, por lo general, no pueden liderar un equipo exactamente de la misma manera día a día, ya que los titulares suben al montículo una vez cada cinco días. Smoltz señaló que sus equipos de los Braves eran una excepción porque Greg Maddux, Tom Glavine y él mismo aportaban colectivamente a Atlanta un liderazgo significativo desde la rotación de lanzadores.
Lo que quería decir, en definitiva, es que los equipos campeones suelen necesitar a un jugador de campo que esté presente todos los días y que pueda convertirse en la voz principal de la plantilla.
Esa distinción ayudó a Smoltz a entender por qué el capitán de los Yankees, Judge, podía considerar a Schlittler el mejor lanzador del béisbol sin por ello situarlo necesariamente en lo más alto de una votación para el MVP.
Eso no quiere decir que los lanzadores no puedan ganar el MVP.
Kershaw se llevó tanto el premio Cy Young de la Liga Nacional como el de MVP en 2014 tras terminar con un balance de 21-3 y una efectividad de 1,77. Justin Verlander logró el mismo doblete en la Liga Americana en 2011.
La opinión de Judge, en cambio, parece reflejar una distinción filosófica sobre cómo deberían funcionar ambos premios.
Eso es lo que hace que su respuesta sea especialmente interesante.
Pocos jugadores tienen más autoridad en un debate sobre el MVP que Judge, que ya ha ganado el premio tres veces. Y pocos lanzadores entienden mejor el valor de un abridor de élite que Smoltz, ganador del Cy Young y uno de los lanzadores de postemporada más destacados de su generación.
Schlittler sigue haciendo que el debate sobre el MVP sea difícil de ignorar
Schlittler no ha hecho gran cosa en el montículo para acallar los rumores.
El jugador de 25 años llegó al domingo con un balance de 14-6 y una efectividad de 1,94 —la mejor de la Liga Americana— en 190 2/3 entradas. También tiene un WHIP de 0,91 y 234 ponches, mientras que sus rivales solo le están bateando .184.
Lidera la Liga Americana en ERA e entradas lanzadas, y figura entre los mejores en varias otras categorías importantes de pitcheo.
Incluso la irregular derrota de los Yankees del sábado ante Arizona reforzó en parte sus argumentos.
Schlittler cedió tres carreras en seis entradas, pero solo una fue limpia. Permitió tres hits, dio tres bases por bolas y ponchó a seis, bajando su ERA de 1,95 a 1,94 a pesar de no obtener la decisión en la derrota por 5-3 de Nueva York en la última entrada.
Esta actuación prolongó una racha impresionante en la que los rivales han tenido dificultades para generar una ofensiva significativa contra él.
Esto nos deja con dos cuestiones distintas ahora que la temporada regular llega a su última semana.
La primera es si Schlittler, de los Yankees, ha sido el mejor lanzador de la Liga Americana. Sus estadísticas hacen que cada vez sea más difícil rebatir esa afirmación.
La segunda es si un lanzador que tiene una temporada así debería compararse con los bateadores habituales a la hora de decidir el MVP.
Judge ha dejado bastante clara su postura.
Ahora, Smoltz le ha dado al capitán de los Yankees el apoyo de una de las figuras más destacadas del béisbol en el mundo del pitcheo.
Así que la polémica en torno a Schlittler quizá tenga menos que ver con si su temporada es extraordinaria y más con lo que los votantes creen que debería significar la palabra «valioso».
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Aaron Judge injury explained: What is Yankees star facing? Surgeon talks possible return, risk
item.dc:creator: Randy Miller

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — The Yankees surely were in a somber mood during Sunday night's cross-country flight from Phoenix to New York. The AL East race is all but over and Aaron Judge is hurt again, this time potentially for the season.
The Diamondbacks prevailed 5-3 on Saturday night and 8-4 on Sunday afternoon, costing the Yankees two more games in the standings and leaving them six games behind with seven games remaining in the regular season.
Following Monday's off day, the first-place Rays will be in the Bronx for four games in three days at Yankee Stadium, which will probably lead to champagne corks popping in the visiting clubhouse. The Rays need just one win to clinch the AL East.
At this point, the Yankees will inevitably face the Red Sox a week from Tuesday in Game 1 of a Wild Card Series.
The mystery is whether Judge will be back for this best-of-three.
Here's what we know:
1. The three-time MVP is back on the injured list with a right calf strain less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him for 88 games.
2. The strain is in the soleus muscle.
3. He's eligible to be activated for next Sunday's regular-season finale, game 162.
How bad is it? What did the MRI reveal?
As usual, the Yankees and Judge have remained guarded/secretive about revealing his injury and rehab details.
"It doesn't matter what the grade is," manager Aaron Boone said last Friday in Phoenix. "We're going to get him back or we're not. That's what we're going to work to do and we'll see.''
Judge basically said the same thing to Yankees media on Saturday, while adding, "I'd like to be back for the playoffs. That's definitely the plan."
What can we unpack from what little we know?
NJ.com consulted with an NYU Langone Health sports orthopedic surgeon to provide a clearer picture of what Judge is facing without knowing if the strain is a Grade 1 (mild), Grade 2 (moderate partial tear) or Grade 3 (severe complete rupture).
"If it's a Grade 1, in two weeks you could see Judge doing baseball activities again and then three weeks back playing," Dr. Spencer Stein said. "It's a calf muscle strain and they're annoying injuries."
Judge was injured during last Wednesday's game in Minnesota, so three weeks would be Oct. 7. If the Yankees win their Wild Card Series, that would be Game 3 of their best-of-five Division Series with the Rays.
"But that's really best-case scenario," Dr. Stein said. "That would be the fastest."
Yankees designated hitter Giancarlo Stanton went on the IL in April with a Grade 1 calf strain and still hasn't returned. He had a setback in June, and then while rehabbing, he strained his other calf in August.
If Judge rushes back, he'd also be risking a setback, the doctor warned.
"I've seen studies there's up to 50% chance of re-injury in these muscular injuries — hamstring injuries, calf muscle injuries," Dr. Stein said. "There's a high rate of retear, so it's definitely a balance of not going back too quickly on them."
Rushing back might be why Judge is hurt again. When he was out with his rib injury, he was shut down from baseball activities from June 1 until Aug. 19. Less than three weeks later, Judge was back from the IL and playing right field for the Yankees with no rehab games and a few live batting-practice at-bats packed into a workout the day before his first game back.
"Well, I would say that there should always be a stepwise return to sports where you build things up and that takes time," Dr. Stein said. "When you're under a time constraint because it's end of season and the playoffs are around the corner, sometimes you have to take a risk and go a little faster. But with a risk, you can end up with another injury."
The location of his calf strain is problematic.
"The gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus muscles comprise the calf, and the soleus muscle is a push-off muscle and part of the Achilles tendon," Dr. Stein said. "There's just a lot of force in that area, a lot of strain and stress, especially when you're swinging a baseball bat."
If Judge returns, he'd be much better off DHing instead of playing right field, Dr. Stein added.
"No question," he said. "The soleus muscle constantly is engaged during simple standing and walking."
That's another risk the Yankees would have to take.
Judge would have to play right field rather than be the designated hitter. Ben Rice, who has 39 home runs and 95 RBI, is entrenched at DH, while Luis Garcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt form a potent first base first-base platoon
Here is Dr. Stein's advice for Judge:
"Follow the instructions and take it day-by-day. Work with the therapists and trainers. Make sure your strength is there. You don't want to rush it too much. You don't want a long-term injury that keeps happening.
"You want to be able to come back, and we get that, but you do want to meet the criteria: Good strength with a good amount of flexibility in the knee and ankle area."
Read the original article on NJ.com. Add NJ.com as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees playoff roster prediction: Who makes the cut with division dreams dwindling ahead of Rays series?
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality. “Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East. Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other
item.content:encoded:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.
Pitchers (11): Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Clarke Schmidt, John Schreiber, Tim Hill, Ryan Weathers
As things stand, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are scheduled to pitch against the Rays, in that order. That would give Cole, who has struggled to get swing-and-miss, an extra day of rest if he were to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young frontrunner, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1.
Because the Wild Card round is a best-of-three series, Rodón isn’t needed, especially with Will Warren expected to work out of the bullpen and able to provide length.
Warren, slated to make one more start this season after struggling on Sunday, is one of a few converted starters who could impact the Bombers’ bullpen this postseason. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are the others. Schmidt, being cautious in his return from Tommy John surgery, couldn’t come into Sunday’s game due to some bicep cramping, while Weathers isn’t expected to return from a flexor strain before the regular season ends.
Still, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled out the idea of Weathers’ first game back coming in the playoffs.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”
As for the relievers that the Yankees have leaned on all season, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick headline the group. All have been used heavily, especially Headrick.
The lefty allowed a grand slam to Nolan Arenado and saw his fastball velocity down an average of 1.3 mph during his major league-leading 79th appearance on Sunday, but he insisted that he feels fine physically. Boone also downplayed concerns over Headrick’s ongoing velocity fluctuations, though he did say that he hopes to get him and other relievers “in a good spot” with some rest ahead of the playoffs.
That said, the Yankees still haven’t been eliminated from the AL East race. They’ll keep trying to take the division from the Rays until they are.
“We’re going to show up Tuesday,” Boone said, “and try and kick their butt.”

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se fueron del Chase Field con el tipo de derrota que cambia el panorama de la última semana.
El domingo, Nueva York tuvo a Corbin Burnes contra las cuerdas, remontó un déficit inicial y se puso con una ventaja de 4-1 gracias a tres jonrones en la tercera entrada. Heliot Ramos empató el partido con un jonrón solitario. George Lombard Jr. sumó un jonrón de dos carreras, y Spencer Jones conectó otro justo después de él. Burnes se fue del partido tras 2 2/3 entradas.
La ventaja inicial no duró mucho. Will Warren llenó las bases con un out en la quinta entrada, y el bullpen de los Yankees no pudo evitar que Arizona le diera la vuelta al partido. Brent Headrick ponchó a Geraldo Perdomo y luego concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll con las bases llenas. Nolan Arenado siguió con un grand slam ante una bola rápida de cuatro costuras a 94,2 mph, dando la vuelta a un marcador de 4-2 y poniendo a los Diamondbacks por delante 6-4. Arizona sumó dos carreras más en la séptima y ganó 8-4.
Los Yankees perdieron dos de tres partidos en Arizona y ahora tienen un balance de 89-66. Tampa Bay mejoró su balance a 95-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a seis partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan siete partidos por disputar. Los Rays llegan al Yankee Stadium para una serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes con una doble jornada dividida. Una sola victoria de Tampa Bay en la serie dejaría a los Yankees fuera de la lucha por el título de la división.
Ese contexto hizo que las declaraciones del entrenador tras el partido tuvieran más peso que un simple intento de pasar página. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el club tiene que encontrar el equilibrio entre una lucha por el título de división que se va desvaneciendo y proteger a un cuerpo de lanzadores muy castigado, además de preparar una plantilla plagada de lesiones para octubre.
La afirmación de Boone choca con la clasificación
A Aaron Boone le preguntaron cómo se enfrentarían los Yankees a Tampa Bay y si el hecho de que la lucha por el título de división se esté desvaneciendo podría cambiar su forma de gestionar los minutos de juego. Su respuesta incluyó una amplia defensa de cómo ha respondido su equipo durante una temporada llena de lesiones y una importante racha negativa este verano.
«Y hemos estado a la altura en casi todas las ocasiones», dijo Boone.
Esa es la parte que llama la atención del mensaje de Boone. Aaron Judge estuvo más de tres meses de baja por una lesión en las costillas, volvió el 8 de septiembre y luego volvió a entrar en la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Además, Nueva York sufrió una racha de siete derrotas seguidas durante un tramo de 4 victorias y 14 derrotas, antes de recuperarse y asegurarse una plaza en la postemporada.
El final del partido en Arizona fue el contrapunto. Los Yankees llegaron a la quinta entrada con una ventaja de tres carreras y la terminaron perdiendo por dos. No anotaron nada después de la tercera y encadenaron dos derrotas seguidas tras ganar el primer partido del viernes por 9-2.
Las cifras cuentan dos historias diferentes sobre los Yankees
La clasificación de la MLB a fecha de 21 de septiembre muestra por qué Boone puede hablar de una temporada sólida, mientras que la tabla de la División Este de la Liga Americana presenta un panorama más sombrío.
Los Yankees han marcado 137 carreras más que sus rivales, frente a la diferencia de +83 de Tampa Bay. Según las previsiones de la MLB, Nueva York debería tener un balance de 92-63, tres victorias más que su balance real. Sin embargo, los Rays llevan una ventaja de seis partidos.
Nueva York tiene un balance de 33-32 contra equipos con un porcentaje de victorias igual o superior al 50 %. Tampa Bay tiene un balance de 37-25 en esos partidos. La capacidad de los Yankees para anotar y evitar carreras sugiere que son un equipo más fuerte de lo que indica su segunda posición en la clasificación, pero los Rays han sabido convertir los partidos difíciles en victorias con mayor consistencia.
Ese contraste es lo que le da tensión a la afirmación de Boone. Los Yankees se han recuperado de rachas perjudiciales, pero no con la frecuencia suficiente como para controlar la división de cara a la última semana.
Boone lanza un mensaje contundente a los Rays
Boone también dejó claro que no ve el martes como una puesta a punto inmediata de cara a la postemporada. Dijo que las decisiones sobre el descanso pueden dejarse para más adelante, una vez que los Yankees se enfrenten por primera vez al equipo al que llevan meses persiguiendo.
«Pero lo primero es lo primero: el martes vamos a salir al campo e intentar darles una buena paliza. Así de sencillo. Y lo mantendremos así de sencillo», dijo Boone.
A Tampa Bay le falta una victoria contra los Yankees para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Nueva York tiene que ganar los cuatro partidos para mantener vivas sus opciones de cara al último fin de semana.
Eso hace que Boone tenga que gestionar dos frentes a la vez. A los Yankees aún les queda una posibilidad matemática de ganar la división, pero la plantilla para la postemporada, la carga de trabajo del bullpen y los jugadores lesionados se están convirtiendo en las preocupaciones más prácticas de octubre. Nueva York también empieza la semana ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
La carga de trabajo de Headrick añade urgencia a la decisión de Boone
La 79.ª salida de Headrick el domingo fue la segunda más alta de las Grandes Ligas. La velocidad media de su bola rápida fue inferior a la de esta temporada, aunque él lo achacó a la ejecución más que al cansancio.
Los Yankees han confiado en Headrick durante toda la temporada. El domingo quedó claro lo rápido que esa fortaleza puede convertirse en un motivo de preocupación en octubre. Se encontró con las bases llenas, estuvo a un out de salir del apuro, pero luego concedió la base por bolas y encajó el golpe decisivo de Arenado.
Boone dijo tras la derrota que el descanso podría formar parte del plan una vez que se decida el campeón de la división. Eso podría pasar ya el martes.
Hasta entonces, su postura pública está clara. Los Yankees no van a ceder la serie ante Tampa Bay, ni siquiera después de que el colapso de Arizona haya dejado la clasificación prácticamente decidida. La gran afirmación de Boone es ahora lo que los Yankees deben demostrar en el campo: tras decir que han sabido hacer frente a la adversidad en casi todas las ocasiones, su próxima prueba llega con los Rays en posición de celebrar la victoria en el Yankee Stadium.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [si.com] Why Rushing Aaron Judge Back Isn't Worth It for the Yankees
item.dc:creator: Joe Najarian; Unknown
item.description: Despite landing on the injured list, Aaron Judge is still eager to contribute to the Yankees in the postseason. Judge, who chose to forgo a rehab assignment in favor of rejoining the team earlier in the month, told the media that he wanted to recover from his right calf strain by the start of postseason play. The American League Wild Card Series, which the Yankees would play in if the season ended today, is slated to begin on Sept. 29, just 10 days from now. On Saturday, Judge offered a simple "
item.content:encoded:
Despite landing on the injured list, Aaron Judge is still eager to contribute to the Yankees in the postseason.
Judge, who chose to forgo a rehab assignment in favor of rejoining the team earlier in the month, told the media that he wanted to recover from his right calf strain by the start of postseason play. The American League Wild Card Series, which the Yankees would play in if the season ended today, is slated to begin on Sept. 29, just 10 days from now.
On Saturday, Judge offered a simple "we'll see" when asked if he'd be back in time for the playoff action (h/t Brendan Kuty).
So if Judge were to return before then, his stay on the injured list would effectively last a minimum of 10 days. Unfortunately, it's highly unlikely that he fully recovers by then—and from a team perspective, it's not worth it for the Yankees to rush him back.
The Yankees' best lineup needs Judge in the outfield
Judge's injury will effectively prevent him from playing in right field and limit him to designated hitter duties. However, the Yankees' best lineup needs him playing in right field, as sticking him at DH with the roster currently constructed will force another one of the team's best hitters onto the bench.
After spending the first half of the season as the Yankees' starting first baseman, Ben Rice became the everyday DH when the team traded for Luis Garcia Jr., who subsequently took over at first. Garcia plays much better defense at first than Rice does, but Rice has been more productive overall (h/t Yankees) at the plate.
Regardless, both are among the Yankees' best hitters and will be integral to their postseason run.
By having Judge at DH, either Garcia or Rice would come out of the lineup. If Rice is playing first, the Yankees lose access to Garcia's strong glove at the position as well as a threat for extra bases in the heart of the order. If Garcia is at first, the team loses access to Rice's elite power and outstanding poise in clutch situations.
If one of them is called upon to pinch-hit at any point, then one will take over for the other for the rest of the game.
Having Judge in right field instead of the DH spot allows the Yankees to play both Garcia and Rice. But putting Judge in the field with a bad calf is a recipe for disaster.
The Yankees can't afford a career-altering injury to Judge
Calf strains are notorious for being easy to re-injure; look no further than Giancarlo Stanton, who essentially missed the entire season due to calf strains in both legs, including a re-injury to the original strain when rehabbing.
The calf also leads into the Achilles tendon, which becomes vulnerable to tears if the calf is already injured. Achilles tears are not only season-ending in any sport, but the long-term effects are devastating. In a baseball example, former Phillies first baseman Ryan Howard was one of the game's premier sluggers before an Achilles tear during the 2011 postseason, and he was never the same hitter after.
The Yankees don't want that for Judge, and neither does he (h/t Gary Phillips).
If Judge were to reaggravate the calf or tear his Achilles, he risks missing even more time during the 2027 season. The Yankees already saw how dramatically the offense struggles when he's out long-term, and they simply can't risk that happening again next year, especially for a player approaching his mid-30s. Neither Judge nor the Yankees even know the grade of the calf strain right now, which is further reason not to chance anything and shut him down.
Obviously, Judge still wants to play during the postseason because that's when the games matter the most. But given the nature of his injury—which is to the soleus muscle, a crucial part of his ability to hit and run—playing through it isn't an option.
The only option is for the rest of the team to step up in Judge's absence and make a deep postseason run, and perhaps the Yankees can get their captain back if he's feeling 100% by the AL Championship Series or World Series.
Joe Najarian is a writer for Yankees On SI, having previously covered the Yankees both for SI and additional sites since 2023. He also served as Deputy Editor for the Yankees, Mets and Orioles On SI sites, and additionally contributes to Athlon Sports and Men’s Journal covering Major League Baseball and other trending sports news. Joe is a graduate of Rutgers University in 2022, earning a bachelor’s degree in Journalism and Media Studies.
Follow JoeNajarian

item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.title: [thetimes-tribune.com] SWB RAILRIDERS: End of an era for franchise’s nickname
item.dc:creator: Scott Walsh
item.description: MOOSIC — Edinson Duran became the unlikely answer to a trivia question. item.content:encoded:
MOOSIC — Edinson Duran became the unlikely answer to a trivia question.
Sunday’s season finale between the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders and Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp at PNC Field was canceled due to rain and wet grounds. That meant Saturday night’s game was the last one featuring the RailRiders nickname. The team is rebranding and expected to announce the new identity in November.
So when people ask who was the winning pitcher in the final game of the RailRiders era, it isn’t a top prospect like Elmer Rodriguez or an ace like Brendan Beck. It is Duran, a catcher who spent more time on the development list this season than the active roster.
Whenever the RailRiders would need to use a position player to save arms in the bullpen, they would go to Duran. He’s done it eight times in the past two seasons, including six this season.
In the top of the 10th inning Saturday night, Justin Topa struck out the first two batters with the automatic runner on second base. However, with the count 2-1 to Logan Driscoll, Topa reached his pitch limit. With no other options, manager Shelley Duncan called upon Duran. The 24-year old from Venezuela walked Driscoll, then walked Gage Miller to load the bases, but got Johnny Olmstead to fly out to center fielder Duke Ellis to end the inning. The RailRiders won in the bottom of the 10th, 6-5, when automatic runner Yanquiel Fernandez scored from third base on a wild pitch, making Duran the winning pitcher.
“It was really exciting for Duran to come in and do what he did,” RailRiders reliever Eric Reyzelman said. “It’s fun, kind of reminds you why you play this game. Technically, we had nothing on the line playoff-wise. But we did not want to leave this place without a win.”
And so the RailRiders’ final ride has pulled into the station. The team finished 78-68 overall (37-37 first half, 41-31 second half). Its all-time record wound up 1,028 wins and 834 losses.
From the first pitch by Vidal Nuño to Pawtucket’s Brock Holt on April 4, 2013, to the last one Saturday night — Jacksonville’s Stephen Jones’ wild pitch with Kenedy Corona batting — a lot of memorable moments happened in between.
Six times the RailRiders made the playoffs. Three times they lost in the International League championship series (2017, 2018, 2025). But in 2016, they defeated the Gwinnett Braves in four games to capture the IL title, then beat the Pacific Coast League champion El Paso Chihuahuas to claim the Triple-A national championship.
Many notable players have worn a RailRiders uniform.
Hall of Famer Derek Jeter spent seven games on a rehab assignment in early July 2013 while recovering from a broken ankle. During his time here, it became a daily game to see where he was spotted in downtown Scranton.
Later that month, Alex Rodriguez played three games here while coming back from offseason hip surgery. He hit a two-run home run in the second at-bat of his first game.
Curtis Granderson and D.J. LeMahieu were other notable Yankees who rehabbed here over the years. This season, pitchers Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and outfielder Cody Bellinger had rehab stints.
Current Yankees slugger Aaron Judge played 154 games with the RailRiders in 2015 and 2016 and five more games on a rehab assignment in 2019. He totaled 28 home runs and 95 RBIs. Prospects such as Gary Sanchez, Anthony Volpe and George Lombard Jr. spent time here.
“A lot of great players have played for the RailRiders,” said Beck, who wound up leading the International League in earned-run average (2.93), strikeouts (151), innings (135.1), WHIP (1.06) and opponents’ batting average (.210). “To be the last ones to do it is fun. The future is exciting as well. Looking forward to starting something new next year. But to be the team to end the RailRiders dynasty on a comeback win with a good crowd at home is a lot of fun. Definitely a fun day at the office.”
When Duncan played in Scranton/Wilkes-Barre from 2007-09, the team was known as the Yankees. But in his four seasons as manager, the term “RailRiders” has come to mean a lot to him.
“I just always think about the character of every team that I’ve had,” said Duncan, whose record as RailRiders manager is 327-195. “I’ve been lucky to be a part of some good groups that fought all the way to the end. Some good memories and some good relationships. Each year has been a different team and each year has been very special.”
Clint Frazier was a top prospect who played 213 games for the RailRiders from 2016-19 before a severe concussion and lingering symptoms ultimately sidetracked his career. Because of his frequent shuttling between the minors and the majors, he proclaimed himself a “RailRider for Life.”
He made an appearance at Saturday night’s game, signing autographs for fans and throwing out the ceremonial first pitch.
“It was me being a little facetious,” Frazier said. “I think it started around the time I got optioned to the minor leagues in 2019. I was doing relatively well at the big-league level. When I came down here, there was something in the media about September roster expansion and the Yankees were kind of vague on whether I going to be coming back. I remember parking in a parking garage and seeing this sign that said ‘Scranton Life’ and I was like, ‘Dude, I don’t want to be a Yankee. I want to be a RailRider for Life.’ It was a facetious comment and I ended up running with it because it was kind of funny. People obviously took notice to it because I put it on my Twitter bio and it’s been there for like 10 years.”
Frazier was a little surprised and a bit disappointed when he heard the team was rebranding and retiring the RailRiders nickname.
“I’m not a part of the Yankees anymore and I’m not here in Scranton,” Frazier said. “So if they want to rebrand or it’s something the fans want, you give them it. But other than that, I was kind of like, ‘Damn, I guess I won’t be a RailRider anymore. I’ll be whatever they are.’ But I’ll still be a RailRider at heart.”
The nickname has not only meant something to players.
Kristina Knight has been with the team for 20 seasons. She started as an intern with the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Red Barons, then worked in tickets sales and group sales, sponsor servicing and currently is senior director of partnership management and marketing.
“I think it was extra special because it was a community-thought name,” Knight said. “We surveyed the community and did the poll of submitting your ideas. So I like to think it was the community’s name, which was extra special within itself. The reason we went away from the Yankees name was to give the area more ownership of the team here. I think it did that for sure.
“When we were the Yankees, it was very nice and obviously nice to be included in the Yankees family. But the RailRiders was our very own name and gave our own identity in the minor-league baseball world.”
When the new nickname is announced in November, Knight believes that the community will accept it as well.
“I think it will be as well-received and special to the community,” Knight said. “We are trying to make sure it reflects everything in this area that we find very special and attractive about our area and try to make it a highlight to the nation.”

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Clarke Schmidt to see doctor amid new injury concerns appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees' bid for the AL East crown may be all but lost, as they sit six games behind division-leader Tampa Bay Rays in the standings with seven games remaining in the regular season, but the important thing is that they have secured a spot in the Wild Card round — marking their 27th postseason berth in 34 seasons (they are currently in the middle of a 34-year winning season streak).
The key now for the Yankees is keeping their key players healthy. While the Yankees have been mostly healthy on the pitching side of things, reliever Clarke Schmidt, who returned to big-league action on September 16 after a lengthy layoff, suffered some bicep cramping on Sunday, which then prevented him from suiting up in their 8-4 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks.
While Bob Nightengale of USA Today reported that Schmidt's inability to show up on the mound was merely precautionary, he will be meeting with a doctor back in New York to ascertain that he's not suffering from any underlying serious injury that could keep him out for an extended period once more.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Schmidt didn't make his 2026 season debut until September after he underwent elbow surgery (internal brace procedure), so at least he's not suffering any setbacks in that regard.
The 30-year-old righty struck out two in 0.2 innings of work in his only appearance of 2026 in a 5-4 loss for the Yankees against the Minnesota Twins.
The Yankees have already been dealt a huge injury blow, with Aaron Judge, who only recently returned to action, suffering a calf strain that sent him back to the injured list. They already have Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham among lineup regulars already on the IL.
While New York has enough depth to make up for the absences of a few players, they would want to enter the postseason as close to full strength as they can get. With the Wild Card round set to begin in nine days, they have some time to get it together from a health standpoint.
Related: Yankees' Spencer Jones shuts down injury concern ahead of postseason

item.title: [Newsday] Erik Boland: Yankees' upcoming week all about Aaron Judge
item.dc:creator: Erik Boland
item.description: A 3-3 road trip at this point of the long season for almost any big-league team would be considered at least a minor success. The 3-3 trip for the Yankees that concluded with Sunday’s 8-4 loss to the Diamondbacks was nothing short of disastrous. And potentially season-altering — and not in a good way — depending on the prognosis for Aaron Judge’s right calf. It all starts there, of course. This time it was something other than Judge’s upper body commanding attention. During the previous three mo
item.content:encoded:
A 3-3 road trip at this point of the long season for almost any big-league team would be considered at least a minor success.
The 3-3 trip for the Yankees that concluded with Sunday’s 8-4 loss to the Diamondbacks was nothing short of disastrous.
And potentially season-altering — and not in a good way — depending on the prognosis for Aaron Judge’s right calf.
It all starts there, of course.
This time it was something other than Judge’s upper body commanding attention. During the previous three months-plus, he battled his way back from a right rib stress fracture, missing 84 games.
In the early innings of Wednesday’s loss to the Twins in Minneapolis, Judge felt discomfort in his right calf. He eventually gave way to a pinch hitter in the top of the sixth inning of what turned into a 5-4, 13-inning loss.
That defeat all but put an end to the Yankees’ AL East title hopes. They fell 4 1⁄2 games behind the Rays on Wednesday and now are six back with seven games to play. The Rays’ magic number is down to two, which means that if the Yankees lose even one of the four games against Tampa Bay this week, the division race is over.
So the 3-3 trip essentially cemented the Yankees as a wild-card team and sucked any remaining drama there might have been for this week’s series at the Stadium. The Yankees are a club headed for a best-of-three Wild Card Series showdown with the Red Sox.
Winning three of four against the Red Sox from Aug. 28-30 and outscoring them 26-9 gave the Yankees a 7-6 edge in the season series.
A Yankees-Red Sox matchup at the Stadium in the wild-card round has seemed fairly inevitable since Boston left town the night of Aug. 30 after a 16-1 loss.
As incredible as the Red Sox’s 32-5 stretch was, they have gone 52-67 the rest of the season. They cut the Yankees’ 15 1⁄2-game lead to a half-game with that hot streak but never caught them, and they have gone 20-21 since the streak ended on Aug. 7.
So before the road trip to Minnesota and Arizona, the potential of a wild-card matchup with the Red Sox — aside from the anything-can-happen element that goes with any short series in baseball — hadn’t thrown a huge scare into the fan base.
Now, however, Judge seems questionable at best for that series, which has taken on a far different look — and created additional angst for Yankees fans — with the potential of the three-time American League MVP missing it entirely or being severely limited in it.
While it’s true the Yankees managed that season-series win against the Red Sox without Judge, who did not return until Sept. 8, that late August series was mostly an outlier when it came to the performance of their offense when the outfielder was out.
The Yankees did well enough in Judge’s absence with a more than respectable 45-39 record, but the difference in the offense’s numbers were striking.
Through May 31, the last game Judge played before going on the injured list in early June, Yankees were 36-23, averaging 5.2 runs per game and hitting .243 with a .770 OPS.
Without Judge before his return on Sept. 8? The offense averaged 4.1 runs per game and hit .227 with a .681 OPS in that 45-39 stretch.
The upcoming week now becomes all about Judge. The only question that matters: Just how serious is his calf strain?
In the least surprising development that has occurred since Judge came out of Wednesday’s game, the Yankees, taking their cue from the outfielder, have said little regarding what’s to come.
But even within the vagueness of most of the answers, there was room for tea-leaf reading.
A somber Aaron Boone said after Wednesday’s game (before knowing of the upcoming MRI tests): “Hopefully we get it treated and knock it out and he’ll be a factor at some point.”
The “some point” sent up all kinds of red flags.
Judge, speaking to reporters in Phoenix on Saturday, said, “I’d like to be back by the postseason. That’s definitely the plan.”
Judge saying he’d “like” to be back by the playoffs — which for the Yankees are very likely to begin Sept. 29 — and that doing so is “the plan” is not the same as a “this is a small thing; I’ll be back” guarantee.
That Judge, who did not play in any rehab games before his return, went 4-for-23 with 13 strikeouts and one homer in seven games before returning to the injured list is not relevant.
It’s his mere presence in the lineup — and what it represents in terror factor to opposing pitchers, regardless of whether Judge is in a hot streak or cold streak — that matters.
What kind of a presence Judge will be come Sept. 29 — and whether he will be a presence at all — will take center stage in evaluating the week to come, and not how the Yankees do against the Rays and Orioles to end the season.
Judge’s calf is now all that matters this week, a week that, up until this 3-3 trip, appeared assured of meaning so much more.

item.content:encoded:
There’s a lot on the line before the 2026 regular season wraps up on Sunday, including postseason seeding, statistical milestones and player development. And even for the players and teams who won’t be chasing a World Series title, finishing the season strong is always important.
With the help of MLB.com’s beat writers, here is one player to watch on each team during the final week of the regular season.
American League East
Blue Jays: 1B Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Over and over again, the flashes we’ve seen from Guerrero have fizzled. He was the face of the Blue Jays’ run to Game 7 of the World Series a year ago, but now, he’s the face of their disappointing 2026. It’s still so easy to believe in Guerrero when you see these flashes of his incredible talent, but he’s hit just nine home runs this season and has been living with an OPS under .700, stunning numbers for someone of his stature. Still, he’s the player with the most power to change this team’s trajectory, and if anyone can help salvage this season, it’s Guerrero. -- Keegan Matheson
Orioles: 1B Pete Alonso
Who else? If the O’s are going to make an improbable push into the postseason as a Wild Card team, it will likely be because of Alonso, who has done everything in his power to keep his team in the race down the stretch. There have been only nine 40-plus-homer seasons in Orioles history (since 1954), but Alonso could join the list with a strong finish to his first campaign in Baltimore. -- Jake Rill
Rays: 3B Junior Caminero
With all due respect to Chandler Simpson’s bid for both the AL batting crown and stolen-base title, this one’s pretty simple. Caminero has established himself as a legitimate candidate for the AL MVP Award alongside Yordan Alvarez. He’s leading the AL in home runs. He’s tracking toward starting all 162 games at third base. He’s the best player on the best team in the AL. And as an opening act for his first real moment in the postseason spotlight, he hit the first two walk-off homers of his career -- including one to clinch a playoff berth. Caminero’s power and energy always make him a player to watch, and that’s especially true as the Rays work to lock down their first division title since 2021. -- Adam Berry
Red Sox: LHP Garrett Crochet
The ace lefty is in a race against time to help the Red Sox as a reliever by the Wild Card round of the playoffs. Here is what's on the docket for Crochet: at least one live batting practice session at Fenway Park early in the week. After that, he would likely throw another live BP or a simulated game. An outside possibility would be the Red Sox getting him a tune-up in a regular-season game. Crochet last pitched for the Sox on April 25 before going down with a left shoulder injury. Most players wouldn’t go cold turkey into the playoffs after not pitching for so long, but Crochet has the chance to make the type of impact that could make it worthwhile. -- Ian Browne
Yankees: RHP Cam Schlittler
No matter where you stand on the issue of a pitcher winning the MVP Award, there’s no debating that Schlittler has earned that title within the Yankees’ clubhouse, putting the finishing touches on the club’s best pitching season since Ron Guidry in 1978. Those Yankees won a championship, and now the current group will lean on the 25-year-old from Walpole, Mass., to lead them toward the Canyon of Heroes for the first time since 2009. -- Bryan Hoch
AL Central
Guardians: 3B José Ramírez
Ramírez has produced below his superstar standard this season, in which he has dealt with the aftereffects of left hamate surgery he underwent in June. It’s something he’ll have to manage the remainder of 2026, but the 34-year-old might be turning it on at the right time. Ramírez is 8-for-17 with three doubles, one home run and three RBIs in his past four games. -- Tim Stebbins
Royals: C Carter Jensen
Jensen’s breakout rookie season has cemented him alongside Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone as a core piece for a club looking to compete again in 2027. He’s already set Royals rookie records for home runs (25) and extra-base hits (60). Oh, and he’s done it while batting leadoff (he holds another record there, too) and taking over everyday catching duties from Salvador Perez. -- Jackson Stone
Tigers: SS/3B Kevin McGonigle
This could be the week that McGonigle wraps up the AL Rookie of the Year race. He’s the first rookie since Aaron Judge in 2017, and the fifth since 1990, to reach base safely 256 times in a season. He has more walks (94) than strikeouts (92) and is just the fifth rookie in the Divisional Era (since 1969) with that many walks in a season. And he joins Ted Williams as the only rookies in history to post at least 95 runs, 26 doubles, 17 homers, 70 RBIs and 93 walks. He has a chance to lead all AL position players in Baseball-Reference WAR, entering Sunday atop the AL at 6.8. -- Jason Beck
Twins: OF Emmanuel Rodriguez
Rodriguez has already shown his all-around skill set, from power to plate discipline to speed and defense. The only thing that has held him back over his pro career has been health, and now that he’s on the field, he’s hard to take your eyes off. Rodriguez is one of a slew of young Twins trying to cement their spots on the 2027 roster. -- Courtney Hollmon
White Sox: 1B Munetaka Murakami
Right-handed reliever Mike Vasil, also known as the Windy City Wizard for his dugout wand magic, said it best about Murakami: When he goes, the team goes. Murakami changed this franchise upon his arrival from Japan, taking the focus off a 6-13 team start and putting it upon his strong exploits on the field. Murakami has struggled since the start of August but showed his importance via a mammoth three-run home run in the first inning of a 3-1 victory over Detroit on Thursday. If Murakami can get hot over these final two series, the White Sox could punch their unexpected playoff ticket. -- Scott Merkin
AL West
Angels: C/1B/DH Moisés Ballesteros
Ballesteros got off to a slow start after being acquired in a trade that sent reliever Ryan Zeferjahn to the Cubs at the Trade Deadline but has been heating up offensively in September. He’s also been faring better than expected defensively at both catcher and first base. The 22-year-old was ranked as a Top 100 prospect by MLB Pipeline before each of the last two seasons, and the Angels would love to see him develop into a much-needed power bat from the left side. -- Rhett Bollinger
Astros: DH Yordan Alvarez
Shortstop Jeremy Peña said it best Thursday: “Obviously, Yordan is our horse.” After a 35-game stretch (Aug. 3-Sept. 13) in which he slashed .242/.380/.383 with three homers (since Aug. 3) to loosen his grip on the AL MVP Award, Alvarez homered in two of three games against the Royals last week and is still in contention for the Triple Crown. Alvarez leads the AL in batting average (.313) and is second in homers (40) and RBIs (99). -- Brian McTaggart 
Athletics: OF Henry Bolte
The A’s saw a five-tool talent in Bolte when they drafted him out of high school in 2022, and that has played out this year as he’s become just the third rookie in franchise history with at least 10 home runs and 20 stolen bases in a season and the first since Mitchell Page in 1977. Still just scratching the surface of his abilities, Bolte is building for what could be true star potential from him in 2027. -- Martín Gallegos
Mariners: INF/OF Michael Arroyo
Seattle's No. 3 prospect and MLB Pipeline's No. 42 overall prospect has played sparingly -- just five starts in the team’s 13 games since he made his MLB debut on Sept. 6. But that's been primarily due to a lack of positional runway. He came up as a second baseman but has transitioned more to left field this season. However, both those spots are occupied (by Cole Young and Randy Arozarena, respectively). Arroyo is a big part of the club's longer-term plans and has shown what he can do with the bat. How he's used in this final week could be a springboard for 2027. -- Daniel Kramer
Rangers: SS Corey Seager
Seager is the engine that keeps the Rangers offense going, and his absence has been felt throughout his three separate stints on the injured list this season (twice with back issues, once with a concussion). As he played sporadically in the first half, Seager hit just .182/.292/.374 as he battled injuries. Since returning from his last IL stint on July 31, he’s hitting .285 with an .837 OPS and eight homers in 45 games. The Rangers will only go as far as Seager takes them. And lately, he looks like the player who can put the team on his back. -- Kennedi Landry
National League East
Braves: RHP Robert Suarez
Suarez made a rehab appearance on Sunday with Triple-A Gwinnett, striking out one in a scoreless inning. The veteran reliever hasn’t pitched in the Majors since he was shut down in late June with a 0.56 ERA. There’s hope he will pitch in a big league game before the postseason begins, but the Braves haven’t committed to activating him before the regular season concludes. -- Mark Bowman
Marlins: SS Otto Lopez
A 2026 All-Star, Lopez needs 15 hits over his final six games to become the first Marlin since Luis Arraez in 2023 to reach 200 hits. Lopez (.305) trails Arraez (.313) and D-backs catcher Gabriel Moreno (.307) for the National League batting title. If Lopez can somehow leapfrog that pair, he would be the fourth NL batting champion in franchise history, joining Arraez ('23), Dee Strange-Gordon ('15) and Hanley Ramirez ('09). -- Christina De Nicola
Mets: RHP Jonah Tong
Few Mets players have as much to prove as Tong, who spent most of this season in the Minors before recently returning and flashing some much-improved form. If Tong can finish the year with another solid start, he will position himself well for what’s sure to be a lively rotation competition next spring. If he falters, he’ll only give the Mets more reason to be wary of him. -- Anthony DiComo
Nationals: OF James Wood
Wood slugged his way into his second All-Star selection, then missed 27 games because of a left oblique strain. He returned from the IL on Sept. 2 and is batting .259 with a .698 OPS this month. Wood, who just turned 24 on Thursday, will look to make up for the time he lost to injury and close out the final week of the season strong. -- Jessica Camerato
Phillies: LHP Jesús Luzardo
Luzardo is on the 15-day injured list with inflammation in his left shoulder. He’s eligible to be activated on Sunday, the final game of the regular season. It doesn’t necessarily matter if he pitches or not that day. It matters if the Phillies think Luzardo, who began throwing on Sunday, can pitch in the NL Wild Card Series, which begins on Sept. 29. If he can pitch, can he start? Or does he come out of the bullpen? He’s been arguably baseball’s best pitcher for months, so the Phillies need him one way or another. -- Todd Zolecki
NL Central
Brewers: RHP Jacob Misiorowski
Misiorowski probably has the National League Cy Young Award locked up. And his final regular-season start later this week will probably be tapered, since there’s no need to push his pitch count into dangerous territory. But the outing is still important, because it offers the Brewers’ young ace one final opportunity to build confidence going into what will surely be a Game 1 start in the NL Division Series. No club better showcases the fact that baseball is a team sport, but there’s little doubt that Misiorowski is singularly important to Milwaukee’s October hopes. -- Adam McCalvy
Cardinals: 1B Alec Burleson
Outfielder Jordan Walker received a lot of publicity because of his breakout season and winning the T-Mobile Home Run Derby, but Burleson is the man on the Cardinals, currently leading the Major Leagues with 111 RBIs. The last Cardinal to lead the big leagues in that department was Joe Torre (137) in 1971, and the last to lead the National League was Albert Pujols (118) in 2010. Burleson also leads the Majors with 61 hits with runners in scoring position, the most by a Cardinal since Brian Jordan (62) in 1996. -- Bill Ladson
Cubs: OF Pete Crow-Armstrong
All the “P-C-A” chants at Wrigley Field have transformed into “M-V-P” chants every time Crow-Armstrong steps to the plate for the North Siders. Crow-Armstrong is vying to become just the seventh player in MLB history to finish with at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases. Beyond keeping an eye on how high he can get those numbers, Cubs fans want to see just how high Crow-Armstrong’s MLB-leading WAR (10.5, per FanGraphs) can get before season’s end. And then, of course, the question will be whether the star center fielder can play like an MVP in October. -- Jordan Bastian
Pirates: SS Konnor Griffin
Pittsburgh fans have received small samples of what Griffin can do as baseball’s former top prospect. After missing most of the summer due to two separate IL stints, Griffin has become a regular at shortstop and in the leadoff spot to finish out his rookie campaign. To put it simply, Griffin is both the present and the future. Keep a close eye on his continued ascension in the final week. -- Aiden Stepansky
Reds: 1B Sal Stewart
Stewart will be trying to put the finishing touches on a season that should net him the NL Rookie of the Year Award. The 22-year-old is the 14th rookie since 1920 to post a 30-homer, 100-RBI season, and each of the last nine that did it since the award started in 1947 have won it, the most recent being Pete Alonso for the Mets in 2019. Stewart is currently second in MLB overall in RBIs with 110. If he can overtake Burleson, he would be the third rookie to finish a season leading in that category since RBIs became an official statistic in 1913, joining Ted Williams (1939) and Walt Dropo (1950). -- Mark Sheldon
NL West
D-backs: OF Corbin Carroll
Carroll battled a lower back issue which clearly hampered him at the plate, but after taking a couple of days off to rest, he has begun to swing the bat much better. As the D-backs have seen many times in the past when Carroll gets hot, it’s something to see. If they get his bat going and Gabriel Moreno and Nolan Arenado continue to swing it the way they have, the D-backs will have a puncher’s chance during the final week. -- Steve Gilbert
Dodgers: TWP Shohei Ohtani
Ohtani landed on the 15-day IL for the first time as a Dodger when his ongoing right biceps and left knee issues lingered into the beginning of September. He is done for the season as a pitcher, but he's expected back as a hitter. The final week of the regular season will be important for Ohtani, whether he returns in time to play a few games or tunes up his swing behind the scenes. -- Sonja Chen
Giants: 1B Bryce Eldridge
Now that Rafael Devers is out for the season, Eldridge -- once he clears concussion protocol --  has the chance to play first base every day for the Giants. The 21-year-old rookie has made some impressive strides with his defense, but his calling card remains his big bat, which has produced several majestic homers this year, including a 461-foot blast on Tuesday night at Busch Stadium. The Giants have struggled to develop star hitters in recent years, but Eldridge’s tantalizing power should give them plenty to dream on heading into 2027. -- Maria Guardado
Padres: RHP Nick Pivetta
Pivetta missed nearly five months with a flexor strain in his right elbow. His first few starts since returning have been mostly solid. The Padres have serious rotation questions heading into the postseason and will be assessing Pivetta’s final outing with a keen eye on what kind of usage might lie ahead for him in October. If they can get the dominant version of Pivetta that finished sixth in NL Cy Young voting last season, it would go a long way. -- AJ Cassavell
Rockies: 1B TJ Rumfield
Blocked in the Yankees organization, Rumfield flourished after being acquired in a quiet deal last offseason. His stingy at-bats -- with the patience to draw a walk, fight off tough pitches and shorten up and go the other way -- are examples of the offensive culture shift the Rockies are seeking. There is power potential. He has hit home runs in spurts this year, and a year's experience -- not just on the field, but dealing with the grind of a Major League season -- could lead to even more pop. -- Thomas Harding

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees' Paul Goldschmidt Has Gone From Disposable to Indispensable
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: For a short while there, it appeared that Paul Goldschmidt was a prime candidate to be left off the New York Yankees' postseason roster. The addition of Luis Garcia Jr. had completely clouded Goldschmidt's role, and it appeared that the impending returns of Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton would make the former NL MVP rather disposable. item.content:encoded:
For a short while there, it appeared that Paul Goldschmidt was a prime candidate to be left off the New York Yankees' postseason roster.
The addition of Luis Garcia Jr. had completely clouded Goldschmidt's role, and it appeared that the impending returns of Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton would make the former NL MVP rather disposable.
My, how things have changed.
Yes, Goldschmidt's at-bats have still been somewhat sparse since the arrival of Garcia at the MLB trade deadline, but with Judge and Stanton now both potentially out for the playoffs (or at least the Wild Card Series), Goldschmidt's value just increased exponentially.
Suddenly, Goldschmidt is now one of the Yankees' very best options against left-handed pitching, and he may get some starts in the playoffs now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf.
Goldschmidt has always mashed southpaws, owning a lifetime 1.006 OPS against them. This year, he is slashing .309/.404/.592 versus lefties, making him a must on New York's playoff squad.
It should also be noted that after a miserable month of July and after barely playing in August, Goldschmidt has gone 6-for-18 at the plate this month, so he is starting to rediscover his stroke as October draws near.
And with the Boston Red Sox — New York's likely Wild Card opponent — being loaded with left-handers, Goldschmidt will likely get significant playing time early on in the postseason.
In that scenario, Ben Rice would serve as the DH — a role that almost certainly would have gone to Stanton had he been available — and Goldschmidt will play over at first base. Garcia would then come off the bench as a pinch hitter against righties.
Goldschmidt's overall numbers this season look solid, as he is slashing .253/.316/.455 with 18 home runs and 50 RBI across 370 trips to the dish. Not bad for a 39-year-old.
However, a massive chunk of Goldschmidt's damage was done back in May and June, when he combined for 13 homers and 37 RBI and was a borderline All-Star.
Goldschmidt's production has nose dived since then, but he appears to be kicking it back into gear just in time for the playoffs.
And now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf, you can expect Goldschmidt to play a pivotal role.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — The Yankees’ chances of winning the AL East are on life support.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Of greater concern is whether their bullpen meltdown Sunday was just a bad day or represents cracks emerging in a heavily worked unit.
Brent Headrick served up a grand slam to Nolan Arenado in the fifth inning, flipping the game on its head and all but wrapping up the Yankees’ spot in the AL wild-card series next week after an 8-4 loss to the Diamondbacks at Chase Field.
By dropping the series finale, a game they once led 4-1, the Yankees (89-66) fell to six games back of the Rays with seven to play.
They will welcome the Rays to Yankee Stadium on Tuesday for a four-game showdown, needing a sweep to stay alive in the division race. One win by the Rays in The Bronx will secure them the AL East title.
The Yankees would then turn their attention to securing the top AL wild card, ending Sunday leading the Red Sox by 5 ¹/₂ games, though Aaron Judge’s questionable status for that series because of a calf strain looms over everything.
In the meantime, Sunday’s loss — on the heels of Saturday’s walk-off win by the Diamondbacks (82-74) — was another regrettable one after third-inning home runs by Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones had staked them to a 4-1 lead.
In the bottom of the fifth, Will Warren loaded the bases with one out, at which point Aaron Boone called on reliable lefty Headrick for his 79th appearance of the season — the second most in the majors.
Before Sunday, Headrick had inherited 50 runners this season and allowed only five of them to score.
But after striking out the first batter he faced, Headrick walked Corbin Carroll to force in a run, which brought Arenado to the plate.
Shop Yankees Merch
Arenado crushed Headrick’s 2-0 fastball just to the left of the left field foul pole, but then straightened it out on the very next pitch (another fastball), clobbering a grand slam to put the Diamondbacks ahead 6-4.
The Diamondbacks later added a pair of insurance runs off John Schreiber in the seventh inning, the first earned runs Schreiber has allowed as a Yankee.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Aaron Judge encabeza la lista de lesionados más importantes que afectan a los contendientes de la MLB
