item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees made two moves at the MLB trade deadline, acquiring a pair of bats in Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos.
Both deals were puzzling at the time given the awkward fit, but now, with Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton potentially both out for the playoffs, it makes sense.
We've already spoken enough about Garcia, so let's focus on Ramos for a second.
Ramos has not been good since arriving in the Bronx.
Heading into Saturday night's matchup against the Arizona Diamondbacks, Ramos was slashing .165/.311/.306 with two home runs and eight RBI over 103 plate appearances in pinstripes. That came after he slashed .264/.304/.424 in San Francisco this season.
Not that Ramos was exactly lighting it up with the Giants, posting a .728 OPS, but he was certainly more productive than he has been with the Yankees.
But there is one area in which Ramos has surprisingly elevated his game since the trade: plate discipline. More specifically, taking pitches.
Ramos owned a 13.6 percent walk rate with New York going into Saturday, which is well above his lifetime median of 7.3 percent.
In fact, in spite of the fact that Ramos is hitting nearly 100 points lower with the Yankees than he did with the Giants this season, his on-base percentage in New York has been higher.
Ramos has never been one for free passes. He topped out at 52 walks last season, finishing with a 7.5 percent walk rate. His OBP in 2025 was .328. He lays claim to a lifetime .316 OBP.
Is it possible there is a legitimate reason why it's suddenly improving with the Yanks? Or is this a classic case of small sample size?
Perhaps being surrounded by better hitters has helped. Ramos is still striking out, having fanned 29 times. But he is doing a much better job of working the count and, as a result, finding other ways to get on base.
Ramos is under club control through 2029, so barring an offseason trade, he could be with the Yankees for a while. If he can start making contact again and hit closer to his career average of .252 while still walking, perhaps New York might have something here.
And with Judge now possibly sidelined for the postseason due to his calf strain, Ramos might have an even bigger role than expected in October.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What the Yankees' Lineup Should Look Like Without Aaron Judge In October
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno; Unknown
item.description: Aaron Judge's regular season may be over, but that doesn't mean the Yankees' has to be. A mystery calf ailment popped up suddenly on Wednesday and has resulted in the Yankees captain being placed on the injured list. It's unclear whether he will return in 2026, even if he's eligible to return next weekend. Aaron Boone did not give any information on the severity of the calf issue, but the timeline is likely not good due to how tricky those injuries prove to be. A scenario is now potentially unfo
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge's regular season may be over, but that doesn't mean the Yankees' has to be.
A mystery calf ailment popped up suddenly on Wednesday and has resulted in the Yankees captain being placed on the injured list. It's unclear whether he will return in 2026, even if he's eligible to return next weekend. Aaron Boone did not give any information on the severity of the calf issue, but the timeline is likely not good due to how tricky those injuries prove to be.
A scenario is now potentially unfolding that would have only appeared in Boone's nightmares: a postseason without the best hitter in baseball, with a lineup that struggled mightily without him. Even if they seemed to gradually improve as time went on, particularly in August, it would be a massive blow if he cannot return.
You can't replace a guy like Judge midseason; you can merely do your best to make up for his absence. Fortunately, on a platoon-heavy team like this, they should have plenty of options to build a lineup without him for the playoffs.
What the playoff lineup should look like against right-handed pitching
- Ben Rice (DH)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Luis García Jr. (1B)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Austin Wells (C)
- Ryan McMahon (3B)
This lineup simultaneously features the easiest decisions, but also the roughest circumstances. Having a guy like Judge as the ultimate lineup balancer who mashed both lefties and righties allowed you to use plenty of left-handed hitters at the top of the order, something that the team has in abundance.
The best right-handed hitter on the roster without Judge is hard to pinpoint, especially since all of them are significantly worse against same-handed pitching. Heliot Ramos might just be the best option to bat highest among them, which would be cleanup in this scenario.
It's not an ideal situation in the slightest. Even if you don't think it makes sense to bat Ramos that high because of his struggles against righties, there is some merit to breaking up the team's many left-handed bats. In a lineup that will likely only feature one other righty, it has to be considered.
The fate of this lineup when they're out there, which would likely be mostly after a potential Wild Card Series with the Red Sox, would hinge on the middle. Spencer Jones and Jazz Chisholm Jr. got hot in August and helped the offensive turnaround begin, but both are heavily streaky bats with contact issues. If they go cold, this lineup might limp through games like they did in July.
What the playoff lineup should look like against left-handed pitching
- Paul Goldschmidt (1B)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Ben Rice (DH)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- Anthony Volpe/José Caballero (3B)
- Austin Wells (C)
Here's where it gets interesting. How far do you lean into the platoons on a team with several players designated to specifically hit lefties, especially against a team that will likely lean heavily on those types of pitchers in Boston?
Many Yankees fans believe that it would be improper to take a guy like García, who is likely the team's second-best pound-for-pound hitter with Judge injured, out of the lineup, but you don't really have a choice here. He's slashing just .238/.274/.363 against lefties, while Goldschmidt has been among the team's best hitters against them for the last two seasons. Add in Rice's improvements against same-handed pitching, and it just needs to be done.
Using him in a different position is also just not happening. He has not played second base, where he was extremely poor, since 2025. The only position he's played this season is first base. If he wasn't so dreadful out there, maybe he could replace Chisholm, a mediocre hitter against lefties in his own right.
Speaking of defense, you might notice the lack of Amed Rosario, and that's intentional. Rosario's use on this roster was almost exclusively predicated on his ability to hit left-handed pitching, but he's been significantly worse at it this season. Add in his truly dreadful defense, and you have a conundrum.
Anthony Volpe is a better hitter than José Caballero, but there are questions about how his arm strength would play at third, where he's also very inexperienced with just three games played in Triple-A. Caballero would probably get the nod here, but he's someone who just plays better off the bench with his speed and versatility.
It's also an aggressive placement for Lombard, batting fifth in his first career playoff game. The results haven't quite been there yet for him, but he's always been significantly better against lefties and should be slid up the lineup and be treated as one of those platoon bats who are there to hit that handedness, even if it might lead to consequences in the bullpen.
Boston is loaded with left-handed pitching from the rotation to the bullpen, so there will be few opportunities to get to a guy like García on the bench. The rest of the bench would be situational with pinch runners and pinch hitters.
Things ultimately look particularly shallow, but is there a chance that some last-minute reinforcements could help out?
Could Trent Grisham or Giancarlo Stanton return to provide relief?
It seems unlikely, especially early in the postseason, but the Yankees are refusing to shut the door on either Trent Grisham's or Giancarlo Stanton's return.
Grisham, who suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain earlier this month, was revealed to be "pretty far along" in his running program, and Boone said it's not out of the question that he returns in the season's final days, although an exact timeline for that has not been spelled out. If Grisham is physically ready to get back on the field, it would provide a boost, even if he might not be starting over Jones at this point.
Stanton, who's been out since April due to two separate calf strains and a re-aggravation, has continued to hit through his rehab, but hasn't resumed running as of last Sunday. Considering how it took several weeks for him to even get close to back from injury with his running program last time, this likely doesn't put him in play until the ALCS at the earliest.
While Stanton seems significantly less likely to get into a game again this season, there is a path for Grisham. The team could use him and Ramos in a platoon situation to add yet another lefty to the lineup against right-handed pitching. They could also utilize him as a pinch hitter on a larger bench than usual, due to the team's propensity to carry fewer than 13 pitchers in the Wild Card Series.
The real question for Grisham is defensive. While Jones has absolutely looked shaky in center field, the struggles of Grisham out there are well documented. Add in his diminished athleticism and likely balky hamstring straight off an injury, would it be better if the team just chanced it by throwing him in right field when he plays?
He hasn't played the position since a disastrous error lost the Brewers the 2019 Wild Card Game against the Nationals, but playing it at Yankee Stadium is significantly easier than dealing with the spacious center field. Of course, this is something the Yankees would have to determine their willingness to do beforehand and have him practice the position, so what plans they have will be determined by that.
As for Stanton if he's ever medically able to get back? There just might not be any room for him with Rice as the permanent DH. You don't want to take the bat out of either of their hands, and with the team seemingly having to juggle multiple guys coming off soft-tissue injuries, can they afford to use a roster spot for a designated pinch hitter as they did with 2022 Matt Carpenter?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] “Aaron Judge Is Falling Apart”; “Hang Up the Cleats” – Fans Rip Yankees Captain for Staying Tight-Lipped About Severity of Injury
item.dc:creator: Shantanu Bhattacharjee

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees captain Aaron Judge is facing intense scrutiny online for not revealing the severity of his latest right calf strain. The lack of transparency regarding his MRI results and cliffhanger responses has sparked online frustration, with many calling for Judge to retire for good.
Aaron Judge suffered a severe injury to the soleus muscle in his right calf in his first at-bat Wednesday, playing against the Minnesota Twins. Judge felt a stiffness in his lower right leg during the first inning but continued playing. He was eventually removed in the sixth inning. The club put him on the 10-day injured list, which has now raised serious doubts about his availability for upcoming games.
When asked how serious the injury was, Judge reportedly refused to disclose its severity. An MRI was done, but Judge did not reveal the strain's specific grade.
Baseball insider Bryan Hoch posted Judge's statement regarding the injury on X:
"I'd like to be back by the postseason. That's definitely the plan. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that."
The secrecy of his medical status has only fueled speculation and frustrations among MLB fans.
One user said:
"He's [Aaron Judge] falling apart. This is weirdly familiar to Stanton…."
Another user wrote:
Someone said:
One user wrote:
One more user wrote:
Judge's earliest possible return date is September 27, in the final regular-season game against the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium.
Yankees Manager Addresses Aaron Judge's Injury
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone addressed Aaron Judge's injury, admitting that the team is capable of going the distance without its captain:
"The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
Boone also said:
"I don't have a timeline on him, I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires."
With Judge out, the Yankees, holding the No. 1 wild-card spot, are set to face the Boston Red Sox in a best-of-three series beginning September 29.

item.content:encoded:
The St. Louis Cardinals missed the playoffs this season and will need to head back to the drawing board to build a team that can qualify for the postseason next year.
Moreover, the question is what moves they should make to improve the team to challenge the Chicago Cubs and Milwaukee Brewers in the NL Central.
It’s been a wild 2026 MLB season for Anthony Volpe, who was optioned to Triple-A in August and then recalled in September. Still, it might be in the 25-year-old’s best interest to get a fresh start elsewhere.
Since reaching the majors in 2023, Volpe has been hitting .225 with 432 hits, 54 homers, 218 RBIs, and 241 runs scored in 537 games for the New York Yankees in his career, per StatMuse.
Despite this production during his four seasons in Pinstripes, FanSided’s Robert Murray believes that the Cardinals could be the change of scenery that Volpe needs after a rollercoaster career with the Yankees.
“Anthony Volpe would be a really good, buy-low option for the Cardinals,” Murray wrote in a Sept. 19 article. “Volpe was supposed to be the Yankees’ long-term answer at shortstop. Instead, he struggled mightily and fluctuated between the majors and minors.
“The Yankees still believe in Volpe and want to hold him, so a trade might be considered unlikely. But this is something that other teams will sniff around this offseason, I believe, and Bloom – who has previously worked with the Red Sox and Rays – should have plenty of familiarity in dealing with the Yankees.”
Anthony Volpe Could Boost Trade Value In the Coming Weeks
Since being recalled on Sept. 9, Volpe has performed well. Entering Sept. 20, Volpe has been batting .290 with nine hits, a home run, seven RBIs, and four runs scored in seven games, per StatMuse.
Moreover, if Volpe can end the season on a high note and have a productive postseason, his trade value might increase, and a team like the Cardinals could feel they can tap into his potential.
Volpe will have an opportunity to step up like every Yankee in that lineup, given that Aaron Judge is back on the injured list. New York can’t replace Judge with one batter, but they can do so with everyone chipping in.
Cardinals, Yankees Get Compelling Trade Idea
Recently, Christopher Kline of FanSided floated a trade idea that would send Volpe along with LHP Brent Headrick and LHP Kyle Carr to the Cardinals for 24-year-old shortstop Masyn Winn.
“The Yankees’ lack of fundamental soundness on the defensive end has bitten them in the you-know-what all season, just like it did last year,” Kline wrote in a Sept. 16 article. “The hope was that top prospect George Lombard Jr. could steady the ship at shortstop, but he has stacked up errors left and right.
“It’s too early to write off the 21-year-old long term, but he could serve more comfortably at third or second — which is notable, since Jazz Chisholm Jr. is about to [be a free agent]. Winn immediately alleviates a ton of defensive issues for the Yankees, while his weaker bat would be well-protected in the American League’s most potent lineup.”

item.title: [USA Today] Cam Schlittler laments what he couldn't do for Yankees with AL East hopes slipping away
item.dc:creator: Bob Nightengale
item.description: Cam Schlittler laments what he couldn't do for Yankees with AL East hopes slipping away PHOENIX — It was more than an hour since New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler threw a pitch Saturday evening, and he was still upset with himself. item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler laments what he couldn't do for Yankees with AL East hopes slipping away
PHOENIX — It was more than an hour since New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler threw a pitch Saturday evening, and he was still upset with himself.
He had another strong performance in the Yankees’ 5-3 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks, one that just about every starter in baseball would take − but they’re not Schlittler.
They’re not demanding perfection.
They’re not having one of the greatest seasons in baseball history.
So, when you give up just three hits and one earned run in six innings, it’s not good enough.
Not when you’re cruising to the Cy Young award with a 14-6 record and 1.94 ERA, yielding no more than one earned run in 22 of 32 starts, the best mark in Yankees history.
The 24-year-old has looked like Bob Gibson on the road, yielding an insane 1.16 ERA, the third-lowest in MLB history in a pitcher’s first 17 road starts. The only pitchers with a lower road ERA are Gibson in 1968 and Claude Hendrix in 1914.
Still, Schlittler didn’t care about any of that. All he knows is that the Yankees lost on Pavin Smith’s pinch-hit, two-run homer in the ninth inning, and he blamed himself.
He was livid that he couldn’t field a bunt in the fifth inning by Tim Tawa, and paid the price by giving up a two-run triple to Jordan Lawlar, with both runs unearned, coughing up a 2-1 lead. And after the Yankees took a 3-2 lead in the top of the sixth, he ran into control problems, throwing eight consecutive balls, and gave the lead right back, 3-3.
His night was over after six innings.
And, for the first time since Aug. 3, he gave up more than one run in a game, even though two of the runs were unearned.
“I mean, I wouldn’t say I really gave them a chance,’’ Schlittler said. “That one’s kind of on me, so I’ll take the blame for that. Made an error there, let up two runs.
“I mean, that’s baseball, but yeah, that one’s on me.’’
The loss all but mathematically eliminates the Yankees’ hopes of catching the Tampa Bay Rays for the AL East lead, even with a four-game series scheduled next week at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees (89-65) are five games back with just seven games remaining, with the Rays’ magic number dropping to 4.
“I mean, there’s still a chance,’’ Schlittler said, “but we got to play our (butts) off a little bit.’’
The reality is that the Yankees would have to sweep the Rays, needing to win all four games to win the tiebreaker, and still would need help.
“Mathematically, probably pretty tough,’’ Yankees outfielder Cody Bellinger said, “but you never know. … I mean, they’re playing tremendous baseball so it’s tough to climb up in the standings if they keep winning, right?
“So, mathematically, pretty tough, but got to keep on rolling.’’
The Yankees realize winning the AL East certainly has an inherent advantage with a first-round bye, which would give slugger Aaron Judge four more recovery days. But if they’re going to win their first World Series since 2009, they’re going to have to do it the hard way.
“The goal is obviously to win the division, rest your guys, get those extra off-days,’’ Bellinger said. “But ultimately, the World Series champion has come out of the wild card, so keep on fighting for the division, and we got to keep on rolling.’’
While the Yankees know it’s unrealistic to believe they can still win the division, they can at least start thinking about setting up their rotation for the postseason.
They can have Schlittler make one more start, perhaps even limit his innings, making sure he’s plenty rested, knowing that if they’re going to be playing deep into October, they’ll need to jump on his shoulders. He’ll be starting Game 1 of the postseason for them, being only the ninth pitcher in the 21st century to complete a season with a sub-2.00 ERA.
The Cy Young award belongs to him.
But he wants a World Series ring to go along with that hardware.
“The expectation is to make the playoffs,’’ Schlittler says, “and the expectation is to win a championship. That’s what I care about.’’
The Yankees know he’s special, putting on the greatest season by a Yankees pitcher since Ron Guidry in 1978, and know that when he takes the mound in October, he fully expects to win.
“He's a healthy combination between mature and immature,’’ Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “I say that affectionately because look, he's really confident (in) what he does, which is a critical component to playing this game at this level. But he also doesn't take himself too seriously.
“I think he has a really good way of not being overwhelmed by really good results, which obviously he's had a lot of. Or even the moments and times where he struggled, he processes it real well, kind of matter-of-fact, and moves on.’’
The reality now is that the Yankees will be a wild-card team, and will host the Boston Red Sox in a best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium.
They also will have the greatest pitcher in the American League at their disposal.
“I’ll be ready,’’ Schlittler says.
Follow Nightengale on X: @Bnightengale

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees fell in heartbreaking fashion on Saturday night against the Los Angeles Dodgers, losing on a walk-off two-run shot from Pavin Smith.
New York is now 89-65 on the season and still sits firmly in the top Wild Card spot but trails the Tampa Bay Rays by five games for the AL East division.
Currently, the biggest concern for the Yankees stems from injuries, as Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. are all sidelined. Even rookie slugger Spencer Jones seems to be dealing with some type of foot injury.
Aaron Boone Makes Statement on Jones’ Decision
Fortunately, Jones’ injury does not seem serious as he said pregame it was “no big deal.”
In fact, Boone said that he was available off the bench during Saturday night’s game and ultimately explained why he didn’t use him as a pinch-hitter.
After a reporter asked Boone if Jones was available or if he was trying to stay away from him because of the injury, Boone made it clear that he would’ve gone to him if the right spot emerged.
“He was available, like I would’ve… if a spot came up to hit or we needed to do something I would’ve gone to him,” Boone said.
Aaron Boone speaks to the media following the Yankees 5-3 loss tonight in Arizona. pic.twitter.com/aeBBxybvHN
— YES Network (@YESNetwork) September 20, 2026
Looking at the Yankees
New York will play the Diamondbacks one more time on Sunday and then, after a day off Monday, will begin a massive four-game set with the Rays. If they can sweep the series, they could get back into the race over the final three games of the regular season.
On Tuesday, the two teams will play a doubleheader and then wrap it up across Wednesday and Thursday, with the Yankees likely throwing their top four guys in Max Fried, Carlos Rodon, Gerrit Cole, and Cam Schlittler.

item.content:encoded:
Los New York Yankees respondieron con autoridad en su primer partido sin Aaron Judge y derrotaron 9-2 a los Arizona Diamondbacks este viernes en Chase Field. Nueva York fabricó cinco carreras en la primera entrada, Ben Rice y George Lombard Jr. conectaron cuadrangulares y Gerrit Cole lanzó seis entradas de calidad para llevarse una victoria que también tuvo un significado histórico para el derecho.
LEER MÁS SOBRE: ¡Aaron Judge vuelve a la lista de lesionados de los Yankees!
LEER MÁS SOBRE: ¡Los Dodgers ya son campeones de la División Oeste!
Suscríbete al Newsletter de Unanimo y recibe gratis las últimas noticias. Dale click aquí
La jornada comenzó con una noticia importante para los Yankees: Judge fue colocado nuevamente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Sin su principal figura ofensiva, Nueva York necesitó encontrar producción desde el primer turno y la respuesta llegó inmediatamente frente al abridor de Arizona, Eduardo Rodríguez.
Los primeros cinco bateadores de los Yankees lograron embasarse. Ben Rice recibió una base por bolas y posteriormente Amed Rosario conectó un sencillo productor para abrir la pizarra. Después llegaron más oportunidades para la ofensiva neoyorquina, hasta que George Lombard Jr. conectó un sencillo de dos carreras que llevó el marcador a 5-0 antes de que terminara el primer episodio. Rodríguez necesitó 45 lanzamientos para conseguir los tres outs de la entrada, la mayor cantidad de su carrera en un primer inning.
Arizona intentó reaccionar en el segundo capítulo. Corbin Carroll conectó un cuadrangular de dos carreras para acercar a los Diamondbacks a 5-2 y darle algo de vida al público de Chase Field. Sin embargo, Cole logró contener la ofensiva local y evitó que la reacción se transformara en una amenaza mayor.
La respuesta de los Yankees llegó en la tercera entrada. Ben Rice volvió a aparecer y conectó un cuadrangular solitario, su número 39 de la temporada, para recuperar la diferencia de cuatro carreras y colocar el encuentro 6-2. El batazo también completó una noche ofensiva sobresaliente para Rice, quien terminó con dos imparables, dos bases por bolas, dos carreras y dos carreras impulsadas.
Mientras la ofensiva seguía produciendo, Cole encontró estabilidad desde la lomita. Después del cuadrangular de Carroll, el derecho no permitió otra carrera y completó seis entradas con cuatro hits, dos carreras limpias, ninguna base por bolas y seis ponches. Venía de dos aperturas en las que había permitido siete jonrones combinados, por lo que su actuación en Phoenix representó una recuperación importante en su temporada.
Lombard Jr. volvió a aparecer en la sexta entrada. El campocorto conectó su tercer jonrón de la temporada, esta vez solitario, para ampliar la ventaja de Nueva York a 7-2. El joven infielder terminó la noche con dos imparables y tres carreras impulsadas, convirtiéndose en otra de las figuras ofensivas del triunfo visitante.
Ver esta publicación en Instagram
Los Yankees agregaron dos carreras más en la séptima entrada para terminar de sentenciar el encuentro. La ofensiva visitante terminó con ocho hits y nueve carreras, mientras que Arizona consiguió siete imparables, pero no volvió a pisar el plato después del segundo inning.
Para Cole, la victoria tuvo un valor especial. El derecho llegó a 162 triunfos en su carrera, superando a Mike Moore y convirtiéndose en el lanzador con más victorias entre los jugadores que fueron seleccionados con el primer pick global del Draft. Cole fue elegido por los Pittsburgh Pirates con la primera selección en 2011.
La derrota, en cambio, complicó todavía más el panorama de Arizona en la recta final de la temporada. Los Diamondbacks llegaron al encuentro buscando mantenerse en la pelea por el último boleto de comodín de la Liga Nacional, pero la caída ante Nueva York significó su tercera derrota consecutiva. Al término de la jornada quedaron cinco juegos por detrás del último puesto de Wild Card, con ocho encuentros restantes.
Los Yankees, ya clasificados a los playoffs, mejoraron a 89-64 y se colocaron a cuatro juegos de los Tampa Bay Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con nueve partidos por disputar. Nueva York además consiguió su octava victoria en sus últimos 10 encuentros.
El triunfo llegó, además, en una noche en la que los Yankees tuvieron que afrontar la ausencia de Judge. Rice y Lombard Jr. aportaron los batazos largos, mientras que Cole respondió desde el montículo para que Nueva York tomara el primer partido de la serie en Arizona con una victoria contundente de 9-2.

item.content:encoded:
Redacción FOX Deportes
Aaron Judge confía en que podrá volver en los playoffs
El jardinero y cañonero de los Yankees fue colocado en la lista de lesionados
Después de ser enviado a la lista de lesionados por diez días debido a una distensión en el músculo sóleo derecho, Aaron Judge expresó su deseo de regresar para los playoffs.
“Me gustaría estar de vuelta para la postemporada; ese es definitivamente el plan”, declaró el capitán de los Yankees. El jardinero confirmó que mantendrá sus rutinas de tiro y entrenamiento físico “para volver de inmediato en cuanto estemos listos” y afrontar el cierre del campeonato.
Respecto a la gravedad de la lesión, el estelar bateador admitió que la localización de la molestia ha dificultado su movilidad en el terreno. “He lidiado con distensiones antes y he jugado así, pero esto fue en un lugar diferente que lo hizo un poco más difícil”, explicó Judge, añadiendo que el sóleo “es más crucial para correr y batear”. Sobre su tiempo de baja, reconoció que no tiene certeza: “El cuerpo médico no me ha dicho el grado aún y no tengo respuestas sobre plazos”.
Los Yankees colocaron a Aaron Judge en la lista de lesionados
El equipo neoyorquino se quedará sin su máxima estrella en la parte final de la temporada
Por su parte, el mánager Aaron Boone adoptó una postura pragmática y evitó ofrecer un diagnóstico médico o una fecha estimada para el retorno de su figura. “No importa qué grado sea, nos quedan nueve partidos”, afirmó el estratega ante los medios de comunicación. “Vamos a trabajar para tenerlo de regreso o no; eso es lo que vamos a hacer y ya veremos qué sucede”, enfatizó sobre las posibilidades de volver a contar con el jugador en el roster.
La fecha más cercana para la reactivación de Judge es el 29 de septiembre frente a los Orioles, día en que también inicia la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana. El vigente Jugador Más Valioso busca reincorporarse a tiempo para los playoffs tras una campaña afectada por los problemas físicos, en la que registra un promedio de .241 con 18 cuadrangulares y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos disputados esta temporada.
LO MÁS VISTO

Aaron Judge recibió un nuevo golpe en una temporada marcada por las lesiones. El capitán de los New York Yankees regresó a la lista de lesionados debido a una distensión muscular en la pantorrilla derecha, situación que genera incertidumbre sobre su participación en el cierre de la campaña y en los Playoffs de las Grandes Ligas. El mánager Aaron Boone confir
item.content:encoded:
¡Alerta en los Yankees! Aaron Judge regresa a la lista de lesionados
Aaron Boone reconoció que todavía no existe una fecha para su regreso.
Aaron Judge recibió un nuevo golpe en una temporada marcada por las lesiones. El capitán de los New York Yankees regresó a la lista de lesionados debido a una distensión muscular en la pantorrilla derecha, situación que genera incertidumbre sobre su participación en el cierre de la campaña y en los Playoffs de las Grandes Ligas.
El mánager Aaron Boone confirmó que el equipo todavía no cuenta con un calendario definido para la recuperación del bateador.
“No tengo un plazo definido para su recuperación”, dijo el piloto, quien tampoco pudo garantizar la presencia de Judge en la postemporada. Ante la pregunta sobre si estará disponible para los Playoffs, su respuesta fue contundente: “No lo sé”.
Judge apenas había regresado el 8 de septiembre, después de perder tiempo por una fractura en la costilla derecha. En seis encuentros desde su vuelta, registró cuatro imparables en 23 turnos, además de un cuadrangular, para un promedio de .174.
El problema físico apareció durante el duelo del miércoles ante los Mellizos de Minnesota. Judge abandonó el encuentro por molestias en la pierna derecha.
“Intenté restarle importancia y ver cuánto tiempo podía aguantar, porque estos partidos son importantes en la recta final de la temporada”, explicó Judge. “Pero, tras analizarlo, pensé que lo correcto era salir del juego para no perjudicar al equipo en el campo ni en las bases”.
Los Yankees, que buscan asegurar su lugar en la Postemporada. La temporada regular concluirá el 28 de septiembre, mientras que la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana comenzará el 29.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — In case the Yankees weren’t dealing with enough injury headaches for a 6-foot-7 slugger, Spencer Jones was out of the lineup Saturday with a sore left foot/heel.
The rookie outfielder claimed it was “no big deal” and chalked it up to the wear and tear of playing on Chase Field’s turf Friday night after jamming his heel in Minnesota earlier this week.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
But after the Yankees just lost Aaron Judge to the injured list again with a right calf strain, the last thing they needed was Jones nursing an injury of his own.
“Just a little banged up,” Jones said before Saturday’s game against the Diamondbacks. “Playing on turf is different, hard on the feet.”
Aaron Boone also downplayed it, adding that he still almost kept Jones in the lineup before sitting him in favor of José Caballero, who started in center field for the second time this season.
“Just felt like especially being on the turf here, he kind of jammed that heel in Minnesota and being on the turf [Friday], so I think it’s just a day-to-day kind of thing,” Boone said. “I even view him as available tonight.”
Boone said he preferred to keep Cody Bellinger in left field instead of shifting him to center.
“I considered moving him to center, but Belli’s grinding too and the turf here kind of beats you up,” he said. “There’s some scenarios where I would move him to center. Tonight, just being on the turf and as much as he’s been through this year, I didn’t want to move him.”
When the Yankees officially placed Judge on the 10-day injured list Saturday, they opted for defensive versatility over offensive upside in his replacement.
That meant calling up Max Schuemann instead of Jasson Domínguez, giving the former another shot in the big leagues for at least a few days beginning this weekend against the Diamondbacks.
“Adding his versatility to our bench makes some sense,” Boone said. “And then obviously some different roster complications moving forward with the playoffs around the corner.”
Schuemann’s stay may be brief, with Jazz Chisholm Jr. potentially returning from the IL as soon as the upcoming series against the Rays at Yankee Stadium that begins Tuesday.
If Schuemann goes back to Triple-A to make room, he would not be available to be recalled for 10 days (unless he was replacing an injured player again), essentially ruling him out as an option for the AL wild-card series.
That may have played a part in Domínguez not getting the call this time, in case the Yankees wanted to use him as a pinch-running threat on their playoff roster.
The 23-year-old also offers value as a switch-hitter, but he has proven to be a defensive liability in the outfield.
The Yankees’ trip to Chase Field gave them a chance to reunite with former teammate Jonathan Loáisiga, who has finally stayed healthy for a full season in the Diamondbacks bullpen.
Shop Yankees Merch
The right-hander often flashed his talent during his eight-year tenure with the Yankees, but injuries too often got in the way.
This season, though, after signing a minor league deal with the Diamondbacks, Loáisiga has avoided the IL and pitched in a career-high 64 games with a 2.32 ERA entering Saturday.
“Been through a lot of battles over the years with Jonny,” Boone said. “It’ll be great to see him. Hopefully we can ding him a little bit here. I know he’s had a really strong year, which I’m excited about for him. He’s such a talented guy that for him, it’s always been about just being healthy. So the fact that he’s gone out there and had a largely healthy season, I’m not surprised at the success he’s had.”
The Diamondbacks held a 25th-anniversary celebration Saturday of their 2001 World Series team that beat the Yankees in seven games.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Aaron Judge, Yankees claim they know nothing about severity of superstar’s calf strain
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: PHOENIX — The Yankees continued to treat Aaron Judge’s calf strain like classified CIA intel on Saturday, as neither the back-to-back MVP nor Aaron Boone shared a grade for the injury. Actually, both claimed that they don’t even know the answer to that question before the Bombers played the Diamondbacks. “I gotta talk to the trainers and figure that out,” Judge said when asked for the grade after officially going on the 10-day injured list. “They got all the reports on that.” Wait, the Yankees’
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — The Yankees continued to treat Aaron Judge’s calf strain like classified CIA intel on Saturday, as neither the back-to-back MVP nor Aaron Boone shared a grade for the injury.
Actually, both claimed that they don’t even know the answer to that question before the Bombers played the Diamondbacks.
“I gotta talk to the trainers and figure that out,” Judge said when asked for the grade after officially going on the 10-day injured list. “They got all the reports on that.”
Wait, the Yankees’ training staff hasn’t told Judge the grade of his strain?
“They haven’t told me yet,” said the captain, who is only seven games removed from a 99-day absence for a fractured rib that he approvingly skipped a rehab assignment for.
Okay, but surely the trainers told Boone, right?
Wrong, said the manager, as Boone stated that he hasn’t bothered to ask for the grade.
“It doesn’t matter what grade it is,” Boone said. “We’re at nine games left [in the season].
“If and when he’s able to be back, he will.”
It doesn’t matter? The Boston Sports Medicine & Research Institute begs to differ, stating a first-degree, or mild, calf strain comes with a 1-3-week timeline. A second-degree, or moderate, strain requires 3-6 weeks of rest and recovery before returning to full activity. A third-degree, or severe, strain “can take many weeks or months to fully heal.”
The severity of Judge’s injury is important because the second-place Yankees’ postseason will begin with the Wild Card round on Sept. 29 if the current standings hold. Judge is obviously instrumental to their chances of fulfilling their championship goals, but it is unclear if he’ll be back in time for the Wild Card round or any postseason action.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason. That’s definitely the plan,” said Judge, noting that the earliest he can return is the last game of the regular season. “So we’ll see. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that.”
Judge, who is continuing to throw, work out and get treatment, added that he’s “gonna do everything we can to get back as soon as we can.” Boone, meanwhile, said that he wouldn’t speculate on Judge’s timeline, but he’s “hoping for the best.”
“We’re gonna get him back or we’re not,” the skipper said. “That’s what we’re gonna work to do, and we’ll see.”
It is no surprise that the Yankees have not revealed many details since Judge hurt his calf in the first frame of Wednesday’s loss to the Twins, a game he did not exit until the sixth inning.
Judge has been notoriously withholding when talking about his various injuries over the years, and he prefers that the Yankees follow suit. They tend to oblige; Boone used the phrase “I don’t know” eight times while discussing Judge’s calf strain before Friday’s game.
The Yankees typically provide a grade within a day or two when a player suffers a strain.
One detail that Judge did share is that he strained the soleus muscle in his calf, as opposed to the gastrocnemius muscle. Judge’s understanding is that the soleus muscle is more “crucial” to running and hitting.
He also said that he “usually” deals with “calf stuff all year long,” but it doesn’t become public, and he doesn’t miss games.
It had been his hope that history would repeat itself, but a return to the injured list couldn’t be avoided this time around.
“I’m definitely frustrated,” said Judge, who has only played in 66 games this season. “I’ve dealt with strains before and kind of played through them, but this was kind of in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult.
“The focus is still the same: to get ready to go for October.”

item.title: [The Big Lead] Yankees make sudden change to lineup, remove breakout star
item.dc:creator: Lou Landers
item.description: The Yankees are already dealing with the loss of Aaron Judge, and now they have another outfielder on the MLB roster who is temporarily unavailable. Spencer Jones, one of New York’s biggest breakout stories over the past month, is out of Saturday’s lineup against the Arizona Diamondbacks with left foot soreness. The rookie told MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch that he expects it to be a one-day issue, which should provide some relief for a Yankees team that cannot afford another significant injury. Spencer
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees are already dealing with the loss of Aaron Judge, and now they have another outfielder on the MLB roster who is temporarily unavailable. Spencer Jones, one of New York’s biggest breakout stories over the past month, is out of Saturday’s lineup against the Arizona Diamondbacks with left foot soreness.
The rookie told MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch that he expects it to be a one-day issue, which should provide some relief for a Yankees team that cannot afford another significant injury.
Spencer Jones has become a key part of Yankees’ lineup
Jones’ emergence has been one of the more encouraging developments for New York this season. After struggling early in his rookie campaign, the 25-year-old has started to find his footing at the plate and has become the Yankees’ everyday center fielder.
Through his first 80 games, Jones is hitting .248/.318/.433 with 10 home runs and a 109 wRC+. More importantly, his September has been particularly impressive. He entered Saturday batting .340/.415/.532 with two homers, 12 RBIs and seven runs through his first 13 games of the month.
The Yankees have also been encouraged by the adjustments Jones has made against Major League pitching. Manager Aaron Boone previously compared his developmental path to Judge’s, noting that Jones’ enormous 6-foot-7 frame could become a major advantage as his adjustments continue to translate.
That makes Saturday’s lineup change particularly notable.
Yankees cannot afford another outfield injury
Jones is being held out as a precaution, with José Caballero taking over in center field Saturday. Jones has indicated that he expects to return Sunday, so there is currently no indication that the foot issue is expected to become a lengthy absence.
Still, the timing is less than ideal.
Judge officially returned to the injured list Saturday with a right calf strain and has no established timetable for his return. The Yankees recalled Max Schuemann to fill his roster spot, while the club is expected to rely more heavily on its remaining outfield options.
New York has already dealt with significant injuries across its roster this season. With the postseason approaching, the Yankees need Jones healthy and available because his recent production has given the lineup another legitimate offensive option.
For now, the hope is that Jones’ absence truly is nothing more than a one-day precaution.

That was a
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Without any guarantees of it happening, Aaron Judge is holding out hope of returning from a calf strain in time for the playoffs.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason; that’s definitely the plan,” Judge said Saturday afternoon. “We’re going to do everything we can to get back as soon as we can.”
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
That was a slightly less definitive statement than what Judge consistently said during the summer when he was trying to come back from a right rib stress fracture, which he did after three-plus months on Sept. 8.
But now the clock is ticking even louder, with Saturday marking 10 days away from Game 1 of the American League wild card series.
“Definitely frustrated,” said Judge, who played seven games after missing 84 on the IL with the rib injury. “Dealt with strains before and kind of played through them, but this was in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult.”
Judge did not reveal what grade the strain was, but said it involved his Soleus muscle, which he indicated was more important to running and hitting compared to the gastrocnemius muscle.
“The focus is still the same, to be ready to go for October,” Judge said.
In the meantime, the Yankees are banking on their summer without Judge paying off now that he is back on the IL.
“Lean on each other,” Cody Bellinger said. “The game itself is hard; if you add too much pressure on yourself, the game becomes even harder. So we really just have to play for each other, lean on each other, pass the baton, do your job and control what you can control.”
The Yankees did that on Friday night, racing out of the gates to score five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 win against the Diamondbacks, just hours after the team announced Judge was going on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain.
But they also got off well at the beginning of June after Judge landed on the IL with a right rib stress fracture before their lineup became a black hole for an extended stretch during the summer. They had finally started to break out of it shortly before Judge got back on Sept. 8, but after having him back for seven games, they now find themselves in the same spot again, less than two weeks away from the start of the playoffs.
“We’ve played most of the year this way, and I feel like in a lot of cases, especially some of our key guys over the last few weeks have started to, especially offensively, get it going like we know they’re capable of,” manager Aaron Boone said.
During the 84-game span that Judge missed this summer, the Yankees ranked 26th in runs per game (4.06), 29th in batting average (.227), 27th in OPS (.681), and 29th in WRC+ (90).
But over the tail end of that stretch, and into Judge’s return, the Yankees started to hit more like they are capable of. That included the trade deadline addition of Luis García Jr., the emergence of rookie outfielder Spencer Jones, and Bellinger getting back on track after returning from his own hamstring injury in August.
Perhaps most importantly, it has coincided with the reemergence of Ben Rice. The lefty slugger was a game wrecker for the first two months of the season before Judge went down, then cooled off a bit during the summer (albeit with some good stretches along the way) before catching fire again over the last few weeks. Entering Saturday, over his last 22 games, Rice had hit .353 with a 1.037 OPS and five home runs, including his 39th of the season Friday night.
“Special year,” Gerrit Cole said. “Has made some really good adjustments from previous years, going into this year, and I think he’s really started to heat back up here the last few weeks after having to make some adjustments in the middle of the season. Not only is he really proficient with the bat, but he’s a smart player and a hard worker, which is leading him to have a really outstanding season for us.”
The Yankees need that to continue for however long Judge is out (and even if and when he returns) for them to play deep into October, though Rice isn’t looking at it as having to do any more — which got some hitters in trouble during the three-time AL MVP’s first absence.
“I would think that everyone just goes out there and stays within themselves, tries to put together quality at-bat after quality at-bat,” he said. “Pitching is always going to be doing their thing, like they have for us all year. So from an offensive standpoint, just do what we did [Friday]: go out and have a team at-bat, trust the guy behind you and keep the line moving.”
To Rice’s point, the Yankees have leaned on the strength of their pitching staff all season, but that was especially the case during Judge’s three months on the IL this summer, when they were able to scratch out enough wins in low-scoring games, with their pitchers keeping them in it almost every night.
New York Post may be compensated and/or receive an affiliate commission if you buy something through our links.
“We have a lot of confidence in here,” Cole said. “For the most part of the summer, we’ve been tested really, really hard and we responded, by and large, really, really well. We have a lot of perfectionists in here. We’re always striving to be perfect and trying to be the best. But the reality is we’ve had a lot of obstacles we’ve had to overcome and, by and large, we’ve played really well.”

item.description: PHOENIX — New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge, speaking for the first time since going on the injured list with a strained right calf, provided no timeline Saturday for when he could possibly return to the lineup. "I'd like to be back by the postseason, so we'll see," Judge said. "That's definitely the plan. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that.'' Judge, who missed three months with a fractured rib, is eligible to come off the injured list for the regular-season
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge, speaking for the first time since going on the injured list with a strained right calf, provided no timeline Saturday for when he could possibly return to the lineup.
"I'd like to be back by the postseason, so we'll see," Judge said. "That's definitely the plan. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that.''
Judge, who missed three months with a fractured rib, is eligible to come off the injured list for the regular-season finale on Sept. 27. He injured his calf in his first at-bat Wednesday playing against the Minnesota Twins. The injury is in the soleus muscle of the calf, which makes it difficult to participate in any baseball activities, he said, except throwing to keep his arm in shape.
"Definitely frustrated,'' Judge, the three-time MVP, said. "I've dealt with strains before, and kind of played through them, but this was kind of in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult. But definitely frustrated because, you know, the ultimate goal was to try to come back to get a couple of games before the postseason, so it changes it a little bit.''
While Judge opted to resume playing with the Yankees instead of having a traditional minor-league rehab stint after such a lengthy absence, he isn't second-guessing his decision, nor for coming out of Wednesday's game when he first felt his calf strain.
"You know, you feel things every single year,'' Judge said. "I usually deal with calf stuff all year long, and it usually gets to you, and usually don't miss any games. So that was kind of the same thing I was feeling.
"I was feeling it. I was working my way back, and then something kind of grabs you at a strange time. So if this would have happened in the rehab game, I would have been probably a little bit more pissed than I was now.
"So, it is what it is.''
The Yankees, who are in the No. 1 wild-card spot, are expected to host the Boston Red Sox in a best-of-three series beginning Sept. 29 in the wild-card round at Yankee Stadium. The winner would play the first-place Tampa Bay Rays in the Division Series.
Follow Nightengale on X: @Bnightengale

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Spencer Jones' remarkable stats vs. lefties are better than Yankees fans' wildest dreams
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level. The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching. He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye
item.content:encoded:
There were many questions the New York Yankees needed Spencer Jones to answer this season. Now, we've seen enough of him, even if it's been in a couple of disjointed stints, to get a good idea of who he is at the major league level.
The answer: pretty damn good. After struggling early, Jones has found his footing. A big reason for his ascendancy has been surprising. The Vanderbilt product has mashed left-handed pitching.
He's now logged 51 plate appearances against lefties and has slashed an eye-watering .435/.490/.761 following his homer off Minnesota Twins lefty specialist Taylor Rodgers on Sept. 15. It was the first dinger Rodgers gave up to a left-handed hitter over 133 plate appearances this season.
The sample size isn't huge, but it's relatively significant. For example, Ben Rice has 209 plate appearances against lefties out of his 622 plate appearances. For Jones, the 51 matchups against southpaws are a decent portion of his 255 total plate appearances.
One of the most impressive things about how he's performed against same-handed pitching is the amount of power he's demonstrated. Obviously, the six-foot-seven outfielder is a behemoth, but most lefties, even those who perform well against southpaws, see a drop in power in those situations. Take Rice, for instance; his slugging percentage drops from .561 against righties to .457 against left-handers. That hasn't been the case for Jones.
This has just been one part of Jones' maturation process that should have every fan feeling confident about not only his future, but his ability to contribute now.
Spencer Jones' performance against lefties has Yankees well-positioned for playoffs vs. Red Sox
Overall, Jones is hitting .259/.331/.452 with 10 homers on the season. He's been even better since being recalled on July 22, posting a .271/.337/.490 line with eight of his 10 homers coming during this most recent span.
There should be no more doubt that he should start over Trent Grisham, assuming Grisham is healthy, once the playoffs roll around. A significant part of that reasoning has to do with his performance against southpaws.
Jones has learned a lot from Cody Bellinger on how to handle those tough at-bats since he's been up in the bigs and the star left fielder has been healthy.
“When we are in the dugout, he’s one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, ‘Yo, what did you see?’ He’ll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he’s going to do next time. It’s like, all right, good to know before I go even into my first (at-bat) what this MVP is going to do for his first at-bat. It’s pretty sweet knowing that I’ve got these guys to help me out,” Jones said to The Athletic this week.
He couldn't have a better mentor. Bellinger isn't hitting lefties as much as he did last year, when he put up an insane .353/.415/.601 line, but his .287/.346/.449 performance in 2026 is plenty good, and better than what he's done against righties. In fact, Bellinger is about as balanced as they come with an .804 career OPS against left-handers and an .819 mark against righties.
We spoke about Rice earlier, but the early-season drama about his usage against lefties is a thing of the past. While he has more pop against righties, Rice's .255/.330/.457 line against southpaws is more than serviceable.
Despite having so many lefties in the lineup on a daily basis, the Yankees as a whole don't suffer much from it. The club is hitting a collective .247/.318/.422 against left-handed pitching this season, with a .740 OPS that ranks ninth. Remember, for most of that time, Aaron Judge hasn't been a factor, either.
Looking ahead, the Yankees' most likely opponent in the Wild Card series is the Red Sox, who are loaded with left-handers. In the rotation, they boast southpaws Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez, with their being a possibility that Jake Bennett makes the cut, too. In the bullpen, they'll hope to unleash Garrett Crochet, Erik Miller and old friend Aroldis Chapman.
However, rather than being overmatched, we might say that this plays into the Yankees' hands. New York can handle left-handed pitching, and those lefty bats can tee off against righties. Jones emerging as a threat against southpaws only solidifies the strength and gives the Yankees another regular who doesn't need a platoon partner, allowing them to match up only where they're vulnerable.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] How the Yankees Should Utilize Jazz Chisholm Jr. When He Returns
item.dc:creator: Joe Najarian; Unknown
item.description: With Aaron Judge likely done for the season, the New York Yankees will rely heavily on their other bats to pick up the slack. One of those will be Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is nearing a return from the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Chisholm, who was putting up an .832 OPS and .367 wOBA since August 4, is expected to be activated during the Yankees' final homestand this coming week. Despite a very disappointing season as a whole, the 28-year-old's improved play is an extremely encouragin
item.content:encoded:
With Aaron Judge likely done for the season, the New York Yankees will rely heavily on their other bats to pick up the slack.
One of those will be Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is nearing a return from the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Chisholm, who was putting up an .832 OPS and .367 wOBA since August 4, is expected to be activated during the Yankees' final homestand this coming week. Despite a very disappointing season as a whole, the 28-year-old's improved play is an extremely encouraging sign.
At the same time, Anthony Volpe has taken full advantage of his new opportunity at second base. When Chisholm went down, Volpe's improvements at the plate in Triple-A carried over to the major leagues and his production from the bottom of the order is a boon to the Yankees' offense. The 25-year old is slashing .296/.345/.481 in 29 plate appearances while also stealing four bases.
The problem is that the Yankees have three middle infielders looking for starting spots. George Lombard Jr. is firmly entrenched at shortstop, which necessitated Volpe's transition to second base. Of course, second base is Chisholm's natural position and the Yankees have gotten well-above average defense from him there.
This means one of these three will be the odd man out... or does it?
The Yankees should play Jazz Chisholm Jr. at third base again
When the Yankees acquired Chisholm at the trade deadline in 2024, they already had Gleyber Torres at second base. So they tested Chisholm out at third base to ensure both players would be in the starting lineup. Chisholm also saw time at the hot corner last year when DJ LeMahieu played second, until the Yankees eventually released the aging LeMahieu to move Chisholm back to his natural position.
Chisholm's defense suffered at third in 2025, as he was worth -3 Outs Above Average (per Baseball Savant). But his athleticism and dynamic skillset is far too great to leave him out of the lineup entirely, even if he's endured a down year. On the other hand, it would be foolish for the Yankees to sit Volpe while he's hot at the plate and adapting well to second.
While second base has two strong options, third base is a major weakness. Ryan McMahon has been atrocious since returning to the lineup on Sept. 1, hitting just .154/.214/.179 in 42 plate appearances; the abysmal offensive production far outweighs McMahon's steady defense, even if the Yankees are going to rely on run prevention in the postseason. Jose Caballero is also capable of playing third, but he's best suited as a bench player at this point.
Between Chisholm and Volpe, the former is better suited to play third due to his past experience. The latter has a grand total of three games and 22.0 innings at the hot corner, all of them in Triple-A.
This certainly isn't an ideal situation for Chisholm: he's struggled for much of the season, got injured when he started turning things around, and may need to play at a secondary position to accommodate a teammate.
But this would likely be the Yankees' best lineup without Aaron Judge, and if Chisholm wants to both win a World Series and secure a future in the Bronx, then moving over to third is the best thing he can do to help the team right now.
Joe Najarian is a writer for Yankees On SI, having previously covered the Yankees both for SI and additional sites since 2023. He also served as Deputy Editor for the Yankees, Mets and Orioles On SI sites, and additionally contributes to Athlon Sports and Men’s Journal covering Major League Baseball and other trending sports news. Joe is a graduate of Rutgers University in 2022, earning a bachelor’s degree in Journalism and Media Studies.
Follow JoeNajarian

However, Cole’s recent surge on the bump has generated plenty of momentum within the organization. item.content:encoded:
Returning to the mound after missing an entire regular season due to an elbow injury is a daunting task for any pitcher. That context helps explain why Gerrit Cole endured a slow start to his 2026 campaign upon returning to the New York Yankees‘ rotation.
However, Cole’s recent surge on the bump has generated plenty of momentum within the organization. When asked whether the veteran righty would take the ball in the Wild Card round, manager Aaron Boone delivered a resolute answer: “I would expect Gerrit Cole to start, yes.”
Boone faces a compelling rotational dilemma, given the standout performances of his depth chart. Max Fried has anchored his share of gems, while breakout starter Cam Schlittler has delivered a dominant campaign, one that Boone firmly believes warrants American League Cy Young honors.
With Aaron Judge sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, the Yankees are relying heavily on their pitching depth to carry the load into October. That group could get another boost with Ryan Weathers tracking toward a postseason return.
Gerrit Cole #45 of the New York Yankees.
Cole’s rollercoaster season
Cole’s season started with immediate frustration before he ever threw an official pitch. Lingering elbow concerns during Spring Training delayed his season debut, forcing him to miss the opening two months of the championship schedule and putting extra stress on the Yankees‘ starting rotation.
Dominant, double-digit strikeout performances—including a 10-strikeout shutout performance over 6.2 innings against Kansas City and multi-hit gems against Chicago and Atlanta—showed he remains one of the most electric arms in baseball.
A recurring issue throughout Cole’s 2026 campaign has been his home run rate. When Cole misses over the plate, opposing hitters have made him pay, elevating his HR/9 rate above his career averages and making several of his outings much more high-stress than his strikeout numbers would indicate.

item.dc:creator: Fernando Rayo
item.description: Aaron Judge regresará a la lista de lesionados, lo que significa que los Yankees deberán navegar el final de la temporada regular sin su capitán, y potencialmente parte de la postemporada. item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge regresará a la lista de lesionados, lo que significa que los Yankees deberán navegar el final de la temporada regular sin su capitán, y potencialmente parte de la postemporada.
Jude fue inhabilitado oficialmente el sábado, en un movimiento retroactivo al jueves. El infielder/jardinero Max Schuemann fue ascendido desde Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre para ocupar el lugar del capitán en el roster.
«La realidad es que hemos tenido que jugar gran parte de la temporada de este año sin él», dijo el manager Aaron Boone. «No se puede reemplazar a un jugador tan extraordinario como Aaron Judge, pero tenemos grandes expectativas. Esas no cambian ahora».
- Te puede interesar: Jonathan Loáisiga recibe a los Yankees desde el otro dogout
Judge se sometió a una resonancia magnética el jueves en Phoenix que reveló la distensión muscular. Boone dijo que no daría detalles sobre la gravedad de la lesión ni ofrecería una estimación de cuándo se espera que Judge regrese.
Al preguntársele si Judge volvería para los playoffs, Boone respondió: «No lo sé».
Prior to tonight’s game, the Yankees made the following roster moves:
• Recalled INF/OF Max Schuemann (#30) from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre.
• Placed OF Aaron Judge on the 10-day injured list (retroactive to 9/17) with a right calf strain.
— New York Yankees (@Yankees) September 19, 2026
«No tengo un plazo definido para su recuperación», dijo Boone. «No voy a hacer predicciones. Obviamente, le daremos tratamiento y veremos qué sucede».
Por lo general, incluso una distensión de grado 1 en la pantorrilla requiere de dos a tres semanas para sanar.
Judge piensa estar en playoffs
Como mínimo, el momento de la lesión implica que Judge estará inactivo no solo durante la serie de este fin de semana contra los D-backs, sino también en la serie de cuatro partidos contra los Rays la próxima semana en el Yankee Stadium. Los Yankees llegaron a la jornada del viernes a cinco juegos de distancia de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana.
El jugador de cuadro y jardinero Max Schuemann viaja a Phoenix y se unirá a los Yankees para el partido del sábado. Judge no estuvo disponible para hablar con los periodistas antes del inicio de la serie del viernes contra los Diamondbacks en el Chase Field.
«Es un tipo que quiere estar aquí todos los días», dijo Cody Bellinger sobre Judge. «Quiere estar en el campo y ayudarnos a ganar. Sin duda es una noticia frustrante, especialmente cuando trabajas tan duro y durante tanto tiempo para volver, y luego sucede algo así. Me siento frustrado por él. Ojalá sea algo leve y de rápida recuperación».
La fecha más próxima posible para el regreso de Judge sería el último partido de la temporada regular, el 27 de septiembre contra Baltimore. La Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana está programada para comenzar el 29 de septiembre. En este momento, dicho escenario implicaría que los Yankees recibieran a los Red Sox en el Bronx.
«La ausencia de Judge duele. Todos sabemos que es el mejor bateador del juego», dijo Bellinger. «Para nosotros aquí dentro, la mentalidad es que tendremos que encontrar la manera de salir adelante. Creo que el talento en este vestuario habla por sí solo. Confío plenamente en que tenemos suficiente talento aquí para salir al campo, ganar y vencer a cualquiera».
Esa tarea será más difícil sin Judge, quien fue sustituido por un bateador emergente en la sexta entrada durante la derrota de los Yankees por 5-4 en 13 entradas ante los Twins, ocurrida el miércoles en el Target Field.
Judge comentó que sintió rigidez en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha durante la primera entrada.
«Intenté restarle importancia y ver cuánto tiempo podía aguantar, porque estos partidos son importantes en la recta final de la temporada», dijo Judge el miércoles. «Pero tras analizarlo, pensé que lo correcto era salir del juego para no perjudicar al equipo en el campo ni en las bases».
Ha sido una temporada marcada por las lesiones para Judge, el actual Jugador Más Valioso (MVP) de la Liga Americana, quien ha registrado promedios de .241/.360/.511 con 18 jonrones y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos.
Judge se perdió gran parte del verano debido a una fractura en una costilla derecha, lesión que se cree sufrió el 26 de abril en Houston. Jugó con la lesión durante aproximadamente un mes antes de ser colocado en la lista de lesionados tras un partido disputado el 31 de mayo contra los Atléticos en West Sacramento.
Sin pasar por una asignación de rehabilitación en ligas menores, Judge regresó el 8 de septiembre contra los Rockies. En seis partidos, bateó de 23-4 (.174) con un jonrón. Boone afirmó que no cuestionaría la decisión de que Judge se saltara la asignación de rehabilitación, señalando: «Estas cosas suceden, tanto si hay asignación de rehabilitación como si no. Hicimos todo lo posible para tratar de darnos a él y a nosotros mismos la mejor oportunidad de lograr un buen resultado».
Tomado de MLB.com

item.title: [MARCA] Boone’s grim Aaron Judge injury timetable clouds Yankees’ postseason hopes
item.dc:creator: Adriano Boin
item.description: - New York Yankees. Aaron Judge triggers intense panic after sudden injury exit just days into MLB return - New York Yankees. Yankee Stadium among 10 Bronx sites testing positive for deadly Legionnaires’ bacteria after 1 dies, 8 sickened Aaron Judge’s latest injury has turned a postseason question into a major uncertainty for the New York Yankees, with manager Aaron Boone unable to provide even a rough timetable for the slugger’s return. Judge was placed on the 10-day injured list Saturday after
item.content:encoded:
- New York Yankees. Aaron Judge triggers intense panic after sudden injury exit just days into MLB return
- New York Yankees. Yankee Stadium among 10 Bronx sites testing positive for deadly Legionnaires’ bacteria after 1 dies, 8 sickened
Aaron Judge’s latest injury has turned a postseason question into a major uncertainty for the New York Yankees, with manager Aaron Boone unable to provide even a rough timetable for the slugger’s return.
Judge was placed on the 10-day injured list Saturday after an MRI revealed a right calf strain. The move comes only days after the Yankees captain returned from a lengthy absence caused by a right rib fracture.
He rejoined the lineup on Sept. 8 against the Colorado Rockies after missing more than three months.
His comeback had already been a work in progress. Judge went 4-for-23 with a home run and 11 strikeouts across his first six games back, before lower-leg discomfort forced him out of Wednesday’s 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins. 
The Yankees subsequently learned he had suffered the calf strain.
Boone was cautious when asked whether Judge could be available for the playoffs.
“I don’t have a timeline on it,’’ Boone said. “I can’t predict anything. … I mean, we have no idea; we’re in the early stages. We’ll just obviously treat it and see what transpires.”
“Hopefully, we can have him be an option at some point.’’
The uncertainty is particularly concerning given how little time remains before October and how recently Judge returned from his previous injury.
Yankees face October uncertainty without their captain
The timing leaves New York with little margin for error. The Yankees have already clinched a postseason berth, but they’re still chasing Tampa Bay in the American League East.
With their playoff position taking shape, every remaining game carries importance, particularly if New York wants to improve its position before the Wild Card Series.
Former Yankees manager Joe Girardi also described the injury as a significant concern, particularly because Judge had only recently returned and was still trying to regain his timing at the plate.
"Well there's a huge level of concern," Girardi said. "Because they were talking about putting him on the IL and he won't have a chance to play in anymore games this season.
“And he was not to me, ready too go from a timing standpoint and how do you get your timing you gotta play games. So it's a pretty big concern to me.”
Judge remains one of baseball’s most important offensive pieces, and his 2026 numbers currently stand at a .241 batting average with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs in 66 games. 
Even after missing significant time, his presence changes the way opposing pitchers approach the Yankees’ lineup.
New York has already learned how to navigate extended stretches without its captain, but October presents a different challenge. 
A postseason series offers less room for an offense to overcome the absence of its premier hitter, especially against teams with strong pitching.
Boone’s message is essentially wait and see. Judge will receive treatment, and the Yankees hope he can become an option at some point. However, the manager’s refusal to establish a timetable underlines how uncertain the situation remains.
The Yankees don’t need Judge back immediately to reach October, but they’ll surely want clarity before the postseason begins.

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge to IL with calf strain, likely to miss rest of regular season
Aaron Judge was placed on the 10-day injured list with a right calf strain, the New York Yankees announced Saturday, Sept. 19, likely ending his regular season only seven games into his return from a 75-game absence due to a rib fracture.
Judge, the 34-year-old three-time American League MVP, left the Yankees' game at Minnesota on Wednesday with what the Yankees called lower leg tightness. His move to the IL was officially made on Saturday, and Max Schuemann was called up.
Judge would be eligible to return on Sunday, Sept. 27, the final day of the regular season. A return then would be unlikely, but at least Judge could return during the club's likely AL wild-card series matchup against the Boston Red Sox.
That would depend on his body cooperating. Judge was limited to 66 games this season, and injuries prompted the Yankees to acquire outfielder Heliot Ramos and infielder Luis Garcia Jr. at the August trade deadline. Center fielder Trent Grisham is also returning from a hamstring injury and manager Aaron Boone said it was unlikely Grisham will return before the regular season ends.
Like Judge, they can only hope he's ready to go when the playoff lights come on.
Other than the COVID-19 shortened 2020 season and his 27-game debut in 2016, Judge's 66 games played in 2026 marks the only other time in his 11-year career he failed to play at least 100 games. He hit 18 home runs in 237 at-bats, giving him 386 for his career. The Yankees clinched at least a wild-card berth Tuesday, one day before Judge suffered his calf injury.
In 2025, Judge won his second consecutive AL MVP, leading the major leagues in batting average (.331), on-base percentage (.457) and slugging (.688).
