item.content:encoded:
Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). Captain Aaron Judge is less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him more than three months. Judge's status for the rest of the season is up in the air.
"I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires," manager Aaron Boone said (via MLB.com). "... The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
The Yankees are always cagey about Judge's injuries. They declined to reveal the severity of the calf strain or give a timetable for his return. Generally speaking, Grade 1 calf strains (the least severe) require 2-3 weeks on the injured list, though calves are very tricky and easy to reinjury. They must be allowed to heal fully, otherwise you risk a more severe injury.
For all intents and purposes, the Yankees are locked into the top wild-card spot. They're six games up in the loss column on the Boston Red Sox, who currently sit in the second wild card spot, plus the Yankees won the season series and have the tiebreaker, so it's really a seven-game lead. New York can clinch the top wild-card spot as soon as Sunday.
The AL East title remains mathematically possible, but it is a long shot. The Yankees are four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the loss column with four head-to-head games remaining next week in the Bronx. The Rays only need to win one of those four games to clinch the season series and secure the tiebreaker, upping the difficulty for New York.
Just to lay it all out, here's what needs to happen for the Yankees to win the AL East, assuming they sweep those four games against the Rays and clinch the tiebreaker for themselves, which is a pretty big assumption:
- Rays go 6-3 or better: Rays win AL East
- Rays go 5-4: Yankees must go 9-0
- Rays go 4-5: Yankees must go 8-1
- Rays go 3-6: Yankees must go 7-2
- Rays go 2-7: Yankees must go 6-3
- Rays go 1-8: Yankees must go 5-4
- Rays go 0-9: Yankees must go 4-5
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason spot and winning the AL East was a long shot even with Judge. These last nine regular-season games are almost meaningless. If the AL East race gets interesting in a few days, the Yankees can shift gears, but the big picture takes priority this next week. Resting key relievers, lining up the rotation for the Wild Card Series, etc.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game," Cody Bellinger said (via MLB.com). "For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I'm fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody."
With the postseason less than two weeks away, Judge's calf injury creates a lot of questions for both him and the Yankees overall. Here are three questions for the man himself, and his team.
Three questions for Judge
1. Will he return for the postseason? This is really the only question, right? The Yankees are built around Judge being the best hitter in the world, and when he's not, the walls begin to cave in. New York had one of the lowest-scoring offenses in baseball when Judge was out with his rib injury. To paraphrase another New York baseball legend, Judge is the straw that stirs the drink.
Judge is eligible to come off the injured list next Sunday, the final day of the regular season. Roster-wise, he can return in time for the postseason. Health-wise, we have no idea. Calf strains are rarely 10-day absences, but that's what the Yankees have to hope is the case here. There's a very real chance the Yankees are without Judge for at least the Wild Card Series, and maybe longer.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Aaron Judge said. “That’s definitely the plan.”
Said the calf strain involves the soleus muscle — which he said is more crucial to running and hitting — making it more difficult to play through.
2. Will he be himself at the plate? Judge did not go on a minor-league rehab assignment before returning from the rib injury and it showed. He went 4 for 23 (.174) with one walk and 13 strikeouts in his seven games back before the calf injury. His timing was not there at all. Judge's one homer came on a hanging breaking ball. Otherwise, pitchers threw fastballs by him consistently.
To put a number on it, Judge missed with 41% of his swings against fastballs in his seven games back, more than double the 19% league average. This is what it looks like when you miss with more than two out of every five swings against heaters:
It is not exactly a surprise a hitter who did not go on a rehab assignment after spending more than three months on the shelf looked out of sorts at the plate. Judge and the Yankees knew it would take him some time to get back up to speed at the plate, and they were willing to live with it. The goal was always to be ready for the postseason, not so much the regular season.
These last nine games aren't particularly important for the Yankees in the standings, but they were incredibly important to Judge. He needed at-bats to rediscover his timing at the plate, and get back to being the dominant hitter he's been throughout his career. The calf strain puts that on pause. Judge now has even fewer at-bats available to get back to being himself.
3. Will he be able to play the field? There is a scenario in which Judge plays through the calf strain as a full-time DH who doesn't run at 100% (or close to it). How the Yankees would align their defense in that scenario, I have no idea. Ben Rice is a full-time DH these days and also New York's best non-Judge hitter. Platoon-mates Luis Gárcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt are first basemen.
Unless the Yankees do something unexpected, like put Gárcia back at second base (where he was terrible defensively) or Rice back behind the plate (where he was also terrible defensively), slotting Judge in at DH means one of the team's most productive hitters will have to sit. This is something the Yankees will worry about when the time comes, and not a second sooner.
Three questions for the Yankees
1. Where will the righty pop come from? The Yankees have a very lefty-heavy lineup and Judge's righty heft provides important balance. Only the Cleveland Guardians have gotten fewer plate appearances from righties this season. Friday's lineup against Arizona Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez could be what the Yankees run out there against lefties in October:
- 1B Paul Goldschmidt, RHB
- LF Cody Bellinger, LHB
- RF Heliot Ramos, RHB
- DH Ben Rice, LHB
- 3B Amed Rosario, RHB
- CF Spencer Jones, LHB
- SS George Lombard Jr., RHB
- C Austin Wells, LHB
- 2B Anthony Volpe, RHB
Goldschmidt and Ramos are lefty mashers. Bellinger and Rice are very productive left-on-left hitters. Jones has performed well against lefties as a big leaguer, though his minor-league track record against southpaws isn't great. Rosario is having his worst season against lefties. The 7-8-9 spots are unlikely to make an impact offensively, regardless of the pitcher's handedness.
That lineup would look much more imposing with Judge in the No. 3 spot. Perhaps this is not such a big concern though? Since trade deadline day, the Yankees have the highest batting average (.289) and on-base percentage (.362) against lefties, and the third-highest slugging percentage (.456) despite Judge not playing much, and not being much of a factor when he did play.
In all likelihood the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and Boston has three quality lefty starters (Jake Bennett, Ranger Suárez, Payton Tolle) and a shutdown lefty relief tandem (Aroldis Chapman, Erik Miller). To beat the Red Sox, the Yankees will need their righty hitters to produce, and now the status of their best right-handed hitter is in question.
2. Will the pitching hold up? Despite not having Judge for more than three months, the Yankees have the American League's best run differential (+143) and second-best record (89-64). They can thank their pitching staff. New York has allowed only 3.68 runs per game this year, the fewest in baseball. Since trade deadline day, it's an incredible 3.37 runs allowed per game.
There are some cracks beginning to form, however. Gerrit Cole has surrendered eight home runs in his last three starts, including five on a four-seam fastball that is no longer the dominant pitch it was at his peak. Max Fried's velocity has been down a tick since returning from a bone bruise in his elbow late last month. That injury has sent him to the injured list twice this year.
Cam Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, has thrown a career-high 184 ⅔ innings with two regular-season starts remaining, plus the postseason. Key late-inning relievers Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, and Brent Headrick have worked a lot -- A LOT -- this season and have all shown a slight dip in velocity in recent weeks, which perhaps is a sign the workload is catching up to them.
Without Judge (and sometimes even with him), the Yankees are a run prevention team. Their superpower is a suffocating pitching staff that is among the best in baseball at limiting hard contact, particularly in the air. With Judge absent, the pitching staff and the ability to prevent runs in general will be of paramount importance. No Judge reduces the margin of error considerably.
3. What about their other injured players? Judge is not the only injured Yankee. Center field Trent Grisham has not played since Sept. 4 due to a Grade 2 hamstring strain. On Friday, Boone said Grisham is pretty far into his running program, and he could make it back before the end of the regular season. That would give the outfield a lift should Judge miss extended time.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. has not played since jamming his thumb sliding into second base on Sept. 8. Boone said Chisholm will come off the injured list when the Yankees return home next week. He's had a down year overall, but Chisholm was playing his best baseball of the season right before the injury. He's an important presence given his speed and defense in particular.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers is working his way back from a flexor strain. He last pitched Aug. 22. Weathers is throwing bullpen sessions, though Boone confirmed he won't return during the regular season. If/when Weathers does return, it will be as a reliever. He has bullpen experience and the Yankees could use middle relief help, but Weathers has to make it back first.
At minimum, Chisholm and Grisham would give the Yankees more options for their Judge-less lineup, even if they only platoon. It wouldn't be hard to find a role for Weathers, who had allowed no more than one run in six of his last seven starts before the injury. Bottom line though, the Yankees need Judge. Everything else is secondary to his return and effectiveness.

item.content:encoded:
Gerrit Cole's two-game stretch against the San Diego Padres and the New York Mets raised concerns. With the postseason weeks away for the New York Yankees, Cole, who should be their two starter heading into the postseason, allowed seven home runs and nine earned runs in 11.1 IP. It was a ghastly set of performances, and it may have left the organization wondering how the rest of the season would shake out for their former Cy Young winner.
If there were any questions about Cole's abilities, his start against the 80-74 Arizona Diamondbacks may have alleviated a few worries. It may also have put to rest any internal debates. Cole did allow a home run this time out, but it was just one. Corbin Carroll pulled a 388-foot home run off Cole's bat at 110.7 MPH.
Headed into the postseason, pitching in Game 1 is an easy decision. Aaron Boone needs to hand the ball to Cy Young frontrunner and prospective MVP candidate Cam Schlittler. There's no reason to really overthink that one.
If Cole starts struggling again, though, the question of who the second starter is gets a little trickier. That might still be a conversation worth having if things go differently to close out the year, but for now, if Cole pitches the way he did against the Diamondbacks, there's no reason to save him for another series.
Cole's big test will be against the Tampa Bay Rays, since he lines up to face them in their next series. If he pitches well against them, he'll further solidify his spot as the team's two-starter.
A better outing for Gerrit Cole
When Aaron Boone was asked about Cole after the game, he said he wasn't too worried. He chalked his struggles up to a long season.
"I think a lot of people probably overreacted to a couple of outings that, frankly, are inevitable in a long season," Boone said, according to the New York Post's Greg Joyce. "The reality is he's having an outstanding season, he's throwing the ball really well, and a great pitcher like him is going to be able to make some adjustments when you have a couple where they get to you."
The Carroll blast was Cole's lone blemish. He pitched six innings of two-run ball, striking out six, allowing no walks, and four hits.
On the back end, he gave up a ton of soft contact. The Diamondbacks had an average exit velocity of 86.8 MPH against him. That's way down from his last two starts, when batters averaged 96.8 MPH against him.
This is the type of Cole the Yankees need in the postseason. Who knows what's happening with Aaron Judge, so the rotation and bullpen have to essentially be perfect if this team is going to make any noise this postseason.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
By Field Level Media
Sep 19 (Field Level Media) – The New York Yankees placed outfielder Aaron Judge on the 10-day injured list Saturday due to a right calf strain.
The move is retroactive to Thursday, one day after the Yankees’ captain and three-time American League MVP was removed from a game against the Minnesota Twins after the sixth inning due to tightness in his lower right leg.
Judge told reporters afterward that he felt the injury during the first inning and “tried to play it off” before reporting it to manager Aaron Boone.
Also on Saturday, the Yankees recalled infielder/outfielder Max Schuemann from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre.
Judge, 34, missed more than three months of the season due to a rib injury and only returned on Sept. 8.
“Once you start ramping up, things pop up,” Judge said. “Hopefully, it’s just one little thing and we’re back out there soon.”
Because the move is backdated to Thursday, Judge would be eligible for activation on Sept. 27, the final day of the regular season.
Judge has appeared in just 66 games this season, batting .241 with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs. In his seven games back from his previous IL stint, he was just 4-for-23 (.174) with one homer and three RBIs.
Schuemann, 29, batted .194 with two homers and eight RBIs in 41 games earlier this season with the Yankees.
(–Field Level Media)

item.content:encoded:
For a historic franchise like the New York Yankees, rotation stability is paramount over the long haul of a 162-game season. That makes Cam Schlittler’s dominant breakout campaign all the more remarkable—so much so that manager Aaron Boone believes the young right-hander has built a compelling case to take home the American League Cy Young Award.
When asked about Schlittler’s transformative presence in the rotation, Boone didn’t mince words: “Well, he’s gonna win the Cy Young!” The manager’s ringing endorsement underscores just how dominant Schlittler has been on the mound this year.
While Boone continues to navigate rotation depth with Ryan Weathers sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, Schlittler gives the Yankees a legitimate ace to rely on as they gear up for October.
On the offensive side, Boone is also monitoring the return timeline for slugger Aaron Judge, who was sidelined with a calf strain. In the meantime, the Yankees skipper has relied on depth options like Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger to keep the lineup producing.
Key milestones driving Schlittler’s Cy Young case
A stellar 2026 breakout campaign with the Yankees has vaulted Schlittler directly into the front-runner conversation for the American League Cy Young Award. Stepping up as the de facto ace while Gerrit Cole missed time, Schlittler has delivered elite run suppression, swing-and-miss stuff, and exceptional durability.
Here is a breakdown of the key numbers and milestones anchoring Schlittler’s Cy Young candidacy:
- 1.95 ERA: Schlittler took over the MLB ERA lead in September, standing as the only qualified starter with an ERA under 2.00.
- Historical run: His 1.71 ERA through his first 16 starts marked the lowest ERA by a Yankees starter through that stretch since Hall of Famer Whitey Ford in 1964.
- 228 Strikeouts in 184.2 IP (11.1 K/9): Schlittler eclipsed the 200-strikeout mark on August 28 against Boston, becoming the fourth-youngest pitcher in franchise history to achieve the feat.
- Signature outings: Highlighted by a career-high 13-strikeout performance against the Cincinnati Reds on June 19, along with double-digit strikeout shutouts against Philadelphia (12 K) and Atlanta (11 K).
Other top Cy Young contenders
Schlittler isn’t running unopposed in a tightly contested American League race. Strong campaigns from power arm Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and left-hander Garrett Crochet of the Boston Red Sox keep them firmly in the mix.
Over in the National League, the Cy Young field features plenty of heavy hitters, headlined by Milwaukee Brewers phenom Jacob Misiorowski, Atlanta Braves veteran Chris Sale, and the Philadelphia Phillies duo of Cristopher Sanchez and Jesus Luzardo.

item.dc:creator: Lou Landers
item.description: The New York Yankees were dealt another major injury blow earlier this week, and it came at the worst possible time in the MLB season. Days later, on Saturday, the team placed Aaron Judge officially back on the injured list with a right calf strain, just 11 days after returning from a lengthy absence caused by a fractured rib. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees were dealt another major injury blow earlier this week, and it came at the worst possible time in the MLB season.
Days later, on Saturday, the team placed Aaron Judge officially back on the injured list with a right calf strain, just 11 days after returning from a lengthy absence caused by a fractured rib.
At the same time, however, the Yankees received encouraging news on Jazz Chisholm Jr., who could be back in the lineup before the end of the regular season.
Aaron Judge heads back to injured list
Sep 11, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees right fielder Aaron Judge (99) runs back to the dugout in the sixth inning against the New York Mets at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Wendell Cruz-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
The Yankees announced Saturday that Judge was placed on the 10-day injured list, retroactive to Sept. 17, with a right calf strain. New York recalled infielder/outfielder Max Schuemann from Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre to take his roster spot.
Judge first experienced tightness in his lower right leg during Wednesday's game against the Minnesota Twins and was removed after the sixth inning. An MRI performed Thursday revealed the calf strain.
The bigger concern is the timing. Judge only returned Sept. 8 after missing more than three months with his rib injury. He went 4-for-23 with one home run across six games following his return.
Manager Aaron Boone has not provided a timetable for Judge's return and would not speculate about whether he will be available for the postseason. His earliest possible return is Sept. 27, the final day of the regular season.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return next week
Jun 2, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (13) walks off the field after the top of the seventh inning against the Cleveland Guardians at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
The Yankees did receive some positive injury news regarding Chisholm, who has been sidelined with a sprained right thumb since Sept. 10.
Boone said Chisholm is "doing well" and should be activated during the team's current homestand. MLB reports that Chisholm has hit for four consecutive days and has also resumed throwing, putting him on track for a potential return around Sept. 22-24.
That would give the Yankees a much-needed boost, particularly with Judge now sidelined again. New York is chasing Tampa Bay in the AL East and has a crucial four-game series against the Rays next week.
The Yankees now face the difficult task of navigating the final stretch of the regular season without their captain while hoping Chisholm can return as expected.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Aaron Boone drops hugely discouraging Aaron Judge update after IL move appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are back in the playoffs, but will Aaron Judge join them?
Just after returning from a three-month absence, Judge was placed on the 1o-day injured list with a right calf strain. With October around the corner, Yankees manager Aaron Boone gave a bleak outlook on whether Judge will return, per Bob Nightengale of USA Today.
When asked if Judge will return for the playoffs, he said, "I don't know.''
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"I don't have a timeline on it,'' Boone said. "I can't predict anything. … I mean, we have no idea; we're in the early stages. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires."
"Hopefully, we can have him be an option at some point.''
For three months, Judge was out with a rib injury. He returned to the lineup on Sept. 8 against the Colorado Rockies.
From there, Judge went 4-for-23 with 13 strikeouts. Then, Judge experienced leg discomfort during the three-game series against the Minnesota Twins. He last appeared on Wednesday, going 0-for-2 in a 5-4 loss to the Twins.
The Yankees are 89-64 and are leading the American League Wild Card standings. To win the Wild Card, the Magic need six wins with nine games left.
Making it through October without Judge will be a challenge.
"The reality is that we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him,'' Boone said. "There's no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but you know we have high expectations that don't change now. We have a lot of confidence in the people we run out there every day. We're going to match up day in and day out, and the goal doesn't change.''
Judge is batting .241 with 57 hits, 18 home runs, and 41 RBIs.
Related: Yankees' Gerrit Cole makes history in win vs. Diamondbacks

item.content:encoded:
On Saturday, the New York Yankees will play the second game of their series with the Arizona Diamondbacks in Phoenix.
They are coming off a 9-2 win on Friday.
Ahead of Saturday’s game, the Yankees will place three-time MVP Aaron Judge on the injured list.
Gary Phillips of NY Daily News Sports wrote (on Friday): “Aaron Judge will be placed on the 10-day injured list tomorrow with a right calf strain, the #Yankees say. A corresponding move will take place at that time.”
Roster Move Admits How Yankees Feel About Domínguez
It’s been revealed that the Yankees will use the open roster spot (from Judge) to call up Max Schuemann.
Bryan Hoch of MLB.com wrote (on Friday): “Aaron Boone said he would not place a timeline on Aaron Judge’s calf strain. Asked if Judge would be back for the postseason, Boone said, “I don’t know. I’m not going to predict anything.” Max Schuemann is en route and will join the Yankees tomorrow.”
It’s fair to point out that Jasson Domínguez (who was recently sent to Triple-A) would have been a good option.
He has started in right field 42 times this year.
Here’s what people were saying:
@RealPaulyRyder: “Dominguez is crushing the ball, but Schumann is coming up…”
@JackMcTraddles: “Do they not want to waste a Dominguez option or do they really like Schuemann more?”

item.content:encoded:
grandes ligas
Ben Rice dispara su jonrón 39 y los Yankees superan a los D-Backs
El artillero remolca 2 vueltas, llega a 94 y Nueva York se impone 9 por 2 a Arizona, equipo que se aleja de la batalla por clasificar
Ben Rice conectó su 39no jonrón de la temporada, Gerrit Cole se convirtió en la primera selección global del draft con más victorias y los Yankees de Nueva York aprovecharon una primera entrada de cinco carreras para tomar el control temprano y vencer 9-2 a los Diamondbacks de Arizona la noche del viernes.
Los Yankees ganaron por octava vez en 10 juegos después de enterarse de que Aaron Judge, tres veces Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana, regresaría a la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Nueva York, que ya aseguró un puesto en los playoffs, está a cuatro juegos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en el Este de la Liga Americana con nueve juegos por disputar.
Los D-backs han perdido tres seguidos y sus esperanzas de playoffs están en serios aprietos. Están a cinco juegos del último comodín de la Liga Nacional con ocho juegos restantes.
Los primeros cinco bateadores de Nueva York se embasaron ante el zurdo All-Star de los D-backs, el venezolano Eduardo Rodríguez, y un sencillo de dos carreras de George Lombard Jr. puso la pizarra 5-0. Lombard añadió un jonrón solitario en la sexta y terminó con tres carreras impulsadas.
Cole (9-9) se recuperó tras un par de aperturas en las que permitió siete cuadrangulares —la mayor cantidad que ha concedido en un lapso de dos juegos. Permitió dos carreras y cuatro imparables en seis entradas, y ponchó a seis.
Elegido primero por Pittsburgh en 2011, Cole consiguió su victoria número 162. Es una más que Mike Moore, seleccionado como número 1 por Seattle en 1981.
Rodríguez (15-7) eligió un mal momento para tener, posiblemente, su peor apertura de la temporada: necesitó 45 lanzamientos para conseguir tres outs, su cifra más alta en una primera entrada. Permitió siete carreras, cinco hits y otorgó cuatro bases por bolas en 5 1/3 entradas. _

item.content:encoded:
The Bronx Bombers secured their spot in the 2026 MLB postseason, but it hasn’t all been smooth sailing. Cody Bellinger lamented Aaron Judge’s recent injury, which has left the New York Yankees awaiting an update on his timeline, but he remains confident in the roster’s talent and its ability to keep moving forward.
“Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he’s the best hitter in the game,” Bellinger said via MLB insider Bryan Hoch on X. “For us in here, our mindset is, we’re going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I’m fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody.”
The Pinstripes want to return to the World Series, and they will have to do it with the players available to them. For now, Aaron Boone has both depth and talent on his roster to accomplish big things in the Bronx.
What injury did Aaron Judge suffer?
Aaron Judge is back on the injured list after suffering a right calf strain during Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins. He initially left the game early with leg tightness, but an MRI revealed the strain, forcing the Yankees to put him back on the 10-day IL.
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees looks on.
Making matters worse, he had just returned a week prior from a broken rib that kept him out for over three months. While he could technically be eligible to return for the regular-season finale on September 27, Aaron Boone hasn’t set a timeline, leaving his availability for the postseason up in the air.
Bellinger steps into a bigger role
With Aaron Judge sidelined, Cody Bellinger must step up as the primary offensive anchor and versatile anchor for the New York Yankees. Batting .273 with 16 home runs, 71 RBIs, and an .788 OPS across 126 games, Bellinger brings crucial run production to the middle of the order.
His elite defensive flexibility will be just as vital, as he is expected to shift seamlessly between right field to cover Judge’s usual post, center field, and first base depending on daily lineup needs.
Cody Bellinger at the 2026 MLB All-Star Game.
Yankees’ next challenges
As the regular season wraps up, Cody Bellinger and the Yankees are heading into the home stretch with a busy final week on the schedule. They finish up their road trip out west with two more against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field (September 19 and 20), before returning to the Bronx for a heavy home stand.
They’ll kick that off with a four-game set against the Tampa Bay Rays at Yankee Stadium—including a Tuesday doubleheader on September 22—and then wrap up the regular season at home with a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles from September 25 to 27.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Últimas Noticias Sobre Las Lesiones De Los Yankees: Dos Jugadores Se Perderán El Resto De La Temporada Y Otros Dos Están A Punto De Volver
item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — La lista de lesionados en el vestuario de los Yankees cuenta dos historias a la vez. Por un lado, se está vaciando. Por el otro, acaba de llenarse más. El mismo fin de semana en que dos titulares se acercaban a su regreso, el equipo se enteró de que terminaría la temporada regular sin su capitán.
Para unos Yankees que persiguen el título de división y se preparan para octubre, este momento tiene sus pros y sus contras. Llegan refuerzos tanto para el cuadro como para los jardines. Pero no volverán una pieza clave de la defensa ni un pilar de la rotación de lanzadores.
Chisholm y Grisham, a punto de volver
La buena noticia viene del lado de los jugadores de campo. Jazz Chisholm Jr., de baja desde el 10 de septiembre por un esguince en el pulgar derecho, volverá al equipo durante la serie en casa que empieza el martes contra los Rays. Boone dijo que Chisholm había bateado cuatro días seguidos y que ya había vuelto a lanzar.
Chisholm estaba en racha cuando se lesionó: había promediado un promedio de bateo de 0,375, con un porcentaje de embasado de 0,464 y un jonrón en sus últimos siete partidos. Su regreso devuelve a los Yankees a su segunda base titular justo en el momento más importante de la temporada.
«Veremos cuáles son nuestras necesidades y cómo se le ve, y si creemos que está listo para incorporarse y aportar su granito de arena», dijo Boone.
Grisham le sigue de cerca. El jardinero central lleva fuera desde el 5 de septiembre por una distensión de grado 2 en el isquiotibial derecho, y Boone ha dicho que ya está muy avanzado en su programa de recuperación con carreras. Ahora los Yankees barajan la posibilidad de que vuelva antes de que termine la temporada regular.
Judge, de baja por una distensión en la pantorrilla
La noticia más impactante es la de Aaron Judge. El tres veces MVP de la Liga Americana entra en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha, una decisión que los Yankees hicieron oficial el sábado, aunque con efecto retroactivo desde el jueves. Así que su regreso más temprano podría ser en el último partido de la temporada regular, el 27 de septiembre.
Judge tuvo que abandonar el partido del miércoles, que acabaron perdiendo en la 13.ª entrada en Minnesota, por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha, que, según él, empezó ya en la primera entrada. Una resonancia magnética realizada el jueves en Phoenix confirmó la distensión. Boone no quiso dar detalles sobre la gravedad ni sobre el tiempo de recuperación, y tampoco se comprometió a que volviera para la postemporada.
Cuando le preguntaron directamente si Judge volvería para los playoffs, Boone fue breve.
«No lo sé», dijo Boone. «No tengo un plazo para él. Ahora mismo está en la lista de lesionados. No voy a hacer predicciones. Está recibiendo tratamiento y ya veremos qué pasa».
Su ausencia se nota menos de lo que se habría notado antes. Los Yankees tienen un balance de 48-39 en los partidos que Judge se ha perdido esta temporada y de 41-25 cuando juega. Aun así, Boone se lo puso claro sobre la derrota.
«No hay quien pueda sustituir a un jugador tan bueno como Aaron Judge, pero tenemos grandes expectativas», dijo Boone. «Y eso no va a cambiar ahora».
A Weathers se le acaba la pista
El contratiempo más discreto es el de Ryan Weathers. El zurdo lleva en la lista de lesionados desde el 23 de agosto por una distensión en los flexores del antebrazo izquierdo, y Boone admitió el viernes que es poco probable que lance en un partido antes de que termine la temporada.
Esto descarta que el lanzador, que sin hacer mucho ruido se había convertido en uno de los brazos más fiables de los Yankees, vuelva a jugar esta temporada regular. Weathers terminó con un balance de 5-8 y una efectividad de 3,60 en 25 salidas como titular —su mejor marca personal—, y registró una efectividad de 2,27 en sus últimas siete salidas antes de la lesión.
No está totalmente descartado para lo que queda de temporada. Weathers tenía previsto hacer una segunda sesión de bullpen el sábado, y el siguiente paso sería una sesión de bateo en vivo. Todavía es posible que tenga un papel en el bullpen durante la postemporada si su preparación avanza más rápido, aunque los Yankees esperarán para valorar su progreso.
La estadística que cambia el panorama del jardín
El regreso de Trent Grisham parecía complicado antes de que Judge se lesionara, porque el novato Spencer Jones aprovechó la oportunidad. Jones ha bateado .361, con un porcentaje de embasado de .425 y un porcentaje de slugging de .528 en los 10 partidos que lleva jugando en el centro del campo.
La ausencia de Judge cambia las cuentas. Ahora hay sitio para los dos. Grisham podría volver a jugar de centro frente a los lanzadores diestros, lo que dejaría a Jones en el campo derecho, donde de otro modo estaría Judge. Una lesión ha creado discretamente un hueco en la alineación que no existía hace una semana.
El jugador de campo interior y exterior Max Schuemann se ha desplazado a Phoenix para unirse a los Yankees de cara al partido del sábado, aportando profundidad al equipo mientras se va definiendo la alineación.
El martes empieza en el Yankee Stadium una serie de cuatro partidos contra los Rays, que incluye una doble jornada, y que podría decidir el título de la división. Los Yankees la afrontarán sin Judge ni Weathers, pero probablemente con Chisholm y quizá Grisham de vuelta en el equipo.
Por ahora, el panorama es mitad optimista, mitad sombrío. Dos jugadores vuelven a cruzar la puerta del vestuario. Otros dos están pendientes del calendario, con la esperanza de que aún haya tiempo para marcar la diferencia en octubre.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario abajo.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Bill Madden: The 20-something stars are taking over MLB’s award races this season
item.dc:creator: Bill Madden
item.description: In the absence of Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge, the mysterious power outages of Vlad Guerrero Jr. and Cal Raleigh, and the injuries to Tarik Skubal and Garrett Crochet, baseball’s postseason awards are coming into focus by ushering in a new wave of 20-something superstars. Going into the weekend the teams with the best records in each league were the small market Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, both of which with leading candidates for baseball’s postseason hardware who are still years aw
item.content:encoded:
In the absence of Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge, the mysterious power outages of Vlad Guerrero Jr. and Cal Raleigh, and the injuries to Tarik Skubal and Garrett Crochet, baseball’s postseason awards are coming into focus by ushering in a new wave of 20-something superstars.
Going into the weekend the teams with the best records in each league were the small market Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, both of which with leading candidates for baseball’s postseason hardware who are still years away from their prime.
For the Brewers, 24-year-old Jacob Misiorowski is the runaway leader for the NL Cy Young Award, at 15-5 and leading the majors in ERA (1.89), strikeouts (243), WHIP (0.812) and strikeouts per nine innings (13.1) — while the Rays, in their bid to salt away the AL East, have gotten a late boost from their 23-year old third baseman Junior Caminero, who took over the AL home run lead last week and was neck and neck with Houston’s Yordan Alvarez in RBI and total bases.
On the surface, Alvarez, who leads the NL in OPS and batting (.311), would appear to have the overall statistical edge on Caminero for the MVP. But the fact that Alvarez is a DH and Caminero, who’s missed only one game while adding superior defense at third base for a team that is likely to win the division also bodes well for him. This is one race that figures to go down to the last day, with the deciding factor possibly being whether the Astros win the AL West.
As for the AL Cy Young Award, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees’ 25-year-old sophomore, has zoomed ahead of the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease with a season for the ages, including a major league-leading 1.95 ERA and 0.904 WHIP and the most starts in Yankee history allowing one or fewer runs (21). His 1.14 ERA for 16 road starts is also the lowest in American League history.
Over in the National League, with Ohtani shackled with knee and bicep injuries that have prevented him from pitching since July 3, effectively ending his chances for a fourth straight MVP, the Cubs’ 24-year-old Pete Crow-Armstrong has stepped up with a phenomenal breakthrough season. Going into the weekend, Crow-Armstrong, who’s played every game, was leading the majors in slugging, OPS and total bases and was second behind Kyle Schwarber in the NL in homers with 44 and third in RBI with 105. On Aug. 29 he hit three homers in a game and with his 44th homer on Sept. 17 surpassed Hall of Famer Billy Williams as the most by a left-handed hitter in Cubs history.
Sorry, but we’re again unable to refrain from reminding that Crow-Armstrong was the Mets’ 2020 first round draft pick who, the next season, they traded to the Cubs for two months of rental free agent Javy Baez.
When it comes to the Rookies of the Year, I realize in this lost season for the Mets there’s been a lot of buzz for Nolan McLean and Carson Benge, but neither are going to win the NL award. That would have to be Cincinnati’s unsung Sal Stewart, who even if nobody probably had him on their Rookie of the Year bingo card at the start of the season, happens to be leading all NL rookies in homers (32) and RBI (110) and has played every day. An equally strong favorite for the AL Rookie of the Year is Cleveland lefty Parker Messick, a second round draft pick out of Florida State three years ago, who leads all AL rookies in wins (12), ERA (2.57), strikeouts (186) and WHIP (1.04).
IT’S A MADD, MADD WORLD
You have to wonder if the window has already closed on Aaron Judge leading the Yankees to a World Series title. The 34-year-old Yankee captain has missed 317 games (and counting) and had only four full seasons since 2018 and the fact remains he’s 280 pounds — and every time he has to make a diving catch or crash into a wall at his age now that’s 280 pounds of impact on his body. No surprise the rib injury that’s sidelined him most of this season. … For nine decades, Juan Vene was a fixture in the press boxes of Yankee Stadium and Shea Stadium and even though his name may not be familiar to most New York baseball fans, he was a legend, especially in his native Venezuela, but really all over Latin America. Word came last week that Vene passed away Sept. 15 in Miami at age 97. A long-time member of the Baseball Writers Association and a regular Hall of Fame voter, Vene was a friend to all of us. Anyone needing an interview with a Latin player in the offseason could count on Vene to help set it up. RIP. … If the White Sox are somehow able to hold on and win the AL Central it will be a remarkable achievement given the year-long state of their starting pitching. According to the Elias Bureau, White Sox starters have logged by far the fewest innings (639) in the majors to the runner-up Nationals’ 671 1/3, and as they stagger to the finish line they have been employing “openers” 2-3 times a week.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will play the rest of the regular season without slugger Aaron Judge. While they understand the magnitude of his loss, they enter the stretch run with belief.
The Yanks scored five runs in the first inning of a 9-2 victory over the Arizona Diamondbacks in the first game of a weekend series Friday, and the teams meet again Saturday in Phoenix as Arizona attempts to stay alive in the National League wild-card race.
"Obviously losing 'Judgey' hurts," Cody Bellinger said. "We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is we're going to have to find a way. The talent in this room speaks for itself.
"I'm fully confident we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win and beat anybody."
American League Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA) will face Arizona right-hander Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77) in the second game of the series.
The Diamondbacks (80-74) will ask Pfaadt to end a slump in which they have lost five of six. They are five games behind San Diego, the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia (all 85-69) for the three NL wild-card spots with eight games to play.
"We know where we're at," Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said. "We can't afford to worry about things we can't control. I'm going to say there's time. There's always time."
The Yankees (89-64) are 48-39 this season without Judge, who was placed on the injured list Friday with a strained right calf after missing three months earlier with a fractured right rib.
New York is also without injured regulars Jazz Chisholm Jr. (thumb) and Trent Grisham (hamstring), although manager Aaron Boone said Chisholm could return for the Tampa Bay series early next week.
The Yankees, who already have qualified for the postseason, are four games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East, and the teams have a four-game series at Yankee Stadium beginning Tuesday.
"There is no replacing a player as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations that don't change now," Boone said. "One thing we do know is that we are in the dance.
"We've been built on the strength of our starting pitching all year."
No one has been as strong as Schlittler, who is in his first full season and has made every start while Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon have missed time with injuries or recovery time.
Schlittler has won four of his last five starts and has given up one run or fewer in each of his last seven. He was struck on the back of his right leg by Bo Bichette's 111.5 mph comebacker on his 94th and last pitch of a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets last Sunday, but shrugged it off.
"You have an ace at the top that has pitched like that," Boone said. "That's a good place to start. He's been dominant. This is largely in line with who we saw down the stretch last year."
Schlittler has never faced the Diamondbacks, although Jesus Sanchez is 4 for 12 with three walks against him.
Pfaadt is 0-2 with a 5.74 ERA in his last five starts, and he gave up six runs and 10 hits in 6 2/3 innings in a loss to Texas on Aug. 12. He will be pitching on six days' rest after being pushed back so Eduardo Rodriguez could start the first game of the series.
Pfaadt lost his only outing against the Yankees, giving up six runs in 4 1/3 innings of a 7-1 loss as a rookie in 2023. Cody Bellinger is 2 for 7 with two solo homers against him and Luis Garcia Jr. is 3 for 7 with a homer.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yankees Are Creating Their Own Distraction With Aaron Judge Injury Secrecy
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
item.description: The New York Yankees haven't exactly been forthright about what's been going on with Aaron Judge. They didn't offer much information when he was initially pulled during the game against the Minnesota Twins. All the public knew was that Judge had tightness in his lower leg, and that was about it. They didn't alleviate any concerns about Judge after he was placed on the injured list. In fact, things have been just as hush. According to the Daily News' Gary Phillips, Judge wasn't available to speak
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees haven't exactly been forthright about what's been going on with Aaron Judge. They didn't offer much information when he was initially pulled during the game against the Minnesota Twins. All the public knew was that Judge had tightness in his lower leg, and that was about it.
They didn't alleviate any concerns about Judge after he was placed on the injured list. In fact, things have been just as hush.
According to the Daily News' Gary Phillips, Judge wasn't available to speak to the media before the game. He wasn't there for them after their 9-2 win against the Arizona Diamondbacks either. The extent of the calf strain is still unclear.
Aaron Boone didn't offer up much of an answer when asked about Judge. His response was muted and didn't offer insight into whether he'll return in the postseason.
"I don't have a timeline on him," Boone said, according to MLB.com's Bryan Hoch. "I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires."
While the public knowing what's wrong with Judge doesn't change his schedule or the organization's plans heading into the postseason, their secrecy won't keep the team from answering a barrage of questions. In fact, they'll likely get more.
This isn't the type of story that goes away with time, and even though the Yankees beat a tough opponent in Eduardo Rodriguez, that will be the story on all the back pages. There won't be an image of a sullen Rodriguez walking off the mound, but rather an image of Judge plastered on every newspaper. This storm cloud is still following the team.
Ghosting the media is a weird look, too
Plus, Judge avoiding the media looks odd when Jazz Chisholm Jr. or Clint Frazier did the same and took hits for it. When Frazier did it in 2019, a headline in The Athletic said that he "ghosted" reporters. There won't be any of that with Judge.
Not speaking to the media was held against those guys and used to say something about their character. For Judge, their captain, the same standard should apply. If he is going to be the example of how a New York Yankee should carry themselves, he should be front and center for reporters, as anyone else would be.
Obviously, Judge could talk, and the Yankees can offer a realistic timetable for what they think is happening, but that doesn't change his timeline. They'll still have to be without him, and guys like Spencer Jones will need to step up.
Still, come the postseason, it's probably better to mitigate any potential circus around the team. Playing in October is hard enough, and the team already gets enough attention during this time of year. No need to make things harder for themselves.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Jazz Chisholm Jr. Expected to Return for Yankees' Final Homestand Against Rays
item.dc:creator: Miracle Dimwesh

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are getting closer to having Jazz Chisholm Jr. back in the lineup.
Manager Aaron Boone said Chisholm is expected to be activated from the 10-day injured list during New York's final regular-season homestand. The Yankees begin that homestand Tuesday against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Chisholm has been sidelined since Sept. 10 after spraining his right thumb on a head-first slide into second base against the Colorado Rockies.
The second baseman has continued making progress during his recovery. Boone said Friday marked Chisholm's fourth straight day of hitting in the batting cages, while he has also resumed throwing on the field.
The Yankees have been using Anthony Volpe at second base while Chisholm recovers. His return will give Boone another option in the infield as New York manages its lineup during the final week of the regular season.
Chisholm was also swinging the bat well before the injury. He hit .375 with a .464 on-base percentage and .500 slugging percentage over his final seven games.
The 28-year-old has appeared in 134 games this season, batting .232 with 16 doubles, three triples, 19 home runs and 55 RBI in 461 at-bats.
Chisholm has also provided plenty of value on the bases. He has scored 68 runs and stolen 40 bases on 49 attempts while posting a .312 on-base percentage and .403 slugging percentage.
His return comes at an important point for New York. The Yankees entered Saturday with an 88-64 record and sat 4 games behind the Rays in the AL East.
New York is also dealing with the expected absence of Aaron Judge for the remainder of the regular season, making Chisholm's return another potential boost for the lineup.
For now, the Yankees will continue monitoring Chisholm's thumb as he works toward activation. If he remains on schedule, he should be back during the final homestand before the postseason begins.

item.title: [Líder en deportes] Gerrit Cole reacciona y comanda la victoria de los Yankees
item.dc:creator: Diego Torres Contreras
item.description: Gerrit Cole disipó las dudas sobre su rendimiento actual tras firmar una sólida actuación desde el montículo en la victoria 9-2 de los Yankees de Nueva York frente a los Cascabeles de Arizona. El derecho, quien venía de una racha complicada con los cuadrangulares, ajustó y mostró su mejor cara en la jornada del viernes. La ofensiva neoyorquina respaldó de inmediato a su abridor con un racimo de cinco anotaciones en el propio primer episodio ante el criollo Eduardo Rodríguez. Sencillos remolcador
item.content:encoded:
Gerrit Cole disipó las dudas sobre su rendimiento actual tras firmar una sólida actuación desde el montículo en la victoria 9-2 de los Yankees de Nueva York frente a los Cascabeles de Arizona. El derecho, quien venía de una racha complicada con los cuadrangulares, ajustó y mostró su mejor cara en la jornada del viernes.
La ofensiva neoyorquina respaldó de inmediato a su abridor con un racimo de cinco anotaciones en el propio primer episodio ante el criollo Eduardo Rodríguez. Sencillos remolcadores de Amed Rosario y George Lombard Jr., sumados a un boleto con bases llenas de Ben Rice, le dieron la ventaja a los «Bombarderos del Bronx» desde el comienzo.
Lombard Jr. completó una jornada destacada al impulsar tres carreras, incluyendo un bambinazo en el sexto tramo. Por su parte, Rice también lució con el madero al conectar su jonrón número 39 de la temporada regular, consolidándose como el líder del equipo en ese apartado.
El único daño que permitió Cole llegó en el segundo inning mediante un cuadrangular de dos carreras de Corbin Carroll. Sin embargo, el serpentinero ajustó el brazo y maniató por completo a la toletería de los D-backs durante el resto de su labor.
Leer también: Mookie Betts comanda con dos jonrones noche de cinco vuelacercas
Con este resultado, los Yankees (89-64) sumaron su triunfo número 11 en sus últimos 15 compromisos y se colocaron a cuatro juegos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en la pelea por el Este de la Liga Americana, mostrando solvencia ofensiva para suplir la ausencia por lesión de Aaron Judge.

item.title: [ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos] Ben Rice hits 39th homer, Cole becomes winningest No. 1 draft pick as Yanks cruise past D-backs 9-2
item.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
item.dc:creator: ABC News; DAVID BRANDT AP baseball writer
item.description: Ben Rice hits 39th homer, Cole becomes winningest No. 1 draft pick as Yanks cruise past D-backs 9-2 Ben Rice hit his 39th homer of the season, Gerrit Cole became the winningest No. 1 overall draft pick and the New York Yankees used a five-run first inning to take control early and beat the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2 PHOENIX -- Ben Rice hit his 39th homer of the season, Gerrit Cole became the winningest No. 1 overall draft pick and the New York Yankees used a five-run first inning to take control e
item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice hits 39th homer, Cole becomes winningest No. 1 draft pick as Yanks cruise past D-backs 9-2
Ben Rice hit his 39th homer of the season, Gerrit Cole became the winningest No. 1 overall draft pick and the New York Yankees used a five-run first inning to take control early and beat the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2
PHOENIX -- Ben Rice hit his 39th homer of the season, Gerrit Cole became the winningest No. 1 overall draft pick and the New York Yankees used a five-run first inning to take control early and beat the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2 on Friday night.
After learning three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge was headed back to the injured list with a right calf strain, the Yankees won for the eighth time in 10 games. New York, which has already clinched a playoff spot, is four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East with nine games remaining.
The D-backs' have lost three straight and their playoff hopes are in major trouble. They're five games back of the final NL wild card with eight games left.
New York's first five batters reached against D-backs' All-Star left hander Eduardo Rodriguez and George Lombard Jr.'s two-run single made it 5-0. Lombard added a solo homer in the sixth and finished with three RBIs.
Cole (9-9) bounced back from a pair of starts that saw him surrender seven homers — the most he's ever given up over a two-game span. He gave up two runs and four hits in six innings, striking out six.
Selected first by Pittsburgh in 2011, Cole won his 162nd game. That is one more than Mike Moore, picked No. 1 by Seattle in 1981.
Rodriguez (15-7) picked a bad time to have arguably his worst start this season, needing 45 pitches to get three outs, his career high for a first inning. He gave up seven runs, five hits and four walks over 5 1/3 innings.
Corbin Carroll hit a two-run homer to cut the deficit to 5-2 in the second. Rice's solo homer in the third pushed the Yankees ahead 6-2.
The D-backs send RHP Brandon Pfaadt (7-3, 3.77 ERA) to the mound Saturday night while the Yankees counter with RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95).
___

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Complete Yankees Cy Young history as Cam Schlittler inches closer to 2026 award
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski
item.description: Even the biggest of homers couldn’t predict just how dominant Cam Schlittler would be this season. The ace of the New York Yankees has cemented himself as one of the top pitchers in all of baseball and proven that last year was not a fluke. Schlittler’s 2026 season may even go down as one of the best pitching performances in the entire history of the franchise. item.content:encoded:
Even the biggest of homers couldn’t predict just how dominant Cam Schlittler would be this season. The ace of the New York Yankees has cemented himself as one of the top pitchers in all of baseball and proven that last year was not a fluke. Schlittler’s 2026 season may even go down as one of the best pitching performances in the entire history of the franchise. Despite the Yankees’ storied franchise, only six pitchers have won the Cy Young award for the team. Schlittler is likely about to change that.
With 6.0 fWAR accumulated throughout the 2026 season, Schlittler is tied with Milwaukee Brewers’ sensation Jacob Misiorowski for the league lead among pitchers. It’s no coincidence that both hurlers are the favorites to take home the Cy Young in their respective leagues. For Schlittler, he’d not only be the seventh Yankees pitcher to win the award, but he’d also be the youngest.
As the Yankees prepare for another postseason run, they will hope that Schlittler’s historic performance is able to carry over into October. As history has taught us, the Yankees win when their pitchers win.
Yankees Complete History of Cy Young Award Winners
It’s hard to fathom that the Yankees only average a Cy Young award winner every 20 years or so. From Mike Mussina to CC Sabathia, the franchise has certainly featured plenty of Hall of Fame pitchers that have come close to winning the award. Mussina was overshadowed by teammate Roger Clemens during his stellar 2001 campaign with the Yankees. Sabathia got as close to third place in the voting following his 2010 season.
Even the great Mariano Rivera couldn’t quite do enough to sway the voters and win the elusive award as a reliever. He finished in the top three of voting four separate times. This includes two seasons when he finished in the top 10 of the MVP race. It’s rare, but pitchers have occasionally made strong cases for MVP.
We’ll detail the six previous Yankees who actually managed to cross the finish line and why they deserved to take home the top pitching award. And because a Yankees season isn’t complete without a World Series title, we’ll also note how far a Cy Young winner got the team in the postseason.
Gerrit Cole, 2023
As the most recent Yankees pitcher to win the award, Gerrit Cole did something in 2023 that only one other player had accomplished in the team’s history, winning the award by unanimous decision. With all 30 first place votes, Cole more than doubled the amount of points that second-place pitcher Sonny Gray received.
As you might imagine, Cole’s 2023 is his most impressive season with the Yankees since joining the club in 2020. He struck out 222 hitters across 209 innings pitched. Although his 3.16 FIP doesn’t scream “elite pitcher,” he allowed just 157 hits while surrendering just 48 walks.
Despite Cole’s brilliance, the club finished with a mediocre 82-80 record, missing out on the playoffs for the first time since the 2016 season, though you couldn’t blame Cole for that. He boasted a 1.03 ERA and a minuscule 0.686 WHIP over his last five starts of the season, including a two-hit shutdown against the Toronto Blue Jays in his last start of the season. If only Aaron Judge hadn't run toe-first into the wall at Dodger Stadium.
Roger Clemens, 2001
As mentioned earlier, Clemens scooped away a lot of votes from Mussina when he won the Cy Young in 2001. Some would argue that Clemens probably stole that award, but you can’t deny that he still had a very good season.
With more emphasis placed on individual wins back then, Clemens boasted 20 wins to go alongside his 213 strikeouts. Clemens’ 2001 season would probably be considered his weakest of his seven award-winning seasons. But hey, it was the early 2000s. People voted more on vibes than actual performance.
Clemens’ 3.29 FIP that season was enough to help take the Yankees to the World Series, where they lost in heartbreaking fashion to the Arizona Diamondbacks. But we don’t have to dwell on that part.
Ron Guidry, 1978
Before Clemens won the award in 2001, it had been 23 years since a Yankees pitcher won it. But oh man, did Ron Guidry ever earn the award in 1978. With a 1.74 ERA across 273 1/3 innings pitched, his season is what many consider to be the best by a pitcher in team history. His home run per nine rate of 0.4 is almost laughable.
Even by modern metrics, Guidry was the clear-cut winner that season. His 2.19 FIP and 208 ERA+ was leaps and bounds better than any other pitcher up for consideration that year, which is why he became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award unanimously.
Guidry was a large reason that the team won 100 games that year. The Yankees would carry that tremendous momentum into the postseason and defeat the Los Angeles Dodgers in the World Series.
Sparky Lyle, 1977
Unlike the long wait in between Clemens and Guidry winning the Cy Young, the Yankees actually had quite the time in the late 70s when it came to award-winning pitchers. Before Guidry, the team saw reliever Sparky Lyle take home the award in 1977. He became just the second reliever in MLB history to win the honor. Since then, seven more relievers have joined the rare club.
When looking at his numbers, you probably wouldn’t really consider Lyle to be a dominant force out of the bullpen. Despite that, he was certainly one of the most effective pitchers in the league. With just 68 strikeouts in 137 innings, Lyle didn’t just rely on swing and misses to get outs. He collected 13 wins and 26 saves, demonstrating just how pivotal he was to the Yankees.
With Lyle coming out of the pen, the Yankees won 100 games in the regular season. He then helped pave the way to a World Series title over the Dodgers.
Whitey Ford, 1961
With 236 career wins and six World Series rings in his collection, Whitey Ford is one of the foremost Yankees winners in team history. In 1961, he added a Cy Young to his trophy case. At 32 years old, he threw a career-high 283 innings, which included 11 complete games and three shutouts.
Ford’s 1961 season may be outshined in the annals of history by Roger Maris’ record-setting performance, but that doesn’t make it any less impressive. Like other pitchers on this list, Ford didn’t put up mind-boggling numbers or boast off-the-charts metrics. Outside of innings pitched, he didn’t really do one thing extremely well. However, he did do just about everything very well.
Ford was more than enough of a pitcher to be considered the ace of a team that some argue to be one of the best teams in MLB history. With 109 wins and a World Series title, it is hard to argue against that claim.
Bob Turley, 1958
Just three years before Ford won his Cy Young, Bob Turley became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award in 1958. Once again, like a number of other Yankees on this list, Turley’s 1958 season isn’t something that you would circle as an all-time great year. His 4.04 WHIP and 119 ERA+ were shockingly poor in hindsight.
Turley probably became the first Yankees pitcher to steal the award from a more deserving pitcher as well. Sorry, Warren Spahn. While Turley threw 245 1/3 innings, including 19 complete games, he was an especially wild pitcher. Turley walked 128 batters, nearly double the amount of walks surrendered by the second and third place pitchers in the Cy Young voting combined that year.
With all of that said, Turley pitched well enough to help lead the Yankees to 92 wins. They then went on to defeat the Milwaukee Braves in seven games in the World Series. When all is said and done, what more could you ask for?

That would be Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is expected to return from a sprained right thumb on the team’s upcoming and final homestand of the regular season. item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — While Friday wasn’t a positive day in terms of injury news for the Aaron Judge-less Yankees, Aaron Boone did say that the team can count on a reinforcement soon.
That would be Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is expected to return from a sprained right thumb on the team’s upcoming and final homestand of the regular season. Boone said that Friday was the second baseman’s fourth day of hitting in a row. He’s also been throwing the last few days.
“He’s getting very close,” Boone said.
Chisholm previously said that he hoped to come off the injured list when the Yankees returned home from Arizona. He hurt his thumb while sliding into second base on Sept. 8.
Chisholm is an impending free agent in the midst of a disappointing season, but he had rounded into form before getting. He hit .295 with an .832 OPS, three home runs, 10 RBI and 10 stolen bases over his last 29 games. He also had a .391 OPS and a 1.028 OPS over his last 15 games.
The hope is that Chisholm can pick up where he left off, especially with Judge returning to the IL with a right calf strain.
Chisholm is hitting .232 with a .715 OPS, 19 home runs, 55 RBI and 40 steals overall.
GRISHAM ‘COULD BE IN PLAY’
Boone also said that Trent Grisham is pretty far into his running progression and “could be in play at the end of the season.” The center fielder suffered his second right hamstring strain of the season earlier this month.
Prior to that, Grisham hit .211 with a .703 OPS and 18 home runs. He’s also been one of the slowest and worst defensive center fielders in baseball the last two years.
With Grisham not producing on either side of the ball and Spencer Jones more than holding his own, the former was not guaranteed to start in the playoffs prior to Judge’s injury. Now, however, Grisham could play center while Jones handles right. The Yankees can also use Jones in center and Heliot Ramos is right against lefties.
WEATHERS WON’T RETURN BEFORE PLAYOFFS
While the Yankees had hoped otherwise, Aaron Boone said Ryan Weathers is “unlikely” to return before the end of the regular season. The left-handed starter, working his way back from a flexor strain as a reliever, is expected to throw his second bullpen session at Chase Field on Saturday.
Asked if the Yankees would be comfortable having Weathers’ first game off the IL come in the postseason, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled the idea out.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] No Aaron Judge, no problem? Yankees show they're still a force to be reckoned with
item.dc:creator: Bob Nightengale; USA TODAY
item.description: PHOENIX — Just in case anyone thought the New York Yankees would simply fade away into the night, their season drifting out to sea with the news that Aaron Judge may be done for the season, the Bronx Bombers delivered a subtle message Friday night that reverberated around the baseball world. The Yankees, with Gerrit Cole looking more like the 2023 Cy Young winner than the pitcher who looked like he was throwing batting practice earlier this month, smacked around the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2 Frid
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Just in case anyone thought the New York Yankees would simply fade away into the night, their season drifting out to sea with the news that Aaron Judge may be done for the season, the Bronx Bombers delivered a subtle message Friday night that reverberated around the baseball world.
The Yankees, with Gerrit Cole looking more like the 2023 Cy Young winner than the pitcher who looked like he was throwing batting practice earlier this month, smacked around the Arizona Diamondbacks 9-2 Friday, and acted afterwards as if it was simply business as usual.
There was Cole, who had given up seven homers in his last two starts pitching his best game in a month, yielding four hits and two runs in six innings.
There was DH Ben Rice, looking like a top-5 MVP candidate by hitting his 39th home run of the season − just as Yankees manager Aaron Boone predicted in spring training − to go along with 94 RBI.
There was rookie shortstop George Lombard, hitting a homer and playing flawless defense.
And there were the Yankees, talking as if they plan to be playing deep into October, whether Judge is in uniform or on their bench as a cheerleader. Judge is going on the injured list with a strained calf and the Yankees have no idea whether he'll return.
"I mean, it's a tough blow for us to take,'' Rice said. "Obviously, we were missing him for a long time there (three months), so this one is especially hard to swallow, just being back for a brief period and already gone.
"But we got no choice but to just keep playing hard, keeping doing our thing.''
Well, that starts on the mound, and with Cole dominating Friday, with Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler scheduled Saturday, and Max Fried and Carlos Rodon pitching well, there may not be a more formidable starting rotation in the postseason.
Cole, 9-9 with a 3.63 ERA in his first season back from Tommy John surgery, certainly knows there's room for improvement. But after being belted around with a 7.15 ERA his past two starts, giving up seven homers and 15 hits in 11.1 innings, this was a massive improvement.
"I thought he was really good,'' Boone said. "You know he grinded pretty hard. Between the last start and this one, there are subtle adjustments you make that a lot of people probably over-reacted to.
"The reality is he's having an outstanding season. He's throwing the ball really well, and a great pitcher like him is going to be able to make some adjustments.''
Cole, who missed the entire 2025 season and the first 51 games this year, says he modified his mechanics to remake his delivery. Why, except for missing his location on a low fastball to Corbin Carroll in the second inning, resulting in a two-run homer, he was on-point with virtually all of his other pitches. He threw 90 pitches − 62 for strikes − without walking a batter.
"I mean, I don't think we did a perfect job tonight,'' Cole said. "I think we moved the needle in the right direction. I think there's some meat on the bone there. It's not easy, but it's necessary. It's the big leagues.''
Yep, just like no one is going to feel sorry for the Yankees with the loss of Judge. Not the Tampa Bay Rays, who are still in first place with a four-game lead. Not the Boston Red Sox, who the Yankees likely will face in the first round. Not a soul outside the Yankees organization.
"We have a lot of confidence in here,'' Cole said. "I mean, for the most part of the summer, we've been tested really, really hard, and responded − by and large − really well.
"We have a lot of perfectionists in here. We're always trying to be perfect, and always striving to be the best. But the reality is we've had a lot of obstacles that we've had to overcome, and we've played really well. So we're looking forward to more challenges to come.''
Yes, with or without Judge. The Yankees went 46-39 when he was out 100 days with a rib fracture, and they believe they're built for October. They know they have four top-quality starters and a deep bullpen that can dominate anyone.
"That's probably our biggest strength,'' Boone said. "Whoever we hand the ball to every day, we know is going to give us an opportunity to win a game.''
They proved that this night, with Judge merely watching from the bench, knowing he may have played his final game of the season.
"We're obviously bummed for Aaron, and Aaron's probably bummed too,'' Cole said, "but we've been in this position before this year. Unfortunately, it's our reality at this point.''
Follow Nightengale on X: @Bnightengale
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: No Aaron Judge, no problem? Yankees show they're still a force to be reckoned with

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] La Crisis De Aaron Judge, De Los Yankees, Se Agrava Mientras Boone Repite Ocho Veces La Misma Frase Enigmática
item.dc:creator: Inna Zeyger
item.description: PHOENIX — Los Yankees han demostrado cómo se puede ganar sin Aaron Judge. El viernes, en el Chase Field, Nueva York se puso por delante de los Arizona Diamondbacks con cinco carreras en la primera entrada y luego se llevó una cómoda victoria por 9-2. Con esta victoria, los Yankees suman ahora 89 victorias y 64 derrotas, reducen a cuatro partidos su desventaja respecto a Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y mantienen la presión sobre los Rays de cara a la serie de cuatro partidos
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees han demostrado cómo se puede ganar sin Aaron Judge.
El viernes, en el Chase Field, Nueva York se puso por delante de los Arizona Diamondbacks con cinco carreras en la primera entrada y luego se llevó una cómoda victoria por 9-2. Con esta victoria, los Yankees suman ahora 89 victorias y 64 derrotas, reducen a cuatro partidos su desventaja respecto a Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana y mantienen la presión sobre los Rays de cara a la serie de cuatro partidos de la próxima semana en el Yankee Stadium.
Pero esa noche también traía consigo una cuestión mucho más grave, propia de octubre. Judge no estaba en la alineación, no se le pudo ver en el vestuario antes del partido y ya no se limitaba a aprovechar la última semana de la temporada regular solo para afinar su ritmo. Tras siete partidos desde su regreso tras una ausencia de 99 días por una fractura por estrés en la primera costilla derecha, el capitán de los Yankees volvió a convertirse en el centro de la incertidumbre del equipo de cara a la postemporada.
Ese momento es importante porque Judge apenas había empezado a recuperar su swing. Acabó con 4 de 23, un jonrón y 13 strikeouts tras volver el 8 de septiembre. Los Yankees lo habían ido incorporando poco a poco con partidos más cortos, un día como bateador designado y días de descanso, intentando equilibrar la urgencia de septiembre con la realidad de que se había perdido 84 partidos.
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero su camino más probable empieza con la Serie de Comodín de la Liga Americana el 29 de septiembre. Se suponía que la recta final de la temporada regular de Judge incluiría a Arizona, una serie directa de cuatro partidos contra Tampa Bay y la serie de cierre contra Baltimore. En cambio, los Yankees llegaron al fin de semana sin dar ninguna respuesta oficial sobre cuándo podría volver a jugar su mejor bateador.
El patrón de ocho palabras de Boone se convierte en la historia
Los Yankees confirmaron entonces la noticia sobre Aaron Judge que había generado tanta incertidumbre. El capitán fue incluido el sábado en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha, con efecto retroactivo desde el jueves. La fecha más temprana en la que podría volver a jugar es el 27 de septiembre, pero Aaron Boone no dio ningún plazo ni grado de gravedad después de que una resonancia magnética confirmara la lesión.
Durante la rueda de prensa del viernes, Boone usó la frase «no lo sé» ocho veces mientras respondía a preguntas sobre la lesión, el tratamiento, el plazo de recuperación y su disponibilidad para la postemporada. Cuando le preguntaron directamente si los Yankees esperaban que Judge volviera en octubre, Boone dio la misma respuesta.
«No lo sé», dijo Boone.
Boone no quiso fijar una fecha concreta para la recuperación de Judge ni pronosticar si estará listo para cuando empiece la fase final.
«No tengo una fecha prevista para su vuelta», dijo Boone. «No voy a hacer predicciones. Obviamente, lo trataremos y ya veremos qué pasa».
El tratamiento no supuso una mejora suficiente
Judge empezó a notar una molestia mientras jugaba en el jardín derecho en la primera entrada del partido del miércoles en Minnesota. Siguió en el partido hasta que Heliot Ramos entró como bateador suplente en su lugar en la sexta entrada. Judge dijo después que intentó seguir jugando porque los partidos eran importantes.
«No me pareció una buena idea insistir demasiado en esto», dijo Judge.
El tratamiento del jueves no supuso una mejora suficiente, por lo que se decidieron hacer más pruebas. La resonancia magnética reveló la distensión. Judge seguirá con el tratamiento, y una inyección de plasma rico en plaquetas es una de las opciones una vez que los Yankees vuelvan a Nueva York.
Boone también dijo que no cuestionó que Judge se saltara una fase de rehabilitación en las ligas menores tras la lesión en las costillas. Los Yankees le habían limitado las entradas y le habían dado días de descanso.
«Estas cosas pasan tanto si hay una asignación de rehabilitación como si no. Hicimos todo lo que pudimos para intentar darle a él y a nosotros mismos la mejor oportunidad de que todo saliera bien», dijo Boone.
Un balance positivo sin Judge oculta el coste ofensivo
Los Yankees han aguantado sin Judge en la clasificación, pero hay que poner en contexto estos resultados. Nueva York tenía un balance de 41-25 cuando Judge era titular hasta el miércoles y de 47-39 cuando no lo era. La victoria del viernes dejó a los Yankees con un balance de 48-39 sin él, frente al 41-25 en los partidos en los que fue titular.
Desde el 2 de junio hasta el 7 de septiembre, los Yankees ocuparon el puesto 29 de las Grandes Ligas con un wRC+ de 90 y un promedio de bateo de 0,227, mientras que su OPS de 0,681 les situó en el puesto 27. El pitcheo ayudó a mantener la estabilidad de la temporada mientras la alineación sobrellevaba la larga ausencia de Judge.
Judge tiene un promedio de bateo de .241/.360/.511, con 18 jonrones y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos. El tres veces MVP de la Liga Americana también sufrió una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha en 2020, pero los Yankees no han dado a entender que la lesión actual sea igual de grave ni que el tiempo de recuperación vaya a ser el mismo.
Octubre sigue siendo una incógnita
Se espera que Max Schuemann vuelva de la Triple A este sábado. Los Yankees irán alternando sus opciones en los jardines mientras Judge recibe tratamiento, y él se perderá la serie de cuatro partidos contra los Rays.
Cody Bellinger dijo que la alineación no puede permitirse ponerse nerviosa como lo hizo durante la anterior ausencia de Judge. Los bateadores que quedan siguen teniendo las mismas expectativas.
«Vamos a tener que encontrar la manera», dijo Bellinger. «Creo que el talento que hay en este vestuario habla por sí solo, y estoy totalmente convencido de que tenemos suficiente talento aquí como para salir al campo, ganar y vencer a cualquiera».
Judge podría estar listo el 27 de septiembre, dos días antes de la Serie de Comodines, pero estar listo no significa estar preparado. Hasta que la pantorrilla responda y los Yankees establezcan un plan de recuperación, la respuesta que Boone repite una y otra vez sigue siendo la descripción más clara del estado de Judge para octubre: no lo saben.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.
